title: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicidal Ideation - Emergency Department Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 38-year-old male plumber, David Chen, has been brought in by his wife after she found him in the garage with a rope. She reports he has been 'not himself' for the past 4 months since his business collapsed during the recent economic downturn. The triage nurse notes he said 'I just want it all to end'. Your task is to take a focused psychiatric history, assess his suicide risk using the SAFE-T protocol, and perform a mental state examination. You have 8 minutes for this station.
patient_role_instructions: You are David Chen, a 38-year-old married plumber with two children aged 8 and 10. Four months ago, your plumbing business of 12 years collapsed due to mounting debts totaling $180,000. You had to lay off three employees who had worked with you for years, which caused immense guilt. Your wife Sarah now works two jobs to support the family while you stay home unemployed. You feel like a complete failure as a husband, father, and provider. For the past 4 months, you have experienced: waking at 2-3am every morning unable to return to sleep, loss of appetite (lost 12kg), no energy to do anything, inability to concentrate even on TV shows, no interest in activities you used to enjoy (fishing, cricket), and constant feelings of worthlessness. Two weeks ago, you started having thoughts that your family would be 'better off without me' and that your life insurance would at least pay off the debts. Three days ago, you researched methods online and today you took a rope to the garage intending to hang yourself, but your wife came home early and found you. You feel intense shame about this. You have no history of mental illness or previous suicide attempts. You drink 4-6 beers nightly to help you sleep (increased from social drinking). You have access to tools in your garage. When the doctor enters, you avoid eye contact, speak softly and slowly, and appear tearful. If asked directly about suicidal thoughts, you will admit 'I can't see any other way out' and describe the plan. If asked about your children, you become more emotional and say they are the only reason you are still here. You have lost hope that things will ever improve financially.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you tell me what brought you to hospital today? (Expected: Wife found me in garage with rope, I wanted to end my life)
TIMELINE: When did you first start feeling down? (Expected: 4 months ago when business collapsed, owing $180,000)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS - SLEEP: How has your sleep been? (Expected: Waking at 2-3am every morning, unable to return to sleep, total 4-5 hours per night)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS - APPETITE: Any changes in appetite or weight? (Expected: No appetite, lost 12kg in 4 months)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS - ENERGY: How are your energy levels? (Expected: Exhausted all the time, no motivation to do anything)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS - CONCENTRATION: Able to focus on things? (Expected: Cannot concentrate even on TV, mind feels foggy)
ANHEDONIA: What about activities you used to enjoy? (Expected: Used to fish and play cricket, no interest anymore, nothing gives pleasure)
MOOD: How would you describe your mood? (Expected: Hopeless, worthless, feel like a failure)
SAFE-T - SUICIDAL IDEATION: Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life? (Expected: Yes, constant thoughts for 2 weeks that family would be better off without me)
SAFE-T - SPECIFIC PLAN: Have you thought about how you might do it? (Expected: Yes, researched methods online 3 days ago, today took rope to garage to hang myself)
SAFE-T - ACCESS TO MEANS: Do you have access to ways to harm yourself? (Expected: Yes, rope in garage, tools including sharp objects)

SAFE-T - FEELINGS: Feelings of hopelessness? Being a burden? (Expected: Complete hopelessness about financial situation, feel like burden to wife who works two jobs, life insurance would at least pay debts)
SAFE-T - EARLIER ATTEMPTS: Have you tried to harm yourself before? (Expected: No, never, first time)
SAFE-T - THREAT/INTENT: What stopped you today? Do you still want to die? (Expected: Wife came home early, but yes, cannot see any other way out)
PROTECTIVE FACTORS: What keeps you going? (Expected: My two children aged 8 and 10, they are the only reason I am still here)
SUBSTANCE USE: Alcohol or drug use? (Expected: Drinking 4-6 beers nightly to help sleep, increased from social drinking)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous mental health issues? (Expected: No, never)
FAMILY HISTORY: Mental health issues in family? (Expected: Father died by suicide when patient was 15)
SOCIAL HISTORY: Living situation, supports? (Expected: Married, wife Sarah working two jobs, two children, isolated from friends due to shame)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Casually dressed, unkempt appearance, poor self-care, facial hair unshaven for several days
BEHAVIOR: Psychomotor retardation, slumped posture, minimal spontaneous movement, poor eye contact
SPEECH: Reduced rate and volume, monotonous tone, increased latency before responding, short answers
MOOD (SUBJECTIVE): 'Hopeless' 'like a failure' 'cannot go on'
AFFECT (OBJECTIVE): Depressed, congruent with mood, restricted range, becomes tearful when discussing children
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and goal-directed, no formal thought disorder
THOUGHT CONTENT: Active suicidal ideation with specific plan (hanging), feelings of worthlessness and guilt, preoccupation with financial failure, no delusions, no homicidal ideation
PERCEPTIONS: No hallucinations reported or observed
COGNITION: Alert and oriented to time, place, person, impaired concentration reported but able to engage in interview
INSIGHT: Partial - acknowledges feeling depressed but believes suicide is rational solution to financial problems
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - unable to see alternatives to suicide despite protective factors
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: HIGH RISK - Active suicidal ideation with specific plan (hanging), aborted attempt today (interrupted by wife), access to lethal means (rope, tools in garage), severe hopelessness, feelings of being a burden, recent research of methods, family history of suicide (father), current stressors (financial collapse, unemployment), substance use (alcohol), male gender. Protective factors present (children) but insufficient to mitigate risk. HIGH RISK requires immediate psychiatric assessment and likely involuntary admission.
IMMEDIATE SAFETY: Patient requires constant 1:1 observation (Level 1 special) in ED, remove all potential means of self-harm, search belongings, change into hospital gown, nil sharps

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007: Meets criteria for involuntary assessment/admission under Section 19 (Emergency) - (1) appears to have mental illness (Major Depressive Disorder), (2) risk of serious harm to self (active plan and attempt today), (3) requires immediate psychiatric treatment, (4) no less restrictive alternative given high suicide risk. Document decision and complete Mental Health Act paperwork.
URGENT PSYCHIATRIC CONSULTATION: Page on-call psychiatrist immediately for crisis assessment, do not discharge patient before psychiatric review

SAFETY PLAN (for ongoing care): Remove access to means (rope, tools, medications), wife to secure garage and remove potential ligature points at home (if eventual discharge), provide Australian crisis contacts, schedule urgent follow-up
CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide written information - Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety), Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467

COMMENCE ANTIDEPRESSANT: Given severity of depression with biological symptoms, commence Sertraline 50mg mane (morning), increase to 100mg after 1-2 weeks if tolerated, PBS code 2062B. Warn about 2-4 week delay in effect and potential initial increase in agitation (requires close monitoring).

ALCOHOL MANAGEMENT: Screen for alcohol dependence (drinking 4-6 beers nightly for 4 months), risk of withdrawal seizures if ceased abruptly, consider Diazepam reducing regime if admitted (e.g., 10mg QID day 1, reduce by 5mg daily), refer to drug and alcohol service
INVESTIGATIONS: Exclude organic causes - FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, BSL, B12/folate, urinary drug screen. Check for alcohol-related pathology given increased consumption.

PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT: Involve wife Sarah in safety planning and education about depression, refer to social worker for financial counseling and Centrelink benefits assessment (Jobseeker allowance, mental health support), involve Lifeline financial counseling service for debt management
PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPY: Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) once acute risk stabilizes, address cognitive distortions about failure and burden

ADMISSION PLAN: Admit to psychiatric inpatient unit (likely involuntary under Mental Health Act given high risk and impaired insight), multidisciplinary team approach with daily psychiatric review, gradual leave testing before discharge, comprehensive discharge plan with crisis contacts and follow-up appointments

DOCUMENTATION: Comprehensive risk assessment documented including SAFE-T domains, Mental Health Act criteria and rationale for involuntary admission, management plan, discussions with patient and wife, psychiatric consultation notes

FOLLOW-UP (post-discharge): Psychiatric outpatient appointment within 7 days of discharge, GP follow-up within 72 hours with shared care plan, ongoing CBT referral, drug and alcohol clinic review if indicated, case management for financial stressors

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, establishes rapport, explains purpose of interview in empathetic manner
Asks open question about presenting complaint and elicits story of today's events (found in garage with rope)
Establishes timeline - 4 months of symptoms since financial stressor (business collapse)
Systematically asks about biological symptoms of depression (sleep, appetite, energy, concentration) - scores 1 point for each symptom asked, maximum 2 points
Asks about anhedonia and loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities
Asks directly about suicidal ideation in clear, non-judgmental manner
SAFE-T S - Asks about specific plan (hanging) and recent preparation (rope, online research)
SAFE-T A - Asks about access to means (rope, tools in garage)
SAFE-T F - Explores feelings of hopelessness, worthlessness, being a burden
SAFE-T E - Asks about previous suicide attempts and family history of suicide
SAFE-T T - Assesses current intent and what interrupted attempt today
Identifies protective factors (children) and explores significance
Asks about alcohol and substance use (increased drinking to 4-6 beers nightly)
Performs mental state examination including mood, affect, thought content (documents depressed mood, restricted affect, active suicidal ideation)
Correctly categorizes as HIGH suicide risk with specific justification (active ideation + plan + attempt + access + hopelessness + high-risk factors)
States immediate safety measures required (1:1 observation, remove means, search belongings)
Recognizes need for involuntary admission and mentions Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria
States need for urgent psychiatric consultation before any discharge decision
Provides Australian crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue, or Suicide Call Back Service)
Mentions appropriate antidepressant (SSRI such as Sertraline) with approximate dose
Addresses alcohol use and withdrawal risk given increased consumption
Demonstrates empathy, validates patient's distress, maintains non-judgmental approach throughout

learning_points: SAFE-T protocol is mandatory for all suicide risk assessments: Specific plan, Access to means, Feelings (hopelessness/burden), Earlier attempts, Threat/intent. Document findings clearly and categorize risk level (LOW/MODERATE/HIGH).

HIGH suicide risk indicators include: active ideation with specific plan, recent preparation or attempt, access to lethal means, severe hopelessness, feeling like a burden, family history of suicide, recent stressors, substance use, male gender, social isolation.

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 Section 19 (Emergency) allows involuntary admission when: (1) person appears to have mental illness, (2) risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) requires immediate psychiatric treatment, (4) no less restrictive alternative available.
Australian crisis contacts must be provided to all patients with suicidal ideation: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467.

Major Depressive Disorder diagnosis requires: ≥2 weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia PLUS ≥4 additional symptoms (sleep disturbance, appetite/weight change, fatigue, poor concentration, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, psychomotor changes, suicidal ideation). This patient has 4 months of symptoms meeting criteria.

First-line antidepressants for Major Depressive Disorder are SSRIs: Sertraline 50mg mane (increase to 100-200mg, PBS 2062B), Escitalopram 10mg mane (increase to 20mg, PBS 8221K), or Fluoxetine 20mg mane (increase to 40mg). Warn about 2-4 week delay in therapeutic effect and potential initial increase in anxiety/agitation requiring close monitoring.

Alcohol consumption in depression: Screen with AUDIT/CAGE, assess for dependence (tolerance, withdrawal symptoms, loss of control), risk of withdrawal seizures if ceased abruptly especially if drinking heavily for >1 month. Consider benzodiazepine reducing regime if admission required (e.g., Diazepam 10mg QID tapering over 5-7 days).

Protective factors (children, employment, religious beliefs, social support) reduce but do not eliminate suicide risk. In this case, children are the only protective factor but insufficient to mitigate HIGH risk given active plan and interrupted attempt.

Biological symptoms of depression (SIGECAPS): Sleep disturbance, Interest loss (anhedonia), Guilt/worthlessness, Energy loss, Concentration impairment, Appetite change, Psychomotor changes, Suicidal ideation. This patient demonstrates 8/9 symptoms indicating severe depression.

Financial stressors and unemployment are significant risk factors for suicide in men. Involve social work early for financial counseling, Centrelink benefits assessment (Jobseeker allowance, mental health support), debt management services (Lifeline financial counseling). Address both psychiatric illness AND psychosocial stressors.

Family history of suicide (father completed suicide when patient aged 15) is a significant risk factor increasing patient's own suicide risk 2-3 fold. Explore patient's memories and beliefs about father's death as this may influence current suicidal thinking.

Never discharge a patient with HIGH suicide risk from ED without senior psychiatric consultation. If psychiatric services unavailable or delayed, patient must remain under constant observation until assessment completed. Document clearly if Mental Health Act involuntary admission criteria met.

title: Mental State Examination - Speech and Language Assessment in Psychotic Episode
candidate_instructions: You are seeing Marcus Chen, a 28-year-old postgraduate engineering student, in the emergency department. He was brought in by his flatmate who became concerned about his behaviour over the past 2 weeks. The flatmate reports that Marcus has been talking rapidly, using made-up words, and sometimes his speech is difficult to follow. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination with particular attention to speech and language assessment. You have 8 minutes to assess his current mental state, evaluate any speech abnormalities, and formulate an appropriate management plan including risk assessment.
patient_role_instructions: You are Marcus Chen, a 28-year-old engineering PhD student. For the past 2 weeks, you have been experiencing what you believe is a 'breakthrough' in your research. You feel energised and special, chosen to solve complex mathematical problems that will change the world. Your speech is pressured and rapid - you have so many important ideas to share. You occasionally use technical terms you've invented (neologisms) like 'quantumdifferential' and 'neurothetics'. Sometimes you lose your train of thought mid-sentence and jump to related but different topics (circumstantiality and tangentiality). You deny hearing voices but mention that you can 'decode hidden messages' in newspaper headlines. You haven't been sleeping much (2-3 hours/night) because you're too excited about your work. You become irritated if interrupted and insist your speech is perfectly normal. You deny any thoughts of harming yourself or others - you're too important to the world's future. You stopped taking your prescribed risperidone 3 weeks ago because you felt it was 'dulling your genius'.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's systematic approach to speech and language assessment within the mental state examination. Key areas to assess include: recognition of formal thought disorder (circumstantiality, tangentiality, flight of ideas), identification of neologisms and word salad, assessment of speech rate and pressure, evaluation of thought content (delusions of grandiosity), and appropriate risk assessment. The candidate should demonstrate understanding of the relationship between speech abnormalities and underlying psychiatric conditions. Watch for proper documentation of specific examples of speech abnormalities and appropriate use of psychiatric terminology. The candidate should also assess insight and formulate a differential diagnosis including manic episode with psychotic features.

sample_answer.history_summary: Marcus Chen, 28-year-old PhD engineering student, presented with 2-week history of pressured speech, decreased sleep (2-3 hours/night), grandiose beliefs about his research importance, and behavioural changes noted by flatmate. Medication non-compliance (stopped risperidone 3 weeks ago). No current substance use reported. Previous psychiatric history suggests possible bipolar disorder.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: Well-groomed, casually dressed, appears energised. Behaviour: Restless, animated gestures, difficult to interrupt. Speech: Pressured, increased rate, normal volume, circumstantial and tangential. Mood: Euphoric ('excited about breakthrough'). Affect: Elevated, labile when challenged. Thought form: Circumstantiality, tangentiality, neologisms ('quantumdifferential', 'neurothetics'). Thought content: Grandiose delusions about research importance, ideas of reference (newspaper headlines). Perceptions: Denies auditory hallucinations, reports 'decoding messages'. Cognition: Alert, oriented, attention difficult to sustain due to distractibility. Insight: Severely impaired, denies illness. Judgement: Poor.
sample_answer.diagnosis: Manic episode with psychotic features (F31.2 - Bipolar disorder, current episode manic with psychotic features)

safe_t_assessment.specific_plan: Denies suicidal ideation, no specific plan identified
safe_t_assessment.access_to_means: Lives with flatmate, no immediate access to lethal means identified
safe_t_assessment.feelings_hopelessness: Denies hopelessness, reports feeling 'chosen' and important
safe_t_assessment.threat_level: Low risk for suicide, moderate risk for poor judgement/impulsivity

management.immediate: Voluntary admission for stabilisation, remove any potential means of harm, provide crisis contacts, involve flatmate in safety planning
management.medications: Restart antipsychotic - consider olanzapine 10mg daily (PBS 3160K) or risperidone 2mg BD (PBS 8055E), monitor for akathisia and metabolic effects
management.therapy: Psychoeducation about bipolar disorder, medication compliance counselling, CBT referral post-acute phase
management.follow_up: Daily psychiatric review as inpatient, GP follow-up within 3 days of discharge, community mental health team within 1 week
management.crisis_contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, NSW Mental Health Access Line 1800 011 511

sample_answer.mental_health_act: Consider involuntary assessment if refuses voluntary admission - meets criteria for mental illness with risk of serious harm to health due to poor judgement and medication non-compliance

learning_points: SAFE-T assessment: Always conduct systematic risk evaluation even when patient appears euphoric - manic episodes carry impulsivity risks
Speech assessment requires systematic evaluation: rate, volume, pressure, rhythm, plus formal thought disorder patterns
Neologisms are pathognomonic of psychotic process - document specific examples for diagnostic clarity
Circumstantiality (eventual return to topic) vs tangentiality (never returns) vs flight of ideas (rapid topic changes with loose associations)
Medication non-compliance is common trigger for manic relapse - always explore adherence history
Australian crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14 available 24/7, state-specific mental health access lines for immediate psychiatric consultation
Mental Health Act consideration: Euphoric patients may refuse treatment despite obvious impairment - balance autonomy with duty of care

title: First Episode Psychosis - Risk Assessment and Mental State Examination
candidate_instructions: You are working in a metropolitan emergency department at 2am. A 23-year-old male university student, David Chen, has been brought in by police under Section 19 of the Mental Health Act NSW 2007. Police were called by neighbours who reported him shouting from his apartment balcony at 1am, claiming that 'the government is trying to poison me through the water supply' and threatening to 'expose the conspiracy'. His flatmate tells you David has been acting strangely for the past 3 weeks - staying up all night, refusing to eat or drink anything except bottled water he buys himself, and accusing his friends of being 'government agents'. He stopped attending university 2 weeks ago. No previous psychiatric history. Cannabis use 2-3 times weekly for the past year. Your task is to: (1) Conduct a focused mental state examination, (2) Assess his risk to self and others using the SAFE-T framework, (3) Determine whether involuntary admission criteria are met. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are David Chen, a 23-year-old computer science student at UNSW. Three weeks ago, you started noticing strange things happening around you. You became convinced that the Australian government has been monitoring you because you 'discovered' evidence of a mass surveillance program while working on a university coding project. You believe they are trying to poison you through the tap water to stop you from revealing the truth. You can hear voices (2-3 male voices) commenting on your actions throughout the day, saying things like 'He knows too much' and 'We need to stop him'. The voices started 2 weeks ago and are present most of the time. You have been smoking cannabis regularly (2-3 joints daily) for the past year, increasing to daily use in the past month to 'help you think more clearly'. You stopped going to classes 2 weeks ago because you believe your lecturers are part of the conspiracy. You have not been sleeping (2-3 hours per night) because you need to 'stay alert'. You have lost 5kg because you only eat packaged food you open yourself and only drink bottled water. Tonight, you went onto your apartment balcony to 'warn the public' about the conspiracy. You feel frightened and agitated, not aggressive. You have no intention to harm yourself but you feel the government might harm you. When the doctor enters, you are initially suspicious and ask 'Are you one of them?' You make poor eye contact, appear dishevelled, and periodically look around the room as if responding to stimuli. You will answer questions but your speech is pressured and you jump between topics. You have no insight into being unwell - you believe everything you are experiencing is real. You deny suicidal thoughts but say 'I might not be safe if they find me'. Hidden information (reveal only if specifically asked): Your maternal uncle has schizophrenia (diagnosed 15 years ago). You have never used other illicit drugs besides cannabis. You have no access to weapons. Your parents live in Sydney and you have a good relationship with them.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you tell me what brought you to hospital tonight? (Expected: Police brought me in, I was trying to warn people about the government conspiracy)
TIMELINE: When did you first start noticing these unusual things? (Expected: About 3 weeks ago)
DELUSIONAL BELIEFS: Tell me more about the government surveillance - what makes you believe this? (Expected: I found evidence in my coding project, they're watching me, trying to poison the water)
AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS: Have you been hearing anything unusual? Voices when no one is around? (Expected: Yes, 2-3 male voices commenting on my actions, started 2 weeks ago, present most of the time)
COMMAND HALLUCINATIONS: Do the voices tell you to do anything? (Expected: No, they just comment)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS: Sleep patterns? (Expected: 2-3 hours per night for past 3 weeks) Appetite? (Expected: Lost 5kg, only eating packaged food)
SUBSTANCE USE: Cannabis use - when did you start, how often? (Expected: Daily for past year, increased to 2-3 joints daily past month)
FUNCTIONAL IMPACT: University attendance? (Expected: Stopped going 2 weeks ago)
SAFE-T ASSESSMENT: Have you had thoughts of harming yourself? (Expected: No suicidal ideation) Any thoughts of harming others? (Expected: No homicidal ideation, but fearful government will harm him)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous mental health problems? Admissions? (Expected: None)
FAMILY PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any family members with mental health conditions? (Expected: Maternal uncle with schizophrenia)
INSIGHT: Do you think you might be unwell? (Expected: No insight - believes experiences are real)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Dishevelled, unkempt hair, wearing same clothes for several days, poor self-care, appears underweight
BEHAVIOUR: Agitated, restless, poor eye contact, guarded, scanning room (responding to internal stimuli), psychomotor agitation
SPEECH: Pressured rate, increased volume at times, circumstantial with tangential derailments
MOOD: Subjective - 'I'm scared, they're after me'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, fearful, congruent with paranoid delusions, restricted range, labile at times
THOUGHT FORM: Circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations at times

THOUGHT CONTENT: Paranoid delusions (government surveillance, poisoning through water supply), persecutory delusions (government agents monitoring him), referential thinking (believes events relate to him). NO suicidal ideation, NO homicidal ideation
PERCEPTIONS: Auditory hallucinations - 2-3 male voices, running commentary type, present most of the time for past 2 weeks, NO command hallucinations
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time. Attention impaired (distractible). Concentration reduced. Memory not formally tested
INSIGHT: NO insight - does not believe he is unwell, attributes experiences to external conspiracy
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - stopped university, social isolation, risky cannabis use, not eating or drinking safely
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: MODERATE-HIGH RISK to self (indirect risk from malnutrition, dehydration, impaired judgment due to psychosis), LOW risk to others (no homicidal ideation, no history of violence, not currently aggressive). Justification: Active psychosis with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations, severely impaired judgment, functional decline, cannabis use complicating presentation, minimal insight, but protective factors include no suicidal/homicidal ideation, no command hallucinations, cooperative with assessment, family support available.

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA MET for involuntary admission: (1) Apparent mental illness present (first episode psychosis), (2) Risk of serious harm to self (declining self-care, weight loss, dehydration, impaired judgment), (3) Requires immediate psychiatric treatment and assessment, (4) No less restrictive alternative given lack of insight and severity. Document as Section 19 (Emergency) - already initiated by police. Recommend continuation as Section 27 (Involuntary Admission) after psychiatric review.

IMMEDIATE SAFETY: Admit to psychiatric inpatient unit. Observations: 15-minute observations initially. One-to-one nursing if agitation escalates. Remove potential ligature points. Search belongings for weapons/substances.

ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION: Commence Olanzapine 5mg PO nocte (first-line for first episode psychosis, lower risk of extrapyramidal side effects). Consider Olanzapine 5mg PO PRN if acutely agitated (max 20mg/24 hours). Alternative: Risperidone 1mg BD if Olanzapine not tolerated. Explain medication rationale using non-confrontational language ('help you feel calmer, sleep better').
BENZODIAZEPINE PRN: Lorazepam 1-2mg PO/IM PRN for severe agitation (max 6mg/24 hours). Monitor for respiratory depression, especially if cannabis use continues.

INVESTIGATIONS: Urine drug screen (confirm cannabis, exclude other substances including amphetamines). Blood tests: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, glucose, CRP (exclude organic causes). Baseline metabolic monitoring before antipsychotic (weight, BMI, BP, fasting glucose, lipids). CT brain if atypical features, focal neurology, or first seizure.
SUBSTANCE USE ASSESSMENT: Cannabis cessation counselling - explain link between cannabis and psychosis. Motivational interviewing approach. Refer to drug and alcohol service for ongoing support.

COLLATERAL HISTORY: Contact parents (with patient consent or under Mental Health Act provisions) to obtain developmental history, timeline of symptoms, family psychiatric history, premorbid functioning.
NURSING CARE PLAN: Monitor food and fluid intake (encourage eating, provide nutritious meals). Sleep hygiene support. Reality orientation. De-escalation strategies if agitation worsens.

PSYCHOEDUCATION: Explain to David (when calmer) and family that this appears to be first episode psychosis. Discuss good prognosis with early treatment. Explain connection between cannabis use and psychosis. Provide written information about psychosis.
CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide to family - Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support), Headspace 1800 650 890 (youth mental health)

FOLLOW-UP PLAN: Daily psychiatry review during admission. Aim for minimum 2-week admission for stabilisation and medication titration. Arrange Early Psychosis Intervention Service (EPIS) referral for discharge planning. Community mental health team follow-up within 7 days post-discharge. GP follow-up within 2 weeks with psychiatry discharge summary.

DOCUMENTATION: Complete Mental Health Act paperwork (Section 27 continuation). Document Mental State Examination findings. Document SAFE-T assessment. Notify Mental Health Review Tribunal within 24 hours of involuntary admission (legal requirement NSW).

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, explains purpose of assessment in non-confrontational manner
Establishes timeline of symptoms (3 weeks onset, progression over time)
Explores delusional beliefs in detail (content, conviction, systematization) without challenging or colluding
Asks specifically about auditory hallucinations (presence, content, frequency, duration, running commentary vs command)
Assesses biological symptoms (sleep, appetite, weight loss)
Conducts SAFE-T suicide risk assessment (asks about suicidal ideation, plan, means, feelings, earlier attempts)
Assesses risk to others (homicidal ideation, intent, history of violence)
Takes detailed substance use history (cannabis type, frequency, duration, relationship to symptom onset)
Asks about past psychiatric history and family psychiatric history
Assesses insight (awareness of illness, attribution of symptoms)
Correctly identifies Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria are met and explains rationale (mental illness, risk of harm, need for treatment, no less restrictive alternative)
Recommends appropriate antipsychotic medication (Olanzapine 5mg or Risperidone 1-2mg) with rationale for first episode psychosis
Recommends appropriate investigations (urine drug screen, blood tests, brain imaging if indicated)
Plans collateral history from family/friends and follow-up with Early Psychosis service
Demonstrates empathy and non-judgmental approach throughout (maintains therapeutic rapport despite patient's paranoia)

learning_points: First Episode Psychosis (FEP) requires urgent psychiatric assessment and early intervention for best outcomes. Onset typically 18-25 years. Key features: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior, negative symptoms.

Cannabis-induced psychosis vs primary psychotic disorder: Cannabis use can precipitate psychosis in vulnerable individuals. Up to 50% of cannabis-induced psychosis cases develop schizophrenia within 3 years. Always screen substance use in young people with psychosis.

Mental State Examination for psychosis: Systematically assess appearance, behavior, speech, mood, affect, thought form (circumstantial, tangential, loose associations), thought content (delusions - types include paranoid, persecutory, referential, grandiose), perceptions (hallucinations - auditory most common in schizophrenia, distinguish running commentary vs command), cognition, insight, judgment.

SAFE-T protocol for suicide risk: Even in acute psychosis, always assess suicide risk (Specific plan, Access to means, Feelings of hopelessness, Earlier attempts, Threat). Psychosis increases suicide risk 5-fold. Command hallucinations to self-harm are high-risk feature.

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria for involuntary admission: (1) Person appears to be mentally ill, (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) Requires immediate psychiatric treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative. Section 19 (Emergency) allows police/ambulance to bring person to ED. Section 27 (Involuntary) allows admission for up to 3 months.

First-line antipsychotics for FEP: Olanzapine 5-10mg daily or Risperidone 1-2mg BD preferred (lower extrapyramidal side effects than older typical antipsychotics like Haloperidol). Start low dose and titrate. Monitor metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes, lipids). Avoid polypharmacy.

Investigations for first episode psychosis: Always exclude organic causes before diagnosing primary psychiatric disorder. Mandatory: Urine drug screen, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, glucose, CRP. Consider: CT brain (if atypical features, focal neurology, age >40), HIV, syphilis serology (if risk factors), autoimmune encephalitis screen (if atypical presentation).

Early Psychosis Intervention Services (EPIS): Specialized teams providing intensive case management for 2 years post-FEP. Evidence shows early intervention improves long-term outcomes. Referral should be made from inpatient unit before discharge.

Australian crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness helpline), Headspace 1800 650 890 (youth mental health 12-25 years), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety).

Collateral history essential: Patients with psychosis often have limited insight. Contact family/friends (with consent or under Mental Health Act provisions) to establish premorbid functioning, timeline, substance use, family psychiatric history, recent stressors.

title: Acute Alcohol Withdrawal - Emergency Department Management
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working the night shift in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 58-year-old man, Robert Chen, was brought in by ambulance at 2am after his wife found him sweating profusely, shaking, and seeing 'things crawling on the walls'. His wife reports he has been drinking heavily for 20 years but stopped abruptly 36 hours ago after running out of money. On arrival, he is tremulous, diaphoretic, and appears frightened. Your task is to take a focused alcohol use history, assess withdrawal severity and complications, and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this station.
patient_role_instructions: You are Robert Chen, a 58-year-old former plumber who was made redundant 2 years ago. You have been drinking 750ml-1 litre of vodka daily for the past 20 years, usually starting at 10am and drinking throughout the day until you pass out around 10pm. You ran out of money 36 hours ago and haven't had a drink since. You started feeling shaky and sweaty 24 hours ago, and in the last 6 hours you have been seeing small insects crawling on your arms and shadows moving in your peripheral vision. You are terrified and can't stop your hands from trembling. You are married with three adult children who have distanced themselves due to your drinking. You have tried to stop twice before - once you had a seizure 12 hours after your last drink (8 years ago), and another time you were admitted to hospital for 'the shakes' (5 years ago). You lost your plumber's license after a workplace accident when you were intoxicated. When the doctor enters, you say 'Doctor, I can't stop shaking and I'm seeing things that aren't there - am I going crazy?' You are anxious, restless, and keep looking around the room nervously. You feel ashamed about your drinking but are desperate for help. You deny any thoughts of self-harm but admit you have felt hopeless about your situation. If asked about medical history, mention you have high blood pressure (taking Amlodipine 10mg) and had pancreatitis 3 years ago. You smoke 20 cigarettes per day. You haven't eaten properly in 3 days. Your wife is in the waiting room and is exhausted but willing to support you.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: When did you last have an alcoholic drink? (Expected: 36 hours ago, abrupt cessation)
ALCOHOL USE HISTORY: How much do you typically drink each day? (Expected: 750ml-1L vodka daily for 20 years)
WITHDRAWAL TIMELINE: When did symptoms start? What symptoms? (Expected: Tremor/sweating 24 hours ago, visual hallucinations last 6 hours)
PREVIOUS WITHDRAWAL: Have you stopped drinking before? What happened? (Expected: Seizure 8 years ago, hospital admission for withdrawal 5 years ago)
CAGE SCREENING: Have you felt you should Cut down? Do people Annoy you by criticizing your drinking? Do you feel Guilty? Do you need an Eye-opener? (Expected: Yes to all four - CAGE 4/4)
WITHDRAWAL COMPLICATIONS: Any seizures this time? Confusion? Fever? (Expected: No seizures yet, visual hallucinations present, oriented to person/place/time)
MEDICAL COMORBIDITIES: Any heart, liver, or pancreas problems? Other medical conditions? (Expected: Hypertension on Amlodipine, previous pancreatitis)
NUTRITION: When did you last eat? Vitamin supplementation? (Expected: Minimal intake 3 days, no vitamins)
SUICIDE RISK (SAFE-T): Any thoughts of harming yourself? Do you feel hopeless? (Expected: No suicidal ideation, feels hopeless about drinking but wants help)
MOTIVATION: Do you want to stop drinking? What support do you have? (Expected: Motivated to stop, wife supportive)
SOCIAL HISTORY: Living situation? Employment? Family support? (Expected: Lives with wife, unemployed 2 years, estranged from children)
MENTAL HEALTH: Depression? Anxiety? Previous psychiatric treatment? (Expected: Low mood related to drinking, no previous psychiatric history)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, poor self-care, sweating profusely, tremulous
BEHAVIOR: Restless, psychomotor agitation, keeps looking around room, poor eye contact
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume but slightly slurred, coherent
MOOD: Subjective - 'Terrified' and 'ashamed'
AFFECT: Anxious, restricted range, congruent with mood
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and goal-directed, no formal thought disorder
THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with withdrawal symptoms and fear of 'going crazy', no suicidal ideation, no delusions

PERCEPTIONS: VISUAL HALLUCINATIONS - seeing insects crawling on arms and shadows in peripheral vision (formication and visual hallucinations consistent with alcohol withdrawal), insight PRESENT (recognizes not real)
COGNITION: Oriented to person, place, and time. Attention mildly impaired due to anxiety and tremor. No memory deficits noted
INSIGHT: Good - recognizes he has alcohol dependence and needs treatment
JUDGMENT: Appropriate - sought medical help, cooperative with assessment
immediate_management: CLINICAL INSTITUTE WITHDRAWAL ASSESSMENT (CIWA-Ar): Score withdrawal severity - tremor (4), sweating (4), anxiety (5), agitation (4), tactile disturbances (2), auditory disturbances (0), visual disturbances (4), headache (2), orientation (0) = CIWA-Ar 25/67 (MODERATE-SEVERE WITHDRAWAL)
ADMIT TO HOSPITAL: Medical ward with telemetry monitoring - risk of seizures (previous history) and progression to delirium tremens (visual hallucinations present)

BENZODIAZEPINE PROTOCOL: Diazepam loading - 20mg oral stat, then 10mg every 2 hours until CIWA-Ar <10, then symptom-triggered dosing (Diazepam preferred over Oxazepam due to longer half-life and seizure prophylaxis)
THIAMINE REPLACEMENT: Thiamine 300mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days (BEFORE glucose administration to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy), then 100mg oral daily ongoing
MULTIVITAMINS: Vitamin B complex (strong) 1-2 tablets three times daily
HYDRATION: IV normal saline 1L over 4 hours (assess for fluid overload given hypertension), oral fluids encouraged
ELECTROLYTE CORRECTION: Check and replace magnesium (target >0.85 mmol/L), potassium, phosphate - common deficiencies in chronic alcohol use

SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK - No suicidal ideation, no specific plan, protective factors (wife's support, motivated for treatment), feels hopeless about drinking but not about life. Monitor mood as withdrawal progresses
SEIZURE PRECAUTIONS: Nil by mouth initially, padded bed rails, suction available, neurological observations every 2 hours for first 48 hours
MONITORING: CIWA-Ar every 2 hours for first 24 hours, vital signs (BP/HR/Temp) hourly, blood glucose 4-hourly

INVESTIGATIONS: FBC (macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia), UEC (hyponatremia, hypokalemia), LFTs (elevated GGT/AST/ALT, low albumin), coagulation studies (prolonged PT if liver disease), blood alcohol level, magnesium, phosphate, glucose, ECG (prolonged QT), chest X-ray if aspiration risk
MEDICAL COMORBIDITY MANAGEMENT: Continue Amlodipine 10mg daily for hypertension, monitor BP closely as withdrawal causes sympathetic surge
ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL COUNSELING: Once medically stable, refer to Drug and Alcohol Service for detoxification support, relapse prevention, and outpatient follow-up
ALCOHOL SUPPORT SERVICES: Provide contacts - Alcohol Drug Information Service (ADIS) 1800 250 015 (NSW 24/7), Family Drug Support 1300 368 186, Alcoholics Anonymous meetings
FAMILY INVOLVEMENT: With patient consent, involve wife in discharge planning and ongoing support, consider family therapy referral

DISCHARGE PLANNING: Once CIWA-Ar <8-10 for 24 hours and medically stable, arrange outpatient Drug and Alcohol follow-up within 1 week, GP follow-up within 3 days, consider residential rehabilitation referral if motivated

marking_criteria.criterion: Asks about quantity and duration of alcohol use (amount per day, years of use)
Asks about timing of last drink and onset of withdrawal symptoms
Asks about previous withdrawal attempts and complications (seizures, delirium tremens)
Uses CAGE screening questions or equivalent structured alcohol assessment
Asks about current withdrawal symptoms (tremor, sweating, hallucinations, confusion)
Assesses for medical comorbidities (liver disease, pancreatitis, hypertension)
Asks about suicidal ideation and performs basic suicide risk assessment
Assesses motivation to stop drinking and available social support
Recognizes visual hallucinations as withdrawal complication (not primary psychosis)
Recommends hospital admission for moderate-severe withdrawal with seizure risk
Prescribes benzodiazepine protocol (Diazepam loading dose and symptom-triggered dosing)
Prescribes thiamine 300mg IV BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy
Orders appropriate investigations (FBC, UEC, LFTs, magnesium, blood alcohol level)
Mentions CIWA-Ar score for objective withdrawal severity assessment
Provides alcohol support service contacts (ADIS, AA, Family Drug Support)
Demonstrates empathy and non-judgmental approach throughout consultation

learning_points: CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol revised) is the gold standard tool for assessing withdrawal severity (score >15 indicates moderate-severe withdrawal requiring treatment)
Benzodiazepines are first-line for alcohol withdrawal - Diazepam preferred for seizure prophylaxis (long-acting), Oxazepam preferred if liver impairment (no active metabolites)
Thiamine 300mg IV must be given BEFORE glucose administration to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) in thiamine-deficient patients
Seizures occur 6-48 hours post-cessation, delirium tremens 48-96 hours (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability) - both medical emergencies with mortality risk
CAGE questionnaire: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener (≥2 positive = likely alcohol dependence, sensitivity 71-95%)
Formication (tactile hallucination of insects crawling on skin) and visual hallucinations are classic withdrawal features, NOT primary psychotic disorder
Alcohol withdrawal can be FATAL - complications include seizures (3-5% mortality if untreated), delirium tremens (5-15% mortality even with treatment), arrhythmias, aspiration
Australian Alcohol Support Services: ADIS 1800 250 015 (NSW 24/7), National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline 1800 250 015, Family Drug Support 1300 368 186, Alcoholics Anonymous
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome prevention requires thiamine replacement - Wernicke's (acute confusional state) is reversible, Korsakoff's (chronic amnesia) is often permanent
Motivational interviewing techniques improve engagement - explore ambivalence, avoid confrontation, support self-efficacy, recognize change is difficult

RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Management of Alcohol Use Disorder
NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines 2008

title: Acute Psychotic Episode - First Episode Psychosis Assessment and Mental Health Act Application
candidate_instructions: You are the on-call psychiatry registrar in the Emergency Department at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital. A 23-year-old university student, Daniel Chen, was brought in by police at 2am after neighbors called triple zero reporting him shouting at his apartment walls and throwing furniture out his third-floor window. Police report he was difficult to engage, stated 'government satellites are tracking me through my fillings' and attempted to flee. He has no previous psychiatric history. His mother arrived 30 minutes ago and reports he has been 'acting strange' for 6 weeks - stopped attending engineering classes, withdrawn from friends, locks himself in his room, talks to himself. She found cannabis in his room last week but he denies using it. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination, assess acute risk to self and others, and determine if Mental Health Act criteria are met for involuntary admission. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 23-year-old third-year engineering student at University of Sydney. For the past 6 weeks, you have been experiencing terrifying realizations that government intelligence agencies installed tracking devices in your dental fillings during a routine filling 8 weeks ago. You can hear agents communicating through a special frequency that only you can detect - male voices discussing your movements, commenting 'he's going to the kitchen now' or 'target is alone'. The voices are constant and becoming more threatening over the past week, with commands to 'destroy the surveillance equipment' which you interpret as your laptop and phone. Tonight you threw your laptop and phone out the window to stop the tracking. You are frightened, hypervigilant, and make poor eye contact. Your speech is pressured and jumps between topics - dental fillings, surveillance, engineering assignments, your mother's cooking. You believe the doctor might be part of the surveillance network. When asked about cannabis, you become defensive - you smoked it twice last month to 'calm the voices' but it made things worse. You have not slept more than 2 hours per night for a week because you need to 'stay alert'. You have vague thoughts that 'maybe I should just end this' if the surveillance never stops, but no specific plan. You are not oriented to time (think it is afternoon, not 3am) but know place and person. You have no insight you are unwell - you believe your experiences are real. Opening statement when doctor enters: 'Are you one of them? I can see the communication device in your ear.' You become agitated if the doctor dismisses your beliefs but calm slightly if they acknowledge your distress without agreeing the delusions are real.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you tell me what brought you to hospital tonight? (Expected: Police brought me in but they don't understand - I was protecting myself from surveillance)
TIMELINE: When did you first notice these tracking devices? (Expected: 6 weeks ago, after dental appointment)
VOICES: You mentioned communication devices - can you describe what you hear? (Expected: Male voices, commenting on my actions, sometimes commanding me to destroy equipment, constant throughout day)
COMMAND HALLUCINATIONS: Do the voices ever tell you to hurt yourself or others? (Expected: Tell me to destroy surveillance equipment, vague commands to 'end the surveillance')
DELUSIONAL BELIEFS: How do you know government agencies are involved? (Expected: The technology is too sophisticated to be anyone else, the timing after my dental filling proves it)
SUBSTANCE USE: Have you used any drugs or alcohol recently? (Expected: Cannabis twice last month, made voices louder, no other substances)
SUICIDAL IDEATION: You mentioned 'ending this' - what did you mean? (Expected: Passive thoughts that if surveillance never stops maybe death would be better, no specific plan, no intent currently)
FUNCTIONING: How have your studies been going? (Expected: Stopped attending classes 4 weeks ago, can't concentrate with voices, behind on assignments)
SLEEP: How many hours are you sleeping? (Expected: 2 hours maximum, need to stay alert for agents)
PREVIOUS PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous experiences like this or mental health treatment? (Expected: Never, no family history of mental illness mentioned)
INSIGHT: What do you think is happening to you? (Expected: Government surveillance is real, not mental illness)
FAMILY COLLATERAL: Need to interview mother separately for timeline, prodromal symptoms, substance use history
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, 3 days beard growth, wearing mismatched clothing, poor hygiene evident, appears exhausted
BEHAVIOR: Hypervigilant, scanning room constantly, startles at sudden movements, limited eye contact, psychomotor agitation - fidgets with hands, stands suddenly from chair
SPEECH: Pressured rate, increased volume when discussing delusions, tangential - shifts from surveillance to engineering to food without clear connections
MOOD: Subjective - 'Terrified' 'I just want the voices to stop'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, fearful, range restricted, congruent with persecutory thought content, labile - shifts from frightened to angry when beliefs challenged
THOUGHT FORM: Tangential, loose associations, thought disorder present - 'The fillings have microchips, my professor uses surveillance too, my mother's dumplings were cold yesterday'

THOUGHT CONTENT: Paranoid delusions (government surveillance via dental fillings), delusions of reference (voices commenting on actions), delusions of control (tracking devices monitoring him), passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent, no homicidal ideation

PERCEPTIONS: Auditory hallucinations - running commentary (third-person voices commenting 'he is walking', 'target is sitting'), command hallucinations (instructions to destroy surveillance equipment), present constantly, worse at night, no visual hallucinations

COGNITION: Disoriented to time (believes 3am is afternoon), oriented to place and person, attention impaired (cannot complete serial 7s due to distractibility from voices), concentration severely reduced
INSIGHT: No insight - does not believe he has mental illness, attributes experiences to external surveillance, does not see need for psychiatric treatment
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - throwing possessions out window, unable to assess risk of behavior, cannot make treatment decisions safely
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: MODERATE-HIGH RISK - Command hallucinations to 'end surveillance' (vague but concerning), passive suicidal ideation present ('maybe I should just end this'), impaired judgment from psychosis, engaging in dangerous behavior (throwing items from height), hypervigilant and unpredictable, protective factors present (mother engaged, no previous attempts, ambivalent about death)

ACUTE RISK TO OTHERS: MODERATE RISK - Paranoid delusions may lead to defensive aggression if feels threatened, poor impulse control, command hallucinations could escalate, no current homicidal ideation but delusional system involves 'enemies'

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA MET FOR INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION: (1) Mental illness present - First Episode Psychosis with paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized thought; (2) Risk of serious harm - Command hallucinations, dangerous behavior (throwing items from height), passive suicidal ideation, impaired judgment; (3) Requires immediate psychiatric treatment - Antipsychotic medication, inpatient monitoring; (4) No less restrictive alternative - Lacks insight, unable to consent to voluntary admission, risk too high for community management
DOCUMENT SECTION 19 EMERGENCY DETENTION OR SECTION 27 INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION under Mental Health Act NSW 2007 - Complete statutory forms, notify Mental Health Review Tribunal within 3 business days

SAFETY PLAN: Constant 1:1 nursing observation until acute psychosis stabilizes, remove potential ligature points from room, check belongings for weapons or substances, secure mental health unit placement

ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION: Commence Olanzapine 10mg oral nocte (sedating, good efficacy for first episode psychosis, lower EPS risk than typicals), if refuses oral or acutely agitated consider Olanzapine 5-10mg IM stat, PBS Authority Required 3139K for continuing antipsychotic beyond 1 month
BENZODIAZEPINE PRN: Lorazepam 1-2mg oral/IM PRN for severe agitation (maximum 6mg in 24 hours), monitor sedation especially if combined with antipsychotic
SUBSTANCE USE SCREEN: Urine drug screen including cannabis and amphetamines - substance-induced psychosis differential, collateral from mother suggests cannabis use but need objective confirmation

MEDICAL WORKUP: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, Vitamin B12/folate, fasting glucose, lipids (baseline before antipsychotic), ECG (QTc prolongation risk with antipsychotics), consider CT brain if any neurological signs or atypical presentation
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Interview mother separately - prodromal symptoms timeline, substance use history, family psychiatric history, premorbid functioning, recent stressors

ORGANIC CAUSES EXCLUSION: Rule out delirium (acute confusion, fluctuating), CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid disease, medication/substance-induced - but clinical picture consistent with primary psychosis
AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide to mother - Lifeline 13 11 14, SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support), Headspace 1800 650 890 (youth mental health)
EARLY PSYCHOSIS TEAM REFERRAL: Contact hospital Early Psychosis Intervention Service (EPIS) within 24 hours - evidence shows early intensive treatment improves outcomes in first episode psychosis

INVOLUNTARY TREATMENT PLAN: Discuss with consultant psychiatrist regarding treatment authority under Mental Health Act, consider clozapine if treatment-resistant after 2 adequate antipsychotic trials, CBT for psychosis when acute symptoms stabilize

FAMILY PSYCHOEDUCATION: Once Daniel stabilizes, provide education about psychosis, medication importance, relapse warning signs, duration of treatment (12-24 months minimum after first episode), cannabis avoidance critical

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, explains role, obtains consent for assessment (acknowledges involuntary context)
Asks open question about presenting complaint and patient's understanding of why brought to hospital
Explores delusional beliefs non-judgmentally - asks about tracking devices, government surveillance, timeline of beliefs
Assesses auditory hallucinations systematically - content (commentary vs command), frequency, impact on behavior
Asks about command hallucinations specifically - does patient obey them, commands to harm self or others
Screens for suicidal ideation - passive thoughts, active plan, intent, protective factors
Takes substance use history - cannabis, amphetamines, alcohol, timeline relative to symptom onset
Assesses insight - does patient believe experiences are real vs. symptoms of illness, sees need for treatment
Assesses cognition - orientation to time/place/person, attention, concentration
Documents thought form abnormalities - tangentiality, loose associations, disorganization
Correctly identifies Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria are met - mental illness present, risk of serious harm, requires immediate treatment, no less restrictive alternative
Proposes appropriate antipsychotic medication - Olanzapine or Risperidone with correct dose range
Recommends safety measures - 1:1 observation, secure environment, remove ligature risks
Plans collateral history from mother and medical workup to exclude organic causes
Provides Australian crisis contacts - Lifeline 13 11 14, SANE Australia, or Headspace

learning_points: FIRST EPISODE PSYCHOSIS (FEP) typically presents age 18-25 years, requires urgent treatment within 1 month of symptom onset for best outcomes - Duration of Untreated Psychosis (DUP) correlates with poorer prognosis

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION CRITERIA: (1) Person has mental illness, (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) Requires immediate treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative available - Section 19 Emergency (72 hours) or Section 27 Involuntary Admission

ANTIPSYCHOTIC CHOICE IN FEP: Second-generation antipsychotics preferred (Olanzapine 5-20mg, Risperidone 1-4mg, Quetiapine 300-800mg) - lower extrapyramidal side effect risk than first-generation, Olanzapine most sedating (useful for agitation/insomnia), start low dose and titrate, monitor metabolic effects (weight, lipids, glucose)

COMMAND HALLUCINATIONS increase risk - assess content (harm self/others), frequency (constant vs occasional), compliance (does patient obey), ability to resist - HIGH RISK if commands to harm, patient has history of compliance, poor impulse control

SUBSTANCE-INDUCED PSYCHOSIS DIFFERENTIAL: Cannabis and amphetamines most common - usually resolves within 1 week of abstinence, if symptoms persist beyond 1 month consider primary psychotic disorder, urine drug screen essential, collateral history critical

COLLATERAL HISTORY ESSENTIAL in psychosis - patient lacks insight and provides unreliable history, family/friends can clarify timeline (prodromal symptoms: social withdrawal, decline in functioning, odd beliefs for weeks-months before acute psychosis), substance use, premorbid personality, stressors

EARLY PSYCHOSIS INTERVENTION SERVICES (EPIS) improve outcomes - intensive case management, family therapy, CBT for psychosis, vocational support, target <3 years from first episode, reduces relapse and hospitalization

AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support for patients and families), Headspace 1800 650 890 (youth mental health ages 12-25)

SAFETY IN ACUTE PSYCHOSIS: 1:1 constant observation if command hallucinations or suicidal ideation, de-escalation techniques (calm voice, non-threatening posture, offer choices), antipsychotic + benzodiazepine for severe agitation, avoid physical restraint if possible

ORGANIC CAUSES TO EXCLUDE: Delirium (acute confusion, fluctuating consciousness), CNS infection (fever, headache, meningism), autoimmune encephalitis (NMDA receptor antibodies), thyroid disease, medication-induced (steroids, dopamine agonists), substance intoxication/withdrawal - FBC, UEC, TFT, CT brain if atypical features

title: Mental State Examination - Auditory Hallucinations in First Episode Psychosis
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. Sarah Chen, a 22-year-old university student, has been brought in by her flatmate who is concerned about her unusual behaviour over the past 3 weeks. She has been talking to herself, appearing distressed, and hasn't been sleeping. Conduct a focused mental state examination with particular attention to perceptual abnormalities. Assess her immediate risk and formulate an appropriate management plan. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Chen, a 22-year-old psychology student at University of Sydney. For the past 3 weeks, you have been hearing voices - specifically two male voices commenting on your actions and occasionally giving you commands. The voices are clearest when you're alone and seem to come from outside your head, usually from behind you. They tell you things like 'She's not good enough' and 'Everyone can see through her lies.' Yesterday, one voice told you to 'just disappear' which frightened you. You haven't been sleeping well (2-3 hours nightly) and have stopped attending lectures. You're scared and confused but haven't told anyone about the voices until now. You have no previous psychiatric history, no substance use, and no family history of mental illness. You live with two flatmates who have noticed your behaviour change. You feel hopeless about your future but deny any specific suicide plan when asked directly. You're cooperative with the examination but appear anxious and occasionally pause mid-sentence as if listening to something.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's ability to conduct a systematic mental state examination focusing on perceptual abnormalities. Look for proper assessment of: appearance and behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought form and content, perceptions (detailed exploration of hallucinations), cognition, and insight. Pay particular attention to how they explore the auditory hallucinations (onset, frequency, content, command nature, impact). Ensure they conduct a thorough risk assessment including SAFE-T protocol. The patient should appear anxious, occasionally distracted (responding to internal stimuli), with evidence of sleep deprivation. Her speech may pause intermittently. Award marks for systematic approach, appropriate questioning techniques, and comprehensive risk assessment.

sample_answer.history_summary: 22-year-old psychology student presenting with 3-week history of auditory hallucinations, sleep disturbance, and functional decline. No previous psychiatric history, substance use, or family history of mental illness. Lives independently with supportive flatmates.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: Casually dressed, poor self-care, evidence of sleep deprivation with dark circles under eyes. Behaviour: Cooperative but anxious, occasionally appears to be listening to internal stimuli, minimal eye contact. Speech: Normal rate and rhythm with occasional mid-sentence pauses. Mood: 'Scared and confused' with congruent anxious affect, restricted range. Thought form: Coherent and goal-directed, no formal thought disorder. title: Mental State Examination: Assessing Insight and Judgment in Major Depressive Episode
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. Sarah Chen, a 34-year-old accountant, was brought in by her husband after she told him she 'can't go on anymore' and has been researching methods to end her life. She has been treated for depression in the past but stopped her medication 6 months ago because she felt it wasn't helping. Conduct a focused mental state examination specifically assessing her insight into her condition and her judgment regarding her current situation. You have 8 minutes to complete your assessment and formulate a management plan.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Chen, a 34-year-old chartered accountant who has been struggling with worsening depression over the past 6 months. You stopped taking your sertraline because you believed it made you feel 'numb' and wasn't really helping. Over the past 2 weeks, you've been having persistent thoughts that your family would be better off without you and have been researching suicide methods online, specifically looking at overdose information. You feel hopeless about your future and believe your depression is a personal weakness rather than a medical condition. You have poor judgment about your safety but retain some awareness that your thinking might not be entirely rational. You are cooperative but express doubt about whether treatment will help. When asked directly about insight, you acknowledge feeling unwell but minimize the severity and attribute it to work stress rather than mental illness.
examiner_instructions: Assess the candidate's ability to conduct a focused mental state examination evaluating insight and judgment in a patient with major depression and active suicidal ideation. Look for systematic assessment of the patient's understanding of their condition, recognition of the need for treatment, and capacity to make safe decisions. The candidate should demonstrate competency in risk assessment using SAFE-T protocol and develop an appropriate immediate management plan. Pay attention to their ability to distinguish between different levels of insight and assess decision-making capacity in the context of mental illness.
