title: Acute Psychosis with Paranoid Delusions - Mental State Examination and Risk Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department. A 28-year-old male university student has been brought in by police under Section 20 Mental Health Act NSW 2007 after he was found shouting at passing cars outside his apartment at 2am, claiming the government was monitoring him through street lights. His flatmate called police after the patient barricaded himself in his room for 3 days, refusing to eat because he believed the food was poisoned. The patient is now sitting in the interview room, appears suspicious and guarded. Your task is to conduct a mental state examination, assess his level of psychosis and any associated risks, and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this consultation.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 28-year-old computer science PhD student at University of Sydney. Three weeks ago you started noticing that street lights would flicker when you walked past them, and you gradually became convinced this was a surveillance system monitoring your research. You believe ASIO (Australian Security Intelligence Organisation) is tracking you because your PhD project on encryption algorithms contains classified information. Two weeks ago you stopped attending your lectures because you were certain your supervisor was working with government agents. For the past 5 days you've noticed the campus security guards are always positioned where you walk, and they speak into radios whenever you pass. Yesterday your flatmate offered you a sandwich and you noticed it smelled unusual - you're convinced he's been recruited to poison you. Last night you couldn't sleep because you kept hearing voices through the walls discussing plans to 'extract the data' from you. You went outside at 2am to confront the surveillance team operating the street lights. When the doctor enters, you are sitting with arms crossed, repeatedly glancing at the corners of the room (checking for cameras). You answer questions but are guarded and suspicious. You haven't used any drugs - you're adamant about this because 'they want people to think I'm on drugs to discredit me'. You have no history of mental illness. Your mother has schizophrenia but you've never told anyone this. You have no intention to harm yourself or others, but you do want to 'expose the surveillance program'. You haven't eaten properly for 3 days and have slept only 2-3 hours per night for the past week. You believe you're completely rational and the doctor is probably part of the system. Opening statement: 'Why am I here? Who sent you? Are you with ASIO?'

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: 'Can you tell me what's been happening that brought you to hospital?' (Expected: Government surveillance, street lights monitoring, poisoned food)
ONSET AND TIMELINE: 'When did you first notice these concerns?' (Expected: 3 weeks ago with flickering street lights)
SPECIFIC BELIEFS: 'What makes you think ASIO is monitoring you?' (Expected: PhD research on encryption contains classified information)
PERCEPTUAL DISTURBANCES: 'Have you noticed anything unusual with your senses - hearing or seeing things others don't?' (Expected: Voices through walls discussing 'extracting data')
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS: 'How has your sleep been?' (Expected: 2-3 hours per night for past week); 'Appetite?' (Expected: Not eating for 3 days due to poisoning fears)
SUBSTANCE USE: 'Have you used any substances - cannabis, amphetamines, other drugs?' (Expected: Denies all use)
PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: 'Any previous mental health problems?' (Expected: Denies, but family history of schizophrenia in mother)
FAMILY HISTORY: 'Any mental health conditions in your family?' (Expected: Mother has schizophrenia)
RISK ASSESSMENT: 'Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?' (Expected: No suicidal ideation); 'Any thoughts of harming others?' (Expected: No homicidal ideation, wants to 'expose' surveillance)
FUNCTIONAL IMPACT: 'How has this affected your daily life - university, relationships?' (Expected: Stopped attending lectures 2 weeks ago, isolated from flatmate)
INSIGHT: 'What do you think is causing these experiences?' (Expected: No insight - believes surveillance is real, doctor may be part of system)
MEDICAL HISTORY: 'Any medical conditions or medications?' (Expected: None reported)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Casually dressed, disheveled, unshaven, poor self-care over past week
BEHAVIOR: Guarded, suspicious, hypervigilant - repeatedly glancing at corners of room, minimal eye contact, arms crossed defensively
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume, coherent but circumferential when discussing surveillance beliefs
MOOD: Subjective - 'I'm fine, just need people to believe me'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, suspicious, congruent with paranoid content, restricted range
THOUGHT FORM: Logical but with evidence of paranoid thinking pattern

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS - Paranoid delusions (ASIO surveillance, street lights monitoring, poisoned food, flatmate recruited as agent) - systematized, elaborate, firmly held with no insight. No suicidal or homicidal ideation expressed
PERCEPTIONS: HALLUCINATIONS - Auditory hallucinations (voices through walls discussing 'extracting data') - second person/third person, content consistent with delusional theme
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to time/place/person, attention intact though hypervigilant, no obvious memory impairment
INSIGHT: ABSENT - Patient has no awareness of mental illness, attributes experiences to external surveillance, believes doctor may be part of conspiracy
JUDGMENT: IMPAIRED - Not eating due to poisoning fears, confronting 'surveillance team' at 2am, stopped academic activities
immediate_management: SAFETY ASSESSMENT: Patient currently not violent but has impaired judgment, paranoid ideation may escalate. No weapons, no expressed intent to harm self or others. Moderate risk of self-neglect (not eating, sleep deprivation)

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007: Patient meets criteria for involuntary admission under Section 27 - (1) Has mental illness (acute psychotic episode with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations), (2) Risk of serious harm to self (self-neglect - dehydration, malnutrition) or deterioration without treatment, (3) Requires immediate psychiatric treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative available (no insight, refusing treatment)

MEDICAL WORKUP: Urgent bloods - FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12, folate (exclude organic causes); Urine drug screen (amphetamines, cannabis - despite denial, must rule out substance-induced psychosis); CT brain if first psychotic episode to exclude structural lesion

IMMEDIATE PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT: Olanzapine 10mg PO stat (atypical antipsychotic, broad efficacy for positive symptoms, lower EPS risk than typical antipsychotics); Olanzapine 10mg PO nocte ongoing; Monitor vital signs, particularly sedation and metabolic effects
ALTERNATIVE IF REFUSES ORAL: Consider Olanzapine 10mg IM if oral refused (though patient not currently aggressive - attempt therapeutic rapport first)
HYDRATION AND NUTRITION: IV fluids if dehydrated (hasn't eaten/drunk adequately for 3 days); Supervised meals on psychiatric ward; Monitor electrolytes
NURSING OBSERVATIONS: 15-minute observations initially; Monitor for agitation, paranoia escalation, absconding risk; One-to-one nursing if required

COMMUNICATION: Use calm, non-confrontational approach; Avoid challenging delusions directly ('I understand you're concerned about surveillance, but we're here to help you feel better'); Explain need for admission focusing on sleep, nutrition, safety rather than 'mental illness'
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Contact flatmate (with patient consent if possible) for timeline, substance use history, baseline functioning; Contact family re: mother's schizophrenia history and treatment
PSYCHIATRY CONSULTATION: Urgent psychiatry registrar review for formal admission under Mental Health Act and ongoing management plan

LONG-TERM PLAN: Antipsychotic continuation (likely 6-12 months minimum for first-episode psychosis); Early Psychosis Intervention Program referral; Case management; Family psychoeducation; Substance use monitoring
CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide to family/flatmate - Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support), Mental Health Line NSW 1800 011 511

DOCUMENTATION: Complete Mental Health Act paperwork (Section 27 Involuntary Patient form, medical certificate, explanation of rights); Notify Mental Health Review Tribunal within 24 hours; Document detailed MSE, risk assessment, and management plan in ED notes

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, explains role, and attempts to establish rapport despite patient's suspiciousness
Asks open-ended question about presenting concerns and what brought patient to hospital
Explores specific delusional content systematically (ASIO surveillance, street lights, poisoned food)
Asks about perceptual disturbances - specifically auditory hallucinations (content, frequency, first/second/third person)
Assesses biological symptoms - sleep pattern and nutritional intake over past week
Asks about substance use (cannabis, amphetamines, alcohol) to exclude substance-induced psychosis
Asks about psychiatric and family history (mother's schizophrenia critical for diagnosis)
Assesses risk of harm to self and others, including self-neglect
Assesses insight - asks what patient thinks is causing these experiences
Conducts systematic MSE covering appearance, behavior, speech, mood, affect, thought form, thought content, perceptions, cognition, insight
Formulates working diagnosis of acute psychotic episode (first-episode psychosis vs early schizophrenia)
Identifies need for involuntary admission under Mental Health Act NSW 2007 and states criteria (mental illness, risk, need for treatment, no less restrictive option)
Proposes appropriate immediate pharmacological management (Olanzapine 10mg PO or alternative atypical antipsychotic with dose)
Orders appropriate investigations to exclude organic causes (bloods - TFT, B12, glucose, calcium; urine drug screen; CT brain)
Communicates with empathy, avoids confrontation, uses non-judgmental language when discussing delusional beliefs

learning_points: FIRST-EPISODE PSYCHOSIS: Acute onset paranoid delusions (ASIO surveillance) + auditory hallucinations (voices through walls) in 28-year-old with family history of schizophrenia suggests first-episode psychosis. Differential includes schizophrenia, substance-induced psychosis (amphetamines, cannabis), brief psychotic disorder, or organic causes

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA: Involuntary admission requires (1) Mental illness present, (2) Risk of serious harm to self/others OR risk of serious deterioration without treatment, (3) Immediate treatment needed, (4) No less restrictive alternative. This patient meets all criteria - acute psychosis with self-neglect (not eating/drinking), no insight, refusing treatment

ATYPICAL ANTIPSYCHOTICS FIRST-LINE: Olanzapine 5-20mg daily, Risperidone 1-4mg daily, or Quetiapine 300-800mg daily preferred over typical antipsychotics (haloperidol) due to lower extrapyramidal side effects. Olanzapine 10mg nocte good starting dose for acute psychosis. Monitor for metabolic effects (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia)

ORGANIC CAUSES MUST BE EXCLUDED: Always investigate first-episode psychosis for medical causes - TFT (hyperthyroidism/hypothyroidism), glucose (hypoglycemia), calcium (hypercalcemia), B12/folate (deficiency), CT brain (tumor, stroke, encephalitis). Urine drug screen mandatory even if patient denies use

SYSTEMATIZED DELUSIONS: This patient has elaborate, interconnected paranoid delusions (street lights → ASIO → PhD research → poisoned food → flatmate recruited). Systematized delusions with hallucinations suggest schizophrenia spectrum over brief psychotic disorder. Duration >1 week also excludes brief psychotic disorder

SELF-NEGLECT AS RISK: Not all psychiatric risk is suicide/violence. This patient has moderate risk from self-neglect - 3 days without adequate food/water, sleep deprivation (2-3 hours/night for 1 week). Self-neglect justifies involuntary admission under Mental Health Act

INSIGHT ASSESSMENT CRITICAL: Patient has zero insight - believes surveillance is real, attributes experiences to external conspiracy, suspects doctor is 'part of the system'. Absence of insight predicts poor treatment adherence and supports involuntary admission

EARLY PSYCHOSIS INTERVENTION PROGRAMS: First-episode psychosis requires specialized follow-up. Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre (EPPIC model) provides 2-year intensive case management, family therapy, CBT for psychosis, vocational rehabilitation. Referral should be made during admission

CANNABIS/AMPHETAMINE-INDUCED PSYCHOSIS: Important differential in young adults. Cannabis use increases psychosis risk 2-4x, amphetamines can cause indistinguishable paranoid psychosis. Urine drug screen essential even if denied. Substance-induced psychosis usually resolves within 1 month of abstinence

COMMUNICATION WITH PARANOID PATIENTS: Avoid challenging delusions directly ('The government isn't watching you'). Instead: (1) Acknowledge distress ('I can see this is very concerning for you'), (2) Focus on symptoms rather than content ('You seem worried and haven't been sleeping'), (3) Explain need for help in non-confrontational terms ('We want to help you feel safer and sleep better'). Build rapport before discussing involuntary admission
references: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders (2016)
Mental Health Act NSW 2007 - Sections 19, 20, 27 (Involuntary Admission Criteria)
Australian Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - Psychotic Disorders: Olanzapine 5-20mg daily first-line for first-episode psychosis
Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre (EPPIC) Clinical Guidelines
NSW Health Mental Health Line 1800 011 511 for crisis assessment and involuntary admission coordination

title: Acute Psychosis with Auditory Hallucinations - Mental State Examination and Risk Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a tertiary teaching hospital. A 28-year-old male university student has been brought in by police after being found shouting at pedestrians on a busy street corner at 2am. Witnesses reported he was having conversations with people who weren't there and appeared distressed. His flatmate arrived shortly after and reports the patient has been acting increasingly paranoid over the past 3 weeks, believing that his university lecturers are monitoring him through his laptop camera. He stopped attending classes 10 days ago and has been awake for most nights, pacing his room and talking to himself. The flatmate denies any known mental health history but mentions the patient has been smoking cannabis daily for the past 6 months. The patient is now sitting quietly in the assessment room but appears guarded and suspicious. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination, assess risk (including violence and self-harm), and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this station.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel, a 28-year-old third-year computer science student at University of Sydney. Three weeks ago, you began noticing that your lecturers were looking at you strangely during tutorials. You discovered they had installed spyware on your laptop to monitor your assignments because they suspect you of cheating. You can see the red light on your laptop camera turning on when you're alone in your room. For the past 10 days, you've been hearing the voices of two lecturers (Professor Chen and Dr. Williams) discussing you through your laptop speakers even when it's turned off. They say things like 'He's not smart enough for this degree' and 'We need to fail him out of the program.' The voices are clearest at night, which is why you've barely slept - maybe 2-3 hours per night for the past week. You've been smoking cannabis (2-3 joints daily for 6 months) to help calm yourself, but it doesn't seem to help anymore. Tonight, the voices told you to go outside and warn other students about the surveillance program, which is why you were on the street corner. You're not sure why the police brought you here - you weren't doing anything wrong, just trying to help people. When the doctor enters, you make minimal eye contact and appear suspicious. Your opening statement is: 'Why am I here? I haven't done anything illegal. Are you working with the university?' You will only reveal details about the voices if directly asked about hearing things or unusual experiences. You deny wanting to hurt yourself but admit you've thought about confronting Professor Chen in person to make him stop the surveillance. You have no previous psychiatric history, no family history of mental illness, and no other medical conditions. You live with two flatmates, have lost contact with your girlfriend (broke up 4 months ago), and your parents live interstate. You stopped attending classes because you believe the lecturers are trying to sabotage you. You appear anxious, fidgety, with poor eye contact, and become more guarded when asked about the voices.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: 'Can you tell me what happened tonight that brought you to hospital?' (Expected: Patient suspicious, may say 'Nothing happened' or 'Police brought me for no reason')
UNUSUAL EXPERIENCES: 'Have you noticed anything unusual happening recently? Things that others might not have noticed?' (Expected: Patient describes surveillance by university lecturers)

PERCEPTUAL DISTURBANCES: 'Have you been hearing or seeing things that others around you don't seem to hear or see?' (Expected: Auditory hallucinations - two voices of lecturers through laptop speakers even when off)

HALLUCINATION CHARACTERISTICS: 'Tell me about these voices - whose voices are they? What do they say? Are they inside or outside your head?' (Expected: Professor Chen and Dr. Williams, critical content, external, clear at night)
DELUSIONAL BELIEFS: 'You mentioned surveillance - can you explain more about what's happening?' (Expected: Fixed belief that lecturers installed spyware, monitoring through laptop camera)
SLEEP PATTERN: 'How has your sleep been?' (Expected: Severe insomnia, 2-3 hours per night for past week, voices worse at night)
SUBSTANCE USE: 'Have you been using any substances - alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, anything else?' (Expected: Cannabis 2-3 joints daily for 6 months, increased recently)
TIMELINE: 'When did you first notice these things happening?' (Expected: Paranoia started 3 weeks ago, hallucinations for 10 days, stopped classes 10 days ago)
RISK OF VIOLENCE: 'Have you thought about confronting anyone about the surveillance? What would you do?' (Expected: Thought about confronting Professor Chen, no specific plan, no access to weapons)
SAFE-T SUICIDE RISK: 'Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' (Expected: Denies suicidal ideation, no plan, no previous attempts)

FUNCTIONAL IMPACT: 'How has this affected your daily life - study, social activities, self-care?' (Expected: Stopped attending university 10 days ago, isolated from friends, poor sleep affecting function)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: 'Have you ever experienced anything like this before? Any previous mental health treatment?' (Expected: No previous psychiatric history, no hospitalizations)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Casually dressed in jeans and hoodie, appears disheveled, poor hygiene (body odor noted), unshaven for several days
BEHAVIOR: Minimal eye contact, fidgety and restless, hypervigilant (scanning room), guarded posture with arms crossed, occasionally glancing at corners of room as if distracted by stimuli
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume initially, becomes pressured when discussing the surveillance, tone suspicious and guarded
MOOD: Subjective - 'Stressed' or 'People don't believe me'
AFFECT: Anxious, congruent with paranoid thought content, range restricted, not reactive to rapport-building
THOUGHT FORM: Linear but circumstantial when discussing delusions, coherent

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS - Paranoid delusions of surveillance by university lecturers, referential thinking (lecturers looking at him strangely), ideas of persecution. No suicidal or homicidal ideation. Thoughts of confronting Professor Chen (potential violence risk)

PERCEPTIONS: AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS - Two distinct voices (Professor Chen and Dr. Williams) heard through laptop speakers even when device off, third-person commentary, derogatory content ('not smart enough'), worse at night, external (outside head), experienced as real
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time. Attention mildly impaired (distracted by hallucinations). No formal cognitive testing performed but appeared to understand questions
INSIGHT: POOR - Does not believe he has mental illness, attributes experiences to real external surveillance, rejects suggestion of psychiatric explanation
JUDGMENT: IMPAIRED - Acted on delusional beliefs (shouting on street), considering confronting lecturer, poor decision-making regarding cannabis use
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT - MODERATE TO HIGH RISK: Violence risk present - thoughts of confronting Professor Chen without specific plan, poor insight, command hallucinations potential (not explicitly stated but voices giving instructions), substance use disinhibition. Self-harm risk LOW - denies suicidal ideation, no plan, no previous attempts, but impaired judgment from psychosis could lead to impulsive actions

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA MET FOR INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION: (1) Mental illness present - acute psychotic episode with auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions; (2) Risk of serious harm - potential violence toward Professor Chen, impaired self-care, risk of aggressive behavior in community; (3) Requires immediate treatment - antipsychotic medication and safe environment; (4) No less restrictive alternative - refuses voluntary admission, lacks insight. Recommend Section 27 (Involuntary Admission) or Section 19 (Emergency) if immediate detention needed

IMMEDIATE SAFETY: Admit to acute psychiatric inpatient unit under Mental Health Act, 1:1 nursing observations initially to assess for escalation, remove potential weapons from environment, offer voluntary admission first (likely refused given poor insight)

MEDICAL WORKUP: Exclude organic causes before confirming functional psychosis - FBC (infection, anemia), UEC (renal/metabolic), LFT (hepatic encephalopathy), TFT (thyroid-induced psychosis), glucose (hypoglycemia), Vitamin B12/folate, syphilis serology, urine drug screen (cannabis, amphetamines), CT brain if first episode psychosis or neurological signs

ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION: Olanzapine 10mg PO nocte (sedating, helps sleep, PBS 8662K) OR Risperidone 2mg PO BD (less sedating, PBS 8415L). Avoid IM administration unless patient refuses oral medication and becomes aggressive. Counsel regarding side effects (sedation, weight gain, extrapyramidal symptoms, metabolic syndrome)
BENZODIAZEPINE PRN: Lorazepam 1-2mg PO PRN agitation (max 6mg/24hrs), avoid overuse, taper once antipsychotic effective

SUBSTANCE USE MANAGEMENT: Cannabis cessation counseling once acute psychosis stabilizes, explain cannabis-induced psychosis risk (40% of first-episode psychosis associated with heavy cannabis use), monitor for withdrawal symptoms (irritability, insomnia, anxiety)

COLLATERAL HISTORY: Contact flatmate for further timeline details, contact family (parents interstate) to inform of admission and obtain family psychiatric history, contact university student services regarding academic suspension during treatment

PSYCHOEDUCATION (once stabilized): Explain diagnosis of acute psychotic episode, likely first-episode psychosis vs. cannabis-induced psychotic disorder, discuss prognosis (60-70% good outcome with early treatment), importance of medication adherence, avoiding cannabis

CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide after discharge - Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety), Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467, SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support)

MENTAL HEALTH TEAM INVOLVEMENT: Refer to psychiatry registrar for admission clerking, liaison with community mental health team for discharge planning, case manager assignment for early psychosis intervention program

FOLLOW-UP PLAN: Inpatient stay 7-14 days until symptoms stabilize, antipsychotic titration to therapeutic dose, weekly outpatient review by psychiatry registrar for 4 weeks post-discharge, then fortnightly community mental health team follow-up, early psychosis intervention program enrollment (EPPIC model in Australia)

MONITOR FOR COMPLICATIONS: Antipsychotic side effects (extrapyramidal symptoms - use benztropine 1mg BD if needed), metabolic syndrome monitoring (weight, lipids, glucose at baseline and 3 months), agranulocytosis if clozapine later considered, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare but life-threatening)

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self professionally and explains purpose of assessment
Uses open-ended question to explore presenting complaint ('Tell me what happened tonight')
Directly asks about perceptual disturbances (hallucinations) - 'Have you been hearing or seeing things others don't?'

title: Acute Mania with Psychotic Features - Risk Assessment and Emergency Management
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the emergency department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 28-year-old man has been brought in by police at 2am after being found standing in the middle of a busy intersection directing traffic and shouting at passing cars. Police report he was aggressive when approached and stated he was 'organizing the city's energy flow'. His mother has arrived and reports he stopped taking his medication 3 weeks ago. She is extremely worried as he has not slept for 4 days, has spent $15,000 on cryptocurrency in the past week, and believes he has special powers to communicate with technology. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination, assess immediate risks, and formulate an emergency management plan. You have 8 minutes for this station.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel, a 28-year-old software developer who was diagnosed with bipolar disorder 3 years ago. You stopped taking your lithium and quetiapine 3 weeks ago because you felt 'amazing' and believed the medications were 'blocking your true potential'. Over the past 4 days you have not slept at all but feel incredibly energized - better than you have ever felt in your life. You have been working on a 'revolutionary' cryptocurrency project and have invested $15,000 (your entire savings plus maxed credit cards) because you are certain it will make you a billionaire within weeks. Tonight you were directing traffic because you could 'see the energy patterns of the city' and knew you could optimize traffic flow with your mind. You speak very rapidly, jumping from topic to topic - cryptocurrency, your special powers, how you are going to change the world, why doctors don't understand your gifts. You are irritable when interrupted and may become hostile if the doctor suggests you are unwell. You have grandiose delusions that you can communicate with electronic devices telepathically and that you have been 'chosen' to revolutionize technology. You believe the government is monitoring your work because they recognize your genius. You have no insight into being unwell - you feel this is the 'real you' finally emerging. If asked about suicide, you deny this completely as you have 'too much important work to do'. However, you acknowledge driving your car at 150 km/hr yesterday because you 'needed to test your reflexes' for your mission. You are not threatening violence but become agitated if told you need to stay in hospital.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: How have you been feeling recently? (Expected: 'Amazing, the best I've ever felt, finally living up to my potential')
MOOD SYMPTOMS: How is your energy level? (Expected: 'Incredible energy, don't need sleep, been awake 4 days working on my project')
SLEEP: When did you last sleep? (Expected: 'Haven't slept in 4 days but don't feel tired at all')
THOUGHT CONTENT: Tell me about your special powers you mentioned? (Expected: Describes grandiose delusions about telepathic communication with technology)
RISKY BEHAVIOR: Have you made any unusual purchases or decisions lately? (Expected: 'Invested $15,000 in cryptocurrency, will make billions')
INSIGHT: Do you think there might be something wrong or that you need treatment? (Expected: 'Nothing wrong, this is me at my best, doctors don't understand')
MEDICATION HISTORY: When did you stop your medications? (Expected: 'Stopped lithium and quetiapine 3 weeks ago, they were holding me back')
PREVIOUS EPISODES: Have you felt like this before? (Expected: 'Yes, 2 years ago but family and doctors ruined it by forcing medication')
SUBSTANCE USE: Have you used any drugs or alcohol recently? (Expected: 'No drugs, couple of energy drinks but don't need them')
HARM TO SELF: Any thoughts of hurting yourself? (Expected: 'No way, too much important work to do')
HARM TO OTHERS: Have you had any conflicts or aggressive behavior? (Expected: 'Got angry at police for interrupting my work, people don't understand my mission')
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Speak with mother - confirms 3-week medication non-compliance, no sleep, reckless spending, previous manic episode 2 years ago requiring involuntary admission
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, wearing mismatched clothing including suit jacket over pyjama top, multiple electronic devices attached to belt, poor hygiene evident, intense eye contact
BEHAVIOR: Psychomotor agitation, unable to sit still, pacing, intrusive, overfamiliar, touching examiner's equipment
SPEECH: Pressured, loud, difficult to interrupt, flight of ideas evident with rapid topic changes from cryptocurrency to special powers to government surveillance
MOOD: Subjective - 'Euphoric, the best I've ever felt, finally fulfilling my destiny'
AFFECT: Objective - Elevated, expansive, labile (rapidly shifting from euphoric to irritable when challenged), incongruent with situation
THOUGHT FORM: Flight of ideas, tangentiality, circumstantial, loose associations between topics

THOUGHT CONTENT: Grandiose delusions (telepathic powers, chosen one, revolutionary genius), persecutory delusions (government surveillance), no suicidal ideation, no homicidal ideation but acknowledges reckless driving and aggressive behavior toward police
PERCEPTIONS: No clear auditory or visual hallucinations reported, but describes 'sensing energy patterns' which may represent perceptual disturbances
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time, attention distractible, concentration impaired by flight of ideas
INSIGHT: Absent - no recognition of illness, attributes symptoms to 'true potential being realized'
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - evidenced by reckless spending, dangerous driving, stopping medications, risky behavior in traffic
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: HIGH RISK - While no suicidal ideation present, significant risk of harm through reckless behavior (driving 150 km/hr, standing in traffic intersection, aggressive confrontation with police). Impaired judgment secondary to acute mania with psychotic features. Previous history of manic episodes. No protective factors as insight absent and medication non-compliant.
SAFETY PLAN: Immediate one-to-one nursing observation in secure area of ED, remove access to exits and potential weapons, calm de-escalation approach, offer food and non-caffeinated beverages

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007: Patient meets criteria for involuntary admission under Section 19 (Emergency) - Mental illness present (Bipolar Disorder Type I, acute manic episode with psychotic features), risk of serious harm to self through reckless behavior, requires immediate treatment, no less restrictive alternative given absent insight and medication refusal, previous history of treatment response with involuntary admission
IMMEDIATE PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT: Olanzapine 10mg PO immediately (can repeat 5-10mg after 2 hours if needed, maximum 30mg/24 hours), PBS 8271K. Alternative if refuses oral: Olanzapine 5-10mg IM
AVOID: Benzodiazepines alone as first-line (antipsychotic more effective for mania), haloperidol in young males (extrapyramidal side effects risk)
CONTACT PSYCHIATRY REGISTRAR: Urgent review required for Mental Health Act assessment, admission to acute psychiatric unit, consideration of recommencing mood stabilizer once acute agitation settled

RECOMMENCE MAINTENANCE MEDICATIONS: Once acute phase managed - Lithium (previous medication, requires levels), Quetiapine 200-400mg nocte for mood stabilization and sedation. Check previous lithium levels and renal function before restarting
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Obtain detailed history from mother regarding timeline of deterioration, medication compliance history, previous episode triggers and response to treatment, baseline functioning

INVESTIGATIONS: Urgent - BSL, UEC (for lithium if restarting), TFTs (to exclude hyperthyroidism mimicking mania), urinary drug screen (to exclude amphetamine-induced psychosis), FBC, LFTs. Consider CT brain if first presentation or atypical features
CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide mother with Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (for carer support)

DOCUMENT: Mental Health Act Section 19 criteria met with specific justification, attempts at voluntary treatment declined, risks identified (reckless driving 150 km/hr, standing in traffic, aggressive behavior, financial harm $15,000 spent, sleep deprivation 4 days)

FOLLOW-UP PLAN: Acute psychiatric unit admission, daily psychiatry review, lithium level monitoring when restarted (target 0.6-1.0 mmol/L), psychoeducation when stable about medication compliance and early warning signs, involve mother in discharge planning, outpatient psychiatry follow-up within 1 week of discharge, community mental health team engagement
SAFETY FOR STAFF: Maintain exit access, have security nearby if needed, do not physically restrain unless imminent danger, use calm non-confrontational approach
DRIVING: Notify Roads and Maritime Services NSW as patient is medically unfit to drive (acute mania with reckless driving behavior), document advice given to patient and family not to drive

Recognizes need for involuntary admission and correctly identifies Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria (mental illness, risk of harm, requires immediate treatment, no less restrictive alternative)
Prescribes appropriate acute pharmacological management - Olanzapine 10mg PO/IM (or alternative antipsychotic), avoids benzodiazepines as monotherapy
Requests urgent psychiatry consultation and plans acute psychiatric unit admission
Orders appropriate investigations - UEC, TFTs, drug screen, lithium level, BSL (at least 3 mentioned)
Provides safety plan including one-to-one observation and environmental safety measures
Discusses need to notify Roads and Maritime Services regarding driving (medical unfitness)
Provides Australian crisis contacts to family (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636) and offers carer support information
Demonstrates appropriate communication style with agitated patient - calm, non-confrontational, maintains safety boundaries

learning_points: ACUTE MANIA TRIAD: Elevated mood + Decreased need for sleep + Increased goal-directed activity (or agitation). Duration ≥7 days or requires hospitalization qualifies for manic episode (DSM-5).

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA: (1) Mental illness present, (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) Requires immediate treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative. Section 19 (Emergency) allows 24-hour detention, Section 27 (Involuntary) for longer admission.

PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT OF ACUTE MANIA: Antipsychotics (Olanzapine 10mg, Risperidone 2mg, Quetiapine 200mg) more effective than benzodiazepines alone. Can combine with benzodiazepine for agitation. Avoid haloperidol in young males (dystonia risk).

SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: In mania, risk comes from reckless behavior (dangerous driving, financial harm, aggressive confrontations, substance use) rather than suicidal ideation. Still requires HIGH risk classification.

LITHIUM MONITORING: Before restarting - check UEC (renal function), TFTs (thyroid), pregnancy test if applicable. Therapeutic range 0.6-1.0 mmol/L for maintenance. Toxicity risk increases with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Rule out substance-induced (amphetamines, cocaine, steroids), hyperthyroidism, delirium, frontal lobe pathology. Drug screen and TFTs essential.
DRIVING NOTIFICATION: Doctor has legal obligation to notify Roads and Maritime Services NSW when patient poses significant driving risk. Document advice given to patient not to drive.
AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support and carer support).

COLLATERAL HISTORY ESSENTIAL: Patients with mania lack insight. Family provides critical information about baseline functioning, medication compliance, previous episodes, and timeline of deterioration.

PSYCHOTIC FEATURES IN MANIA: Grandiose delusions (special powers, chosen by God, extraordinary abilities) are mood-congruent and support diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder. Distinguish from schizophrenia (mood-incongruent delusions, negative symptoms predominate).

title: Acute Alcohol Withdrawal - Medical Emergency Management
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a tertiary hospital. A 48-year-old man has been brought in by ambulance after being found confused at home by his daughter. His daughter reports he has been drinking heavily for 20 years and ran out of alcohol 36 hours ago. On arrival, he appears tremulous, sweaty, and agitated. His vital signs show: BP 165/95, HR 118, RR 22, temp 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is visibly shaking and appears anxious. Your task is to take a focused history to assess alcohol withdrawal severity, screen for medical complications, perform a mental state examination, and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this station.
patient_role_instructions: You are Robert Chen, a 48-year-old former construction site supervisor who was made redundant 18 months ago. You live alone in a one-bedroom flat after your wife left you 2 years ago, though your adult daughter visits weekly. You have been drinking heavily for 20 years - typically 1-1.5 bottles of vodka daily (approximately 30-40 standard drinks). Three days ago you ran out of money and couldn't buy more alcohol. Your last drink was 36 hours ago. You started feeling shaky and sweaty yesterday morning. This morning you saw shadows moving in your peripheral vision that weren't there, and you're terrified. You haven't been able to eat or keep fluids down for 2 days. You feel your heart racing and can't sit still. You had one seizure 8 years ago during a previous withdrawal attempt but didn't seek medical help. You've never been admitted for detoxification. You desperately want to stop drinking but have tried and failed multiple times. When the doctor enters, you are visibly trembling, picking at your clothes, and say 'Something's really wrong, I can't stop shaking and I keep seeing things that aren't there.' You are anxious and cooperative but easily startled by sudden movements or loud noises. If asked about suicidal thoughts, you deny current ideation but admit you've felt hopeless about your alcohol problem. You're frightened you might die from withdrawal because a friend told you it can be dangerous.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: When did you last have a drink? (Expected: 36 hours ago, typically 1-1.5 bottles vodka daily for 20 years)
WITHDRAWAL TIMELINE: What symptoms have you noticed since stopping? When did they start? (Expected: Tremor and sweating 24 hours ago, visual hallucinations this morning)
SEVERITY SCREENING: Tremor, sweating, agitation, hallucinations, confusion, seizures? (Expected: Moderate-severe withdrawal - tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, visual hallucinations, no seizures yet)
PREVIOUS WITHDRAWALS: Have you stopped drinking before? Any complications like seizures or DTs? (Expected: One seizure 8 years ago during unsupervised withdrawal)
SEIZURE HISTORY: Describe the seizure - what happened, how long, did you lose consciousness? (Expected: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure, brief, no medical assessment at the time)
CONCURRENT MEDICAL ISSUES: Liver disease, pancreatitis, head injury, gastritis, infections? (Expected: No known liver disease but hasn't been assessed recently)
NUTRITIONAL STATUS: When did you last eat? Able to keep fluids down? (Expected: Unable to eat or drink for 2 days - high risk thiamine deficiency)
OTHER SUBSTANCE USE: Cannabis, benzodiazepines, opioids, stimulants? (Expected: Alcohol only)
PSYCHIATRIC COMORBIDITY: Depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, previous psychiatric treatment? (Expected: Hopelessness about alcohol problem, no current suicidal ideation, never treated)
MOTIVATION: Do you want to stop drinking? What support do you have? (Expected: Wants to stop, multiple failed attempts, daughter visits weekly)
SOCIAL SITUATION: Living arrangements, employment, family support? (Expected: Lives alone, unemployed 18 months, daughter is main support)
MEDICAL HISTORY: Hospital admissions, chronic conditions, medications? (Expected: No regular medications, no previous detox admissions)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, poor self-care, clothes worn and stained, appears stated age
BEHAVIOR: Psychomotor agitation, coarse tremor of hands, picking at clothes, easily startled, restless, maintains eye contact but anxious
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume, slightly pressured at times due to anxiety
MOOD: Subjective - 'Terrified, something's really wrong'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, congruent with mood, reactive but labile
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and goal-directed, no formal thought disorder
THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with withdrawal symptoms and fear of dying, denies current suicidal ideation but admits hopelessness about alcohol problem, no homicidal ideation
PERCEPTIONS: Visual hallucinations - 'shadows moving in peripheral vision,' formed but non-threatening, insight that they are not real
COGNITION: Alert but mildly distractible, oriented to person, place, time (check for confusion - marker of delirium tremens risk), concentration impaired
INSIGHT: Good - recognizes alcohol withdrawal, wants treatment
JUDGMENT: Presenting for medical care shows intact judgment in crisis
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK - Denies current suicidal ideation, presenting for help shows protective behavior, hopelessness about alcohol not about life, daughter provides support. No safety plan required but address hopelessness in ongoing treatment.

WITHDRAWAL SEVERITY: MODERATE-SEVERE (CIWA-Ar likely 15-20) - Tachycardia (HR 118), hypertension (BP 165/95), coarse tremor, diaphoresis, visual hallucinations, agitation. HIGH RISK for progression to delirium tremens given: 36 hours since last drink (peak risk 24-72 hours), previous seizure history, prolonged heavy use (20 years), unable to maintain nutrition/hydration.

IMMEDIATE MEDICAL STABILIZATION: IV access, bloods (FBC, UEC, LFT, glucose, magnesium, phosphate, BAL, coagulation studies), ECG (check QTc before benzodiazepines), oxygen if hypoxic, nil by mouth initially

BENZODIAZEPINE PROTOCOL: Diazepam loading regimen - 20mg PO/IV stat, then 20mg every 2 hours until CIWA-Ar <10 (typical total loading dose 60-120mg over 6-12 hours). Rationale: Long-acting benzodiazepine prevents seizures and DTs, cross-tolerant with alcohol at GABA receptors.

THIAMINE REPLACEMENT (MANDATORY): Thiamine 300mg IV TDS for 3-5 days BEFORE glucose administration (prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy - confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia). Follow with Thiamine 100mg PO daily long-term.
NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT: Multivitamins IV (Vitamins B and C), magnesium 10mmol IV (prevents seizures), phosphate replacement if low, commence oral fluids when tolerating
SEIZURE PROPHYLAXIS: Benzodiazepines are primary prevention. If seizure occurs: Midazolam 10mg IM or Diazepam 10mg IV, neurology consult if prolonged or recurrent

MONITOR FOR DELIRIUM TREMENS (72-96 hour peak risk): Confusion, disorientation, severe agitation, fever, autonomic instability (tachycardia >120, hypertension). If DT develops: ICU admission, high-dose benzodiazepines (up to 200-400mg diazepam equivalent/24 hours), haloperidol 5mg IM PRN for severe agitation (caution: lowers seizure threshold)
ADMISSION: Medical ward with psychiatric liaison input (NOT psychiatric ward - medical emergency requiring close monitoring). Continuous CIWA-Ar scoring every 2-4 hours.
EXCLUDE CONCURRENT MEDICAL EMERGENCIES: Head CT if confusion or focal neurology (subdural haematoma common in alcoholics), CXR (aspiration pneumonia), septic screen if febrile

ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE TREATMENT PLANNING: Once medically stable, offer: Naltrexone 50mg daily PO (PBS 2484W - reduces craving, blocks opioid reward from alcohol) OR Acamprosate 666mg TDS PO (PBS 8270K - modulates glutamate, reduces withdrawal symptoms), referral to community alcohol and drug service, Alcoholics Anonymous, psychosocial support (daughter involvement with consent)
PSYCHIATRIC REVIEW: Liaison psychiatry review within 24-48 hours for: Co-morbid depression/anxiety assessment, motivational interviewing, relapse prevention planning, address hopelessness
FOLLOW-UP: GP appointment within 1 week post-discharge with alcohol health worker, ongoing community detox support, consider residential rehabilitation if multiple failed community attempts
AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety), National Alcohol and Drug Hotline 1800 250 015
DOCUMENTATION: Detailed alcohol history, CIWA-Ar scores, benzodiazepine doses, vital signs trends, capacity assessment (likely has capacity if oriented and understands treatment)

marking_criteria.criterion: Establishes timeline of alcohol use and last drink (quantity, duration, time since last drink)
Screens for withdrawal symptoms systematically (tremor, sweating, hallucinations, seizures, confusion)
Asks about previous withdrawal complications (seizures, delirium tremens)
Assesses nutritional status and ability to maintain hydration
Screens for concurrent substance use and psychiatric comorbidity including suicidal ideation
Performs systematic mental state examination including cognition (orientation, confusion) and perceptual disturbances
Correctly identifies moderate-severe withdrawal severity and high risk for progression to delirium tremens
Recommends benzodiazepine loading protocol with specific medication and dose (e.g., Diazepam 20mg dosing regimen)
Orders thiamine 300mg IV BEFORE glucose (Wernicke's prophylaxis) and ongoing replacement
Recommends medical ward admission (not psychiatric ward) with monitoring for complications
Discusses long-term relapse prevention (Naltrexone or Acamprosate with PBS codes, community alcohol service)
Provides Australian crisis contacts (Lifeline, National Alcohol Hotline) and follow-up plan
Demonstrates empathy, non-judgmental approach, and acknowledges patient's motivation to change

learning_points: Alcohol withdrawal is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY - severe cases (DTs) have 5-15% mortality if untreated, <1% with appropriate management
CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol revised) score guides benzodiazepine dosing: <10 mild, 10-15 moderate, >15 severe withdrawal
Benzodiazepine loading regimen prevents seizures and delirium tremens - Diazepam 20mg every 2 hours until CIWA-Ar <10, typical total 60-120mg over 6-12 hours

ALWAYS give thiamine 300mg IV TDS for 3-5 days BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) - can progress to irreversible Korsakoff's syndrome (anterograde amnesia, confabulation)
Delirium tremens peak risk 72-96 hours post-cessation: confusion, severe agitation, fever, autonomic instability - requires ICU admission and high-dose benzodiazepines
Previous withdrawal seizure is major risk factor for recurrence - benzodiazepines are first-line prophylaxis (NOT phenytoin - ineffective for alcohol withdrawal seizures)

Alcohol withdrawal seizures are typically generalized tonic-clonic, occur 6-48 hours after cessation, self-limited - if prolonged or recurrent consider other causes (trauma, infection, structural brain lesion)

Long-term relapse prevention: Naltrexone 50mg daily PO (PBS 2484W) reduces craving by blocking opioid reward pathway, OR Acamprosate 666mg TDS PO (PBS 8270K) modulates glutamate to reduce protracted withdrawal symptoms

Concurrent medical issues common in chronic alcohol use: liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis), pancreatitis, gastritis, subdural haematoma (check for head trauma/confusion), aspiration pneumonia, alcoholic cardiomyopathy
Psychosocial support essential: Alcoholics Anonymous (12-step program), community alcohol and drug services, residential rehabilitation for severe dependence, family therapy, relapse prevention CBT

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG): Diazepam preferred for alcohol withdrawal (long half-life, less risk of rebound), alternatives include Oxazepam (shorter-acting, safer in liver disease) or Lorazepam (parenteral option)
National Alcohol and Drug Hotline 1800 250 015 provides 24/7 confidential information and referral for people concerned about alcohol or drug use
references: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Management of Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Withdrawal
Australian Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - Alcohol withdrawal management
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) - Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol
NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines - Alcohol
CIWA-Ar Protocol (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol revised)
Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) - Naltrexone (2484W), Acamprosate (8270K)
Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) - Approved indications for alcohol dependence pharmacotherapy

title: Acute Panic Disorder with Agoraphobia - Emergency Department Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital in Sydney. A 28-year-old primary school teacher, Sarah Chen, has been brought in by ambulance after experiencing a severe episode at a shopping centre. The paramedics report she was found sitting on the floor hyperventilating, clutching her chest, and saying 'I'm dying, I can't breathe'. Vital signs on arrival: HR 118, BP 145/92, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8°C. ECG performed by paramedics showed sinus tachycardia with no acute changes. She has now been in the department for 20 minutes and her physical symptoms have improved slightly. Your task is to take a focused psychiatric history, assess for panic disorder and any suicide risk, and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this consultation.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Chen, a 28-year-old primary school teacher who lives alone in an apartment in Newtown, Sydney. You've been working at the same school for 4 years and generally enjoy your job, though you find it stressful. You're single, with a close relationship to your parents who live in Chatswood. Six months ago, you experienced your first panic attack while driving across the Harbour Bridge - you thought you was having a heart attack and pulled over, calling an ambulance. Since then, you've had 8-10 similar episodes, each lasting 10-20 minutes. Today's episode happened at Westfield shopping centre during lunch break - you suddenly felt your heart racing, couldn't catch your breath, felt dizzy and had tingling in your hands and feet. You were terrified you were dying. You've started avoiding driving across bridges, going to crowded shopping centres, and using public transport. Last week you called in sick to work twice because you were too anxious to leave your apartment. You haven't seen a GP about this because you're embarrassed and worried they'll think you're 'crazy'. You've been drinking 2-3 glasses of wine most nights to calm your nerves. You deny any suicidal thoughts - you're scared of what's happening but want help. You haven't had any previous mental health problems. Your mother has a history of anxiety and takes 'some medication' for it. When the doctor enters, you appear anxious, sitting upright in bed, making intermittent eye contact. You're cooperative but tearful when discussing how this is affecting your life. If asked specifically about physical symptoms during episodes, describe: pounding heart, chest tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness, tingling in hands and feet, sweating, feeling like you're going to die or lose control. If asked about between-episode anxiety, admit you now have constant worry about having another attack, especially in places where escape might be difficult.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you describe what happened today at the shopping centre? (Expected: Sudden onset pounding heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, thought she was dying)

PANIC SYMPTOMS: During these episodes, what physical symptoms do you experience? (Expected: Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, sweating, trembling, tingling in extremities, feeling of impending doom)
TIMELINE: When did you first experience an episode like this? (Expected: 6 months ago while driving across Harbour Bridge)
FREQUENCY: How often do these episodes occur? (Expected: 8-10 episodes over 6 months, increasing in frequency)
DURATION: How long do they typically last? (Expected: 10-20 minutes, peak intensity within 10 minutes)
TRIGGERS: What situations seem to trigger these episodes? (Expected: Driving over bridges, crowded places like shopping centres, public transport)
AVOIDANCE BEHAVIOR: Has this changed what you do day-to-day? (Expected: Avoiding bridges, shopping centres, public transport; called in sick to work twice last week)
ANTICIPATORY ANXIETY: Between episodes, do you worry about having another attack? (Expected: Constant worry about next attack, especially in situations where escape is difficult)
IMPACT ON FUNCTIONING: How is this affecting your work and social life? (Expected: Missing work, avoiding social situations, difficulty leaving apartment)
MEDICAL ASSESSMENT: Have you seen a doctor about this before? Any medical conditions? (Expected: No previous consultation, embarrassed to seek help, no known cardiac or respiratory conditions)
SUBSTANCE USE: Have you used anything to cope with the anxiety? (Expected: Drinking 2-3 glasses wine nightly to calm nerves)
SUICIDE RISK: Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn't worth living? (Expected: No suicidal ideation, wants help but scared)
PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous mental health problems? (Expected: None)
FAMILY HISTORY: Any family history of anxiety or mental health problems? (Expected: Mother has anxiety disorder on medication)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Well-groomed 28-year-old woman appearing stated age, casually dressed, no self-care concerns
BEHAVIOR: Sitting upright in bed, fidgeting with hands, intermittent eye contact, cooperative with interview
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume initially, becomes slightly pressured when describing panic episodes
MOOD: Subjective - 'Terrified', 'exhausted', 'I just want this to stop'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, tearful at times, congruent with mood, reactive during interview
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and goal-directed, no flight of ideas or loosening of associations
THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with fear of having another panic attack, catastrophic thinking about dying or losing control during episodes, no suicidal ideation, no homicidal ideation, no delusions
PERCEPTIONS: No hallucinations, no illusions
COGNITION: Alert and oriented to person, place, time. Concentration reduced due to anxiety but able to complete interview. No memory impairment noted
INSIGHT: Partial insight - recognizes something is wrong and wants help, but limited understanding that this is anxiety disorder rather than cardiac problem
JUDGMENT: Fair - presented to ED appropriately, willing to engage with treatment
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK - No suicidal ideation, no self-harm history, no plan or intent, good protective factors (employment, family support, wants help). No immediate safety concerns requiring Mental Health Act consideration

REASSURANCE: Provide psychoeducation - explain panic attacks are not dangerous, will not cause heart attack or death, symptoms peak at 10 minutes then resolve. Validate her distress while normalizing the experience

RULE OUT MEDICAL CAUSES: Review ECG (sinus tachycardia, no ischemic changes), vital signs now normalizing, no cardiac risk factors. Consider thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) to exclude hyperthyroidism as outpatient investigation

DIAGNOSIS: Panic Disorder with Agoraphobia (DSM-5 criteria met: recurrent unexpected panic attacks, persistent concern about additional attacks, significant maladaptive change in behavior, avoidance of situations)

BREATHING RETRAINING: Teach diaphragmatic breathing technique now - 'Breathe in through nose for 4 counts, hold for 4, out through mouth for 6 counts'. Practice together. Explain hyperventilation perpetuates panic symptoms
ACUTE MANAGEMENT: No benzodiazepines in ED (avoid dependence risk). Symptoms have already improved with reassurance and supportive environment

MEDICATION PLAN: Commence Sertraline 25mg mane for 1 week, then increase to 50mg mane (starting dose for panic disorder lower than depression), PBS Authority Required 8222K. Warn about 2-4 week delay before effectiveness, possible initial increased anxiety in first week

ALCOHOL ADVICE: Advise cessation of alcohol use as coping mechanism - alcohol withdrawal can worsen anxiety, interferes with SSRI effectiveness. Current use (2-3 standard drinks nightly) below dependence threshold

PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPY REFERRAL: Refer to clinical psychologist for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) - gold standard treatment for panic disorder. CBT addresses catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and graded exposure to feared situations. Provide Medicare Mental Health Care Plan (up to 10 sessions per year)
SAFETY PLAN: Although no suicide risk, provide crisis contacts - Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (anxiety/depression support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263
OCCUPATIONAL ADVICE: Medical certificate for 3 days off work to commence treatment and attend urgent GP follow-up. Advise employer notification optional, can use 'medical reasons' without disclosure

GP FOLLOW-UP: Arrange urgent GP appointment within 3-5 days to review medication tolerance, provide Mental Health Care Plan, monitor response. Review again at 2 weeks, then 4 weeks. Continue follow-up monthly until stable
SICK LEAVE: Provide medical certificate for 3 days

DRIVING SAFETY: Advise not to drive during acute panic episodes. If panic starts while driving, pull over safely and practice breathing exercises. Discuss with GP whether driving restrictions needed during treatment initiation
WRITTEN INFORMATION: Provide Beyond Blue panic disorder fact sheet, SANE Australia resources on panic disorder management

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, explains role and purpose of consultation
Asks open question about presenting episode (What happened today? Describe the episode)

Systematically assesses panic attack symptoms - asks about at least 5 of: palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying
Establishes timeline (first episode, frequency, duration of episodes)
Identifies avoidance behaviors and agoraphobia (avoids bridges, crowded places, public transport, leaving apartment)
Asks about anticipatory anxiety (worry between episodes about having another attack)
Assesses functional impairment (impact on work, social life, daily activities)
Screens for suicide risk using direct questions (thoughts of self-harm, suicide ideation, plan, intent)
Asks about substance use including alcohol as coping mechanism
Asks about past psychiatric history and family history of anxiety/mental illness
Provides psychoeducation - explains panic attacks are not dangerous, symptoms are anxiety not cardiac emergency, reassures patient
Demonstrates breathing retraining technique (diaphragmatic breathing) and practices with patient
Recommends SSRI (Sertraline 25mg increasing to 50mg, or equivalent) with explanation of delayed onset and potential initial increased anxiety
Refers for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) - mentions Medicare Mental Health Care Plan or psychologist referral
Advises against alcohol use as coping mechanism, explains alcohol worsens anxiety
Arranges GP follow-up within 1 week and provides medical certificate for work
Provides crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636) even though low suicide risk
Demonstrates empathy, validates patient distress, uses appropriate body language and tone

learning_points: Panic disorder diagnosis requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern about additional attacks OR maladaptive behavioral change (avoidance). Agoraphobia involves fear/avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult

DSM-5 panic attack criteria: Abrupt surge of intense fear/discomfort reaching peak within 10 minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying)

ALWAYS rule out medical causes before diagnosing panic disorder: Hyperthyroidism (check TSH), cardiac arrhythmia (ECG), pheochromocytoma (rare), caffeine/substance intoxication, medication side effects (bronchodilators, steroids)

First-line treatment is combination of SSRI + CBT. Sertraline or Escitalopram preferred (PBS 8222K Authority Required for panic disorder indication). Start low dose (Sertraline 25mg) due to potential initial increased anxiety, increase after 1 week

CBT for panic disorder targets catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and includes: psychoeducation, breathing retraining, cognitive restructuring, interoceptive exposure (inducing panic sensations in safe environment), graded exposure to feared situations

AVOID benzodiazepines as first-line treatment despite rapid symptom relief - high dependence risk, rebound anxiety, interfere with CBT exposure work. Consider only for short-term use (2-4 weeks maximum) in severe cases while waiting for SSRI effect

Breathing retraining technique: Diaphragmatic breathing (4 counts in through nose, hold 4, 6 counts out through mouth) reduces hyperventilation which perpetuates panic symptoms through respiratory alkalosis

Alcohol commonly used as self-medication for anxiety but worsens panic disorder - alcohol withdrawal increases anxiety, interferes with SSRI effectiveness, risk of dependence. Screen all patients with AUDIT-C

Safety planning even for low suicide risk: Provide crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, SANE 1800 187 263), arrange close follow-up within 3-5 days, medical certificate to reduce acute stressors

Medicare Mental Health Care Plan allows GP referral for up to 10 subsidized psychology sessions per calendar year (6 initially, then review for additional 4). Essential for CBT access which is gold standard psychological treatment

title: Acute Anxiety and Panic Disorder - Emergency Department Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior medical officer working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 28-year-old female primary school teacher has presented via ambulance at 2:30am. The paramedics report she called 000 saying she was having a heart attack. On arrival, she had a heart rate of 132bpm, respiratory rate of 28/min, and was hyperventilating. Oxygen saturations were 99% on room air. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Troponin was negative. The ED consultant has reviewed her and ruled out acute coronary syndrome. Your task is to take a focused psychiatric history to assess whether this presentation represents a panic attack, evaluate for underlying anxiety disorder, screen for depression and suicide risk, and formulate an immediate management plan. You have 8 minutes for this consultation.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Chen, a 28-year-old primary school teacher. You live alone in an apartment in inner Sydney after breaking up with your partner of 4 years, 6 months ago. Tonight at 2am you woke suddenly with your heart pounding out of your chest, struggling to breathe, sweating profusely, and convinced you were having a heart attack and about to die. You called 000 immediately. This is the third time this has happened in the past 2 months - the first was 8 weeks ago at work during lunchtime, the second was 3 weeks ago while grocery shopping. Each time lasts about 15-20 minutes and you feel absolutely terrified during the episode. Between attacks, you constantly worry about having another one, especially in public places or at work. You've started avoiding the staff room at lunch and have been making excuses to avoid social gatherings. You haven't told anyone about these episodes because you're embarrassed. Your sleep has been poor for the past 3 months - you lie awake worrying about work, your breakup, and now these episodes. You've lost 4kg because your appetite is poor. You feel constantly on edge and tense. You don't have suicidal thoughts but sometimes think 'I can't keep living like this'. You don't use alcohol or drugs. Your mother has anxiety and takes medication for it. You haven't seen a GP about this yet. When the doctor enters, you appear anxious, sitting forward in the bed, still breathing slightly fast, looking around nervously. You make poor eye contact. If asked specific questions: You've never had these episodes before 2 months ago. During episodes you experience pounding heart, chest tightness, difficulty breathing (feel like you're suffocating), sweating, trembling hands, dizziness, numbness in your fingers, and overwhelming fear of dying. You don't have any medical conditions, don't take regular medications, and have no family history of heart disease. You drink 2 glasses of wine on weekends only. You drink 3-4 coffees daily (increased recently to cope with fatigue). No illicit drugs. You're worried about losing your job if you keep having these episodes at work.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you describe what happened tonight that brought you to hospital? (Expected: Sudden onset at 2am, pounding heart, couldn't breathe, thought having heart attack, overwhelming fear of dying, lasted 15-20 minutes)

TIMELINE: Have you had similar episodes before? When was the first time? How many total? (Expected: Three episodes total over 8 weeks - first at work during lunch, second while shopping, third tonight at home)

PANIC SYMPTOMS: During these episodes, what physical symptoms do you experience? (Expected: Palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, sweating, trembling, dizziness, paraesthesia in fingers, fear of dying - meets DSM-5 criteria for panic attack: ≥4 symptoms with abrupt onset)
ANTICIPATORY ANXIETY: Between episodes, do you worry about having another attack? (Expected: Yes, constant worry about next attack, especially in public or at work)
AVOIDANCE BEHAVIORS: Have these episodes changed your daily activities or social life? (Expected: Avoiding staff room at lunch, declining social invitations, worried about work performance)

TRIGGERS: Do these episodes happen in specific situations or come out of the blue? (Expected: Unexpected panic attacks - no clear situational trigger, first at work, second shopping, third at home sleeping)

ANXIETY SYMPTOMS: Apart from these episodes, how is your general anxiety level? Sleep? Appetite? (Expected: Constantly on edge for 3 months, poor sleep with rumination, 4kg weight loss from reduced appetite, increased muscle tension)

DEPRESSION SCREENING: How is your mood? Energy? Enjoyment of activities? Concentration? (Expected: Low mood associated with anxiety and breakup, fatigue from poor sleep, reduced social engagement, concentration affected by worry)

SUICIDE RISK (SAFE-T): Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life? (Expected: No active suicidal ideation, but feels overwhelmed 'can't keep living like this' - passive expression of distress, no plan, no intent)
SUBSTANCE USE: Alcohol? Caffeine? Illicit drugs? (Expected: 2 glasses wine weekends only, 3-4 coffees daily recently increased, no illicit drugs - caffeine may be exacerbating anxiety)

PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous mental health diagnoses or treatment? Family history? (Expected: No previous psychiatric treatment, mother has anxiety disorder on medication - significant family history)

MEDICAL SCREENING: Any medical conditions? Thyroid problems? Cardiac history? Current medications? (Expected: No medical conditions, no medications, no cardiac family history - important to exclude thyroid disease, cardiac arrhythmia, hypoglycemia as differential diagnoses)

PSYCHOSOCIAL STRESSORS: What's been happening in your life recently? Work? Relationships? (Expected: Relationship breakdown 6 months ago after 4-year relationship, living alone, work stress as teacher, worried about job performance)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Casually dressed in pajamas and jacket, appropriate for 2am ED presentation. Fair grooming and self-care maintained.

BEHAVIOR: Anxious and restless, sitting forward on bed edge. Fidgeting with hands. Poor eye contact, frequently looking around room. Cooperative with interview. Mildly hyperventilating at start of assessment (respiratory rate 22/min, settling to 16/min during consultation).
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume initially, becomes slightly pressured when describing panic episodes. Normal tone and articulation.
MOOD: Subjectively reports 'anxious' and 'scared'. States 'I feel like I'm going crazy' when describing episodes.
AFFECT: Objectively anxious and tense throughout. Congruent with mood. Reactive - becomes tearful when discussing impact on work and social life. Appropriate range.
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and goal-directed. No formal thought disorder. Some circumstantial detail when describing episodes but returns to point.

THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with worry about having future panic attacks. Health anxiety focused on cardiac concerns despite reassurance. No delusions. No suicidal ideation - denies active thoughts of self-harm, no plan, no intent. Passive expression of distress ('can't keep living like this') in context of feeling overwhelmed. Protective factors: employment, concern about students, wants help.
PERCEPTIONS: No hallucinations. No depersonalization or derealization reported during or between panic episodes (important to assess as can occur in panic disorder).
COGNITION: Alert and oriented to time, place, person. Attention and concentration mildly impaired by anxiety during interview. No memory deficits noted.

INSIGHT: Partial insight. Recognizes symptoms are distressing and seeking help, but limited understanding that episodes are panic attacks rather than cardiac events. Open to psychiatric explanation and treatment.
JUDGMENT: Intact. Appropriate help-seeking behavior (called 000 during acute episode, engaging with psychiatric assessment now).

RISK ASSESSMENT: SAFE-T LOW RISK. S-No specific plan for self-harm. A-No access to lethal means. F-Feels overwhelmed and distressed but no hopelessness or worthlessness. E-No previous suicide attempts. T-No threat of self-harm expressed. Protective factors: employment as teacher, responsibility to students, wants treatment, engaged with assessment.
immediate_management: SAFE-T SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK. Passive expression of distress ('can't keep living like this') but no suicidal ideation, no plan, no intent, no previous attempts. Protective factors: employment, responsibility to students, appropriate help-seeking, engaged with treatment. No immediate safety plan required but provide crisis contacts as routine psychiatric care.

DIAGNOSIS: Panic Disorder (DSM-5 300.01) - recurrent unexpected panic attacks (≥2) with ≥1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks and maladaptive change in behavior (avoidance). Generalized Anxiety Disorder (DSM-5 300.02) likely co-morbid - excessive worry for 3 months, sleep disturbance, restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty.

PSYCHOEDUCATION: Explain panic disorder diagnosis. Panic attacks are not dangerous despite frightening physical symptoms. Symptoms caused by acute autonomic nervous system activation (fight-or-flight response) not cardiac pathology. Reassure ECG and troponin normal. Explain panic disorder is common (3% lifetime prevalence) and highly treatable. Normalize experience and reduce catastrophic misinterpretation of symptoms.

IMMEDIATE ANXIETY MANAGEMENT: Teach slow breathing technique (breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 6) to manage hyperventilation during panic attacks. Explain hyperventilation causes tingling and dizziness, which perpetuates panic cycle. Practice breathing technique now while patient still mildly anxious. Advise against breath-holding or breathing into paper bag (outdated advice).

CAFFEINE REDUCTION: Advise immediate reduction in caffeine intake from 3-4 coffees daily to maximum 1-2. Caffeine increases baseline anxiety and can trigger panic attacks. Suggest gradual reduction over 1 week to avoid withdrawal headaches. Switch to decaffeinated or herbal tea.

ACUTE MEDICATION: Consider short-term benzodiazepine for immediate anxiety relief. Diazepam 2-5mg PO as needed for severe panic attacks, maximum 3 times weekly to avoid dependence. Supply 5 tablets only. Counsel regarding driving restrictions after use (4-6 hours) and avoid alcohol. Alternative: Propranolol 10mg PO PRN for physical symptoms (palpitations, tremor) - non-addictive option. Benzodiazepines NOT long-term solution.

LONG-TERM MEDICATION: Initiate SSRI as first-line treatment for panic disorder. Sertraline 25mg mane (half tablet of 50mg), increase to 50mg after 1 week, then 100mg at week 4 if tolerated and insufficient response. PBS Authority Required code 1366 for panic disorder indication. Warn may temporarily increase anxiety in first 1-2 weeks before therapeutic effect at 4-6 weeks. Continue for minimum 12 months after symptom remission to prevent relapse. Alternative SSRIs: Escitalopram 5-10mg daily (PBS 2049P) or Paroxetine 20mg daily (PBS 8032K).

PSYCHOLOGICAL REFERRAL: Refer for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with clinical psychologist under Better Access Mental Health Care Plan (up to 10 Medicare-rebated sessions per year with GP referral). CBT is first-line evidence-based treatment for panic disorder. Targets catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and avoidance behaviors. Exposure therapy for avoided situations. CBT equally effective as medication, more durable effect, preferred by many patients.

GP FOLLOW-UP: Discharge with urgent GP appointment within 3-5 days. GP to complete Mental Health Treatment Plan for Better Access CBT referral, monitor SSRI response and side effects, and provide ongoing support. Provide written ED summary documenting panic disorder diagnosis, medication initiated, and management plan.
SAFETY NETTING: Advise to return to ED if panic symptoms worsen, develop suicidal thoughts, or unable to cope at home. Provide written crisis contacts.

AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support and suicide prevention). Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression and anxiety support, 24/7). Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467 (24/7 telephone and online counseling). SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support, 10am-10pm weekdays).

WORK CONSIDERATIONS: Advise taking 3-5 days off work initially to commence treatment and reduce acute anxiety. Medical certificate provided. Discuss with GP whether workplace adjustments needed (e.g., reduced hours initially). Reassure panic disorder does not mean she cannot continue teaching - highly treatable condition.

LIFESTYLE ADVICE: Regular exercise (30 minutes moderate intensity 5 times weekly) reduces baseline anxiety. Sleep hygiene (consistent bed/wake times, avoid screens 1 hour before bed, relaxation routine). Limit alcohol as can worsen anxiety rebound. Consider mindfulness or meditation apps (Smiling Mind free Australian app). Gradual return to avoided situations rather than continued avoidance.

REVIEW TIMELINE: GP review at 3-5 days, then weekly for first month to monitor treatment response. Psychologist initial appointment within 2-3 weeks. ED follow-up not required unless acute deterioration. Expected improvement in panic frequency and severity within 6-8 weeks of combined SSRI and CBT treatment.

DOCUMENTATION: Document panic disorder diagnosis, SAFE-T low risk assessment, medical differentials excluded (ECG, troponin normal), medication initiated, referrals arranged, and crisis contacts provided. Notify GP via discharge summary.

Assesses psychosocial stressors (relationship breakdown, work stress, living situation) as precipitating/perpetuating factors

Provides diagnosis of panic disorder with clear explanation in lay terms (not dangerous, treatable, autonomic activation)
