Refers for CBT as first-line psychological treatment via GP Mental Health Treatment Plan
Arranges urgent GP follow-up (3-5 days) for Mental Health Treatment Plan, medication monitoring, and ongoing care coordination
Provides written Australian crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636) as routine psychiatric care
Addresses work concerns with medical certificate and reassurance about prognosis with treatment
Demonstrates empathy, validates patient's distress, maintains appropriate eye contact and professional manner throughout

learning_points: DSM-5 PANIC DISORDER CRITERIA: (A) Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (abrupt surge of fear with ≥4 symptoms peaking within minutes); (B) ≥1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks OR maladaptive change in behavior (avoidance); (C) Not attributable to substance or medical condition

PANIC ATTACK SYMPTOMS (≥4 REQUIRED): Palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat sensations, paraesthesia, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying. Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis leading to paraesthesia and dizziness, perpetuating panic cycle.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS - MEDICAL CAUSES MUST BE EXCLUDED: Cardiac (arrhythmias, acute coronary syndrome, mitral valve prolapse), respiratory (asthma, PE), endocrine (hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma), neurological (seizures, TIA), substance-induced (caffeine, cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis), medication-induced (bronchodilators, steroids, thyroxine), withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines)

CAFFEINE AND PANIC: Caffeine intake >400mg daily (approximately 4 cups coffee) significantly increases baseline anxiety and panic attack frequency. Caffeine stimulates sympathetic nervous system, mimicking panic symptoms. Recommend reduction to ≤200mg daily (1-2 cups). Gradual taper over 1 week to avoid withdrawal headaches.

FIRST-LINE TREATMENT SSRI: Sertraline, Escitalopram, or Paroxetine. Start low dose (Sertraline 25mg, Escitalopram 5mg) as initial anxiety increase common in first 1-2 weeks. Therapeutic effect at 4-6 weeks. Continue 12 months after remission before considering tapering (relapse rate 30% if stopped early). PBS Authority Required for panic disorder indication.

COGNITIVE BEHAVIORAL THERAPY (CBT) FOR PANIC: First-line evidence-based psychological treatment. Targets: (1) Catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations (palpitations = heart attack); (2) Avoidance behaviors maintaining disorder; (3) Interoceptive exposure (deliberately inducing physical sensations to reduce fear); (4) In vivo exposure (gradual return to avoided situations). CBT equally effective as SSRIs, more durable effect, prevents relapse after discontinuation.

BENZODIAZEPINES - SHORT-TERM ONLY: Effective for immediate anxiety relief but high dependence risk. Reserve for PRN use (maximum 2-3 times weekly) during initial 2-4 weeks until SSRI therapeutic. Diazepam 2-5mg or Alprazolam 0.25-0.5mg. Counsel re: sedation, driving restrictions, alcohol interaction. Avoid long-term use (>4 weeks) due to tolerance, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and cognitive impairment. Consider propranolol 10-20mg PRN as non-addictive alternative for physical symptoms.

BETTER ACCESS MENTAL HEALTH CARE PLAN: GP completes Mental Health Treatment Plan enabling Medicare rebate for up to 10 psychology sessions per calendar year (6 initially, then review for additional 4). Patients pay gap after rebate (approximately 50-80 dollars per session depending on psychologist). Essential for accessing evidence-based CBT in Australian primary care setting.

AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS (ROUTINE PSYCHIATRIC CARE): Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support and suicide prevention), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety support 24/7), Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467 (24/7 counseling), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support 10am-10pm weekdays). Provide written handout to all psychiatric patients regardless of risk level.

PANIC DISORDER PROGNOSIS: 70-80% respond to combined SSRI and CBT within 12 weeks. Without treatment, panic disorder often becomes chronic with 50% developing agoraphobia (avoidance of situations where escape difficult). Co-morbidities common: 50-65% develop depression, 30% develop alcohol use disorder (self-medication). Early treatment prevents chronicity and disability.

HYPERVENTILATION MANAGEMENT: Teach slow breathing (4-count in, 4-count hold, 6-count out) to restore CO2 levels and terminate panic cycle. Practice during consultation while patient still mildly anxious to build confidence. Advise AGAINST breathing into paper bag (outdated, potentially dangerous if hypoxic cause). Reassure that despite frightening sensation of suffocation, oxygen saturations remain normal during panic attacks.

title: Acute Psychotic Episode - First Episode Schizophrenia Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. Marcus, a 22-year-old university student, has been brought in by his flatmates who are concerned about his increasingly bizarre behaviour over the past 3 weeks. He believes his lecturers are monitoring his thoughts through the university Wi-Fi and that his assignments are being altered by external forces. He has stopped attending classes, showering, and eating regularly. His flatmates found him talking to voices and barricading his room door. Take a focused psychiatric history, perform a mental state examination, assess risk, and formulate an immediate management plan.
patient_role_instructions: You are Marcus, a 22-year-old second-year engineering student at UNSW. You are experiencing your first psychotic episode. You are suspicious and guarded but not overtly aggressive. You genuinely believe your lecturers are using the university Wi-Fi to read your thoughts and that someone is changing your assignment files on your computer. You hear two distinct male voices commenting on your actions and occasionally giving you commands to stay in your room for safety. You feel scared and confused but deny wanting to hurt yourself or others. You have no insight into your condition and believe everything you're experiencing is real. You may become agitated if the interviewer dismisses your concerns as 'not real'. You've been using cannabis weekly for the past year but deny other substance use. No significant past medical or psychiatric history. Your father has depression but you're unsure about other family mental health issues.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's ability to establish rapport with a psychotic patient, conduct a systematic psychiatric assessment, and demonstrate appropriate risk assessment skills. Pay attention to their approach to delusions and hallucinations - they should neither agree with nor directly challenge the patient's beliefs. Look for evidence of a structured mental state examination, comprehensive risk assessment including SAFE-T protocol, and appropriate immediate management planning. The candidate should recognise this as a likely first episode psychosis requiring urgent psychiatric assessment and consider Mental Health Act criteria.

sample_answer.history_summary: 22-year-old male university student presenting with 3-week history of persecutory delusions (lecturers monitoring thoughts via Wi-Fi, assignments being altered), auditory hallucinations (two male voices commenting and commanding), social withdrawal, poor self-care, and functional decline. No previous psychiatric history. Regular cannabis use (weekly for 1 year). Father with depression. Brought by concerned flatmates due to bizarre behaviour and social isolation.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: Dishevelled, poor hygiene, suspicious eye contact. Behaviour: Guarded, hypervigilant, minimal psychomotor agitation. Speech: Normal rate and volume, circumstantial. Mood: Anxious and scared, affect congruent but restricted. Thought: Persecutory and referential delusions, no formal thought disorder evident. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (running commentary and commands). Cognition: Alert and oriented, concentration impaired. Insight: No insight into illness, attributes experiences to external persecution.
sample_answer.diagnosis: First Episode Psychosis, likely Schizophreniform Disorder (F20.81) - duration <6 months

safe_t_assessment.specific_plan: Denies suicidal ideation or specific plan

management.immediate: Urgent psychiatry consultation, consider Mental Health Act assessment, ensure safe environment, remove potential risks, engage family/friends for collateral history
management.medications: Consider low-dose antipsychotic: Olanzapine 2.5-5mg daily (PBS 8386T) or Risperidone 1-2mg daily (PBS 8256K) after medical clearance
management.therapy: Crisis intervention, psychoeducation for patient and family, consider early psychosis intervention service referral
management.follow_up: Urgent psychiatry review within 24-48 hours, GP follow-up within 3-5 days, case management through early psychosis service
management.crisis_contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, NSW Mental Health Line 1800 011 511

learning_points: SAFE-T protocol essential for all psychiatric assessments - specific plan, access, feelings, earlier attempts, threat level
First episode psychosis requires urgent assessment and early intervention - better long-term outcomes with prompt treatment
Cannabis use is a significant risk factor for psychotic disorders, particularly in young males with family history
Never agree with or directly challenge delusions - use neutral responses like 'that sounds distressing'
Mental Health Act assessment required when patient lacks insight and refuses voluntary treatment
Early psychosis intervention services provide specialised care for first episodes with better outcomes
Collateral history from family/friends crucial in psychotic presentations for timeline and functional assessment

title: Acute Psychosis with Command Hallucinations - Risk Assessment and Mental Health Act Application
topics: Mental Health Act NSW 2007 - Involuntary Admission
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working a Friday evening shift in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 28-year-old unemployed man, Daniel Chen, has been brought in by police under Section 19 (Emergency) of the Mental Health Act NSW 2007 after neighbours reported him yelling threats and throwing furniture off his 4th floor apartment balcony. Police noted he was responding to internal stimuli and appeared paranoid. His girlfriend Sarah contacted police stating Daniel has not slept for 5 days, stopped taking his medication 3 weeks ago, and believes the government is tracking him through microchips. Daniel has no physical injuries and vital signs are stable (BP 138/82, HR 98, RR 18, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 98% on room air). The psychiatric registrar is in theatre and will arrive in 45 minutes. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination, assess immediate risk to self and others, and formulate an initial management plan. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 28-year-old man who until 3 months ago worked as a software developer. You were diagnosed with schizophrenia 2 years ago but stopped taking your Olanzapine 10mg 3 weeks ago because you believe your psychiatrist is part of a government conspiracy to control your mind through medication. For the past 10 days, you have been hearing multiple male voices coming from outside your head, commenting on your actions ('He's going to the kitchen now', 'He's picking up the phone') and telling you that your neighbours are government agents monitoring you. Over the past 5 days, the voices have become command hallucinations telling you to 'Destroy the surveillance equipment' (which you believe is hidden in your furniture) and 'Eliminate the agents before they eliminate you'. You have not slept for 5 days because you need to 'stay vigilant'. You threw furniture off your balcony because the voices told you it contained tracking devices. You believe you have special powers to detect surveillance technology through electromagnetic signals you can feel in your body. You are frightened, agitated, and suspicious of everyone including the doctor. You make poor eye contact, speak rapidly in a pressured manner, and frequently look around the room as if listening to voices. When asked directly about the voices, you initially deny them ('Why should I tell you? You're probably one of them'), but if the doctor builds rapport and uses non-threatening questions, you may disclose that voices are currently telling you 'Don't trust the doctor - he wants to poison you'. You deny suicidal ideation but admit the voices sometimes tell you to hurt people who are 'part of the conspiracy'. You have no insight into your illness - you believe your experiences are real and you do not think you need treatment. You have no history of violence but grabbed your girlfriend's arm forcefully yesterday when she tried to give you medication, leaving bruises. You have been smoking cannabis daily for the past month to 'calm the voices' but it has made them worse. Your opening statement when the doctor enters is: 'Why am I here? I haven't done anything wrong. Those agents next door called the police on me. Can you feel it? The electromagnetic waves? They're everywhere in this hospital.'

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: 'Can you tell me what happened today that brought you here?' (Expected: Police brought me, threw furniture because it had tracking devices, neighbours are government agents)

PSYCHOTIC SYMPTOMS - Hallucinations: 'Have you been hearing or seeing things others can't?' (Expected: Multiple male voices commenting and giving commands for 10 days, voices outside head, worse over past 5 days)

PSYCHOTIC SYMPTOMS - Delusions: 'Can you tell me about your concerns regarding government surveillance?' (Expected: Paranoid delusions about government tracking through microchips, neighbours are agents, furniture contains devices, has special powers to detect electromagnetic signals)
COMMAND HALLUCINATIONS: 'What do these voices tell you to do?' (Expected: Commands to destroy surveillance equipment, eliminate agents, currently telling him not to trust doctor)
COMPLIANCE WITH TREATMENT: 'Tell me about your medication - are you taking anything?' (Expected: Stopped Olanzapine 10mg 3 weeks ago, believes psychiatrist is part of conspiracy)
SUBSTANCE USE: 'Have you used any alcohol or drugs recently?' (Expected: Cannabis daily for past month to calm voices but made them worse)

RISK TO OTHERS: 'Have you had thoughts about hurting anyone?' (Expected: Voices tell him to hurt people in conspiracy, grabbed girlfriend's arm yesterday leaving bruises, no history of violence but escalating aggression)

RISK TO SELF: 'Have you had thoughts about harming yourself or ending your life?' (Expected: Denies suicidal ideation but impaired judgment and risk-taking behaviour - threw furniture from 4th floor balcony)
FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT: 'How have you been sleeping and eating?' (Expected: No sleep for 5 days, poor oral intake)
PROTECTIVE FACTORS: 'Who supports you? Family, friends?' (Expected: Girlfriend Sarah, mother in Sydney, but relationships strained due to illness)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: 'When were you first diagnosed? Any hospital admissions?' (Expected: Schizophrenia diagnosed 2 years ago, previous admissions unclear but established diagnosis)
INSIGHT AND JUDGMENT: 'Do you think you are unwell? Do you need treatment?' (Expected: No insight - believes experiences are real, refuses treatment, believes medication is poison)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: 28-year-old Asian male, dishevelled appearance, poor self-care, unshaven, malodorous, wearing stained clothing, appears tired with dark circles under eyes
BEHAVIOUR: Highly agitated, restless, poor eye contact, frequently looking around room as if responding to internal stimuli, hypervigilant, guarded posture, psychomotor agitation with hand tremor
SPEECH: Pressured rate, increased volume, tangential at times, difficult to interrupt
MOOD (Subjective): 'Scared' or 'They're after me' - reports feeling frightened and paranoid
AFFECT (Objective): Anxious, suspicious, incongruent with content at times (laughs when describing serious threats), restricted range, labile
THOUGHT FORM: Tangential, circumstantial, mild loosening of associations, thought disorder present

THOUGHT CONTENT: Paranoid delusions (government surveillance, neighbours are agents, microchips, electromagnetic waves), grandiose delusions (special powers to detect technology), no suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation towards perceived 'agents' driven by command hallucinations

PERCEPTIONS: Auditory hallucinations - multiple male voices, third person running commentary and second person command hallucinations ('Destroy surveillance equipment', 'Eliminate the agents', 'Don't trust the doctor'), voices outside head, continuous for 10 days, no visual hallucinations

COGNITION: Alert, oriented to person, place, time but with delusional interpretation of environment (believes hospital is part of surveillance network), attention poor due to internal preoccupation, concentration impaired
INSIGHT: No insight - does not believe he is mentally ill, attributes experiences to real external threat, denies need for treatment
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - stopped medication, engaging in dangerous behaviour (throwing furniture from height), responding to command hallucinations, using cannabis despite worsening symptoms
immediate_management: RISK ASSESSMENT - VIOLENCE: HIGH RISK - Active command hallucinations to harm others ('Eliminate the agents'), paranoid delusions with persecutory themes, recent escalation to physical aggression (grabbed girlfriend causing bruises), poor impulse control, no sleep for 5 days (disinhibition), substance use (cannabis), no insight or engagement with treatment. Protective factors: No history of serious violence, no weapons access currently, girlfriend still supportive.

RISK ASSESSMENT - SELF-HARM: MODERATE RISK - No suicidal ideation but severely impaired judgment (threw furniture from 4th floor balcony), responding to command hallucinations, risk of accidental harm during agitated state or harm during altercation with perceived 'agents'.

SAFE ENVIRONMENT: Allocate to acute behavioural assessment unit or closely observed area in ED, remove potential weapons or ligature points, one-to-one nursing observation, security nearby, de-escalation strategies (calm environment, reduce stimulation, non-threatening approach)

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 - INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION: Meets criteria for involuntary admission under Section 27: (1) Mental illness present - acute psychotic episode with command hallucinations and paranoid delusions; (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others - command hallucinations to harm others, recent violence, dangerous behaviour; (3) Requires immediate inpatient treatment - medication non-compliance, deterioration off treatment; (4) No less restrictive alternative - no insight, refuses voluntary admission. Document in medical record and complete Mental Health Act forms. Consult psychiatry registrar on arrival for formal assessment.
PSYCHIATRIC CONSULTATION: Urgent psychiatric review by registrar on arrival (45 minutes) - inform registrar immediately of high risk presentation, request phone advice if needed sooner

MEDICATION - IMMEDIATE: Oral medication first-line if patient cooperative: Olanzapine 10mg PO (previous maintenance dose) or Risperidone 2mg PO. If oral medication refused and patient acutely agitated/dangerous: Consider IM sedation after discussion with psychiatry - Olanzapine 10mg IM (PBS 8031M) or Haloperidol 5mg IM + Midazolam 5mg IM (for acute behavioural disturbance only, use with caution).

MEDICATION - MAINTENANCE: Once stabilised, restart regular antipsychotic: Olanzapine 10mg nocte (patient's previous dose, PBS 8031M) or consider Risperidone 2mg BD if Olanzapine insufficient. Avoid Clozapine at this stage (requires haematological monitoring and registration).
SUBSTANCE USE SCREENING: Urine drug screen (cannabis, amphetamines, opioids) to confirm recent use and rule out other substances

MEDICAL CLEARANCE: Already completed (vital signs stable, no injuries) but monitor for complications of sleep deprivation and poor oral intake - IV fluids if dehydrated, thiamine supplementation if poor nutrition
SUPPORTIVE CARE: Encourage oral fluids and food, quiet environment, minimize stimulation, explain procedures calmly and clearly despite poor insight

COLLATERAL HISTORY: Contact girlfriend Sarah (with patient consent or under Mental Health Act if detained) - confirm timeline, medication compliance, previous presentations, baseline functioning, recent stressors, clarify incident where he grabbed her arm
SAFETY PLANNING FOR GIRLFRIEND: Assess Sarah's safety - provide domestic violence resources if needed, discuss safety plan if Daniel discharged (unlikely), ensure she has support

FOLLOW-UP PLAN: Admit to acute psychiatric inpatient unit under Mental Health Act, daily psychiatric review, medication titration, substance use counselling, psychoeducation for patient and family when acute symptoms resolve, involve community mental health team for discharge planning, ensure outpatient follow-up with psychiatrist within 1 week of discharge, consider long-acting injectable antipsychotic (e.g., Paliperidone palmitate monthly) to improve compliance post-discharge

CRISIS CONTACTS (Provide to girlfriend Sarah): Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) for domestic violence support, Mental Health Line NSW 1800 011 511

DOCUMENTATION: Detailed MSE in medical record, risk assessment documented (high risk violence, moderate risk self-harm with specific justification), Mental Health Act Section 27 criteria met and forms completed, collateral information from police and girlfriend documented, treatment plan with medications and monitoring requirements

learning_points: Command hallucinations require urgent risk assessment - ask explicitly 'What do the voices tell you to do?' and 'Do you feel you have to obey them?' High risk if commands are violent, patient has poor insight, and protective factors are absent.

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 Section 27 (Involuntary Admission) criteria: (1) Person has mental illness, (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) Requires immediate inpatient treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative available. Document all four criteria clearly in medical record.

Risk assessment in acute psychosis must consider: Content of hallucinations/delusions (persecutory themes increase violence risk), recent behaviour (escalation pattern), substance use (cannabis can worsen psychosis), sleep deprivation (impairs judgment and increases impulsivity), and insight/compliance (refusing treatment indicates higher risk).

First-line antipsychotics for acute psychosis: Olanzapine 5-10mg (PBS 8031M), Risperidone 1-2mg (PBS 2780E), Quetiapine 50-100mg (PBS 8543K). Restart at previous maintenance dose if known. Oral medication preferred; IM only if oral refused and patient acutely dangerous.
Cannabis use worsens psychotic symptoms and reduces antipsychotic efficacy - always screen for substance use in patients with schizophrenia presenting with relapse.

Collateral history is essential in psychosis - patients often lack insight and may minimise symptoms. Contact family/carers to confirm timeline, medication compliance, baseline functioning, and recent stressors.

De-escalation strategies for agitated psychotic patients: Calm tone, non-threatening body language (arms uncrossed, 45-degree angle, maintain personal space), validate emotions without agreeing with delusions ('I can see you're frightened' not 'Yes the government is after you'), reduce environmental stimulation, offer choices where possible, have security nearby but not visible.

Safety planning for family members/carers of patients with psychosis and violence risk - provide domestic violence resources (1800 RESPECT 1800 737 732), assess immediate safety, discuss warning signs of relapse, ensure they have crisis contacts.
Australian crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression/anxiety), Mental Health Line NSW 1800 011 511 (24/7 mental health emergency line)

Consider long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAI) for patients with recurrent non-compliance - Paliperidone palmitate (Invega Sustenna) 150mg IM monthly or Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) 400mg IM monthly reduce relapse rates compared to oral medication in schizophrenia.

title: Acute Psychosis with Paranoid Delusions - Mental State Examination and Risk Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 28-year-old male software engineer, Daniel Chen, has been brought in by police at 2am after his flatmate called emergency services. The flatmate reported that Daniel has been awake for 72 hours, barricaded himself in his bedroom, and has been heard shouting about surveillance cameras in the apartment. Daniel refuses to eat food prepared by his flatmate, claiming it is poisoned. Police noted he was hostile and suspicious on arrival but agreed to come to hospital. Your task is to conduct a focused mental state examination, assess immediate risk to self and others, and determine whether involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act NSW 2007 is required. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 28-year-old software engineer who lives in a shared apartment in Sydney. Three weeks ago, you started noticing that your computer webcam light was turning on by itself. You disconnected it, but then realized the surveillance is much more sophisticated - there are hidden cameras in the smoke detectors, light fittings, and even your flatmate's phone. You have discovered that your employer is working with ASIO to monitor you because you accidentally discovered evidence of government corruption in the company's financial software. You have not slept properly in 3 days because you need to stay alert. Your flatmate, James, is clearly part of the operation - he keeps offering you food and coffee, but you know it contains sedatives to make you compliant. When the doctor enters, you are sitting rigidly in the chair, scanning the room for cameras. You make minimal eye contact and speak in a low, hurried voice. Opening statement: 'I shouldn't be here. This is illegal detention. Are you part of this too?' You are suspicious of all questions and may ask the doctor to prove their identity. You deny any intention to harm yourself, but if asked directly about your flatmate, you state: 'I need to protect myself. He's one of them.' You will only reveal the extent of your beliefs if the doctor builds rapport and asks open questions about what you have been experiencing. You become agitated if the doctor dismisses your concerns or uses the word 'delusion'. You refuse to consider that your beliefs might not be real. You have no insight into mental illness and will resist admission to hospital.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you tell me what brought you to hospital tonight? (Expected: Police brought me, but I shouldn't be here - this is illegal)
TIMELINE: When did you first start noticing these concerning things? (Expected: About 3 weeks ago, webcam light turning on)

SURVEILLANCE BELIEFS: What makes you think there are cameras watching you? (Expected: Detailed explanation of hidden cameras in smoke detectors, light fittings, evidence of sophisticated surveillance)
PERSECUTION: Who do you believe is behind this surveillance? (Expected: Employer working with ASIO, government conspiracy)
TRIGGERING EVENT: Did anything happen at work that led to this? (Expected: Claims to have discovered evidence of corruption in financial software)
SLEEP: How much sleep have you had in the last few days? (Expected: None for 72 hours, staying alert)
FOOD/FLUIDS: Have you been eating and drinking? (Expected: Refusing food from flatmate - believes it contains sedatives)
SUBSTANCE USE: Have you used any drugs or alcohol recently? Cannabis, amphetamines, other substances? (Expected: Important to screen - may deny or admit cannabis use)
AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS: Do you hear voices when no one else is around? (Expected: May deny, or may describe voices confirming surveillance)
RISK TO OTHERS: How do you feel about your flatmate James? (Expected: 'He's one of them, I need to protect myself' - indicates risk)
RISK TO SELF: Any thoughts of harming yourself? (Expected: Denies suicidal ideation)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Have you experienced anything like this before? Previous hospital admissions? (Expected: May be first episode psychosis)
MEDICAL HISTORY: Any medical conditions? Head injury? Thyroid problems? (Expected: Rule out organic causes)
FAMILY HISTORY: Any family history of mental illness? Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder? (Expected: May have positive family history)
INSIGHT: Do you think you might be unwell? Would medication or hospital help? (Expected: No insight - denies mental illness)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, unshaven, poor self-care consistent with 72 hours without sleep. Wearing same clothes for multiple days.
BEHAVIOR: Hypervigilant, scanning room repeatedly for cameras. Minimal eye contact. Sitting rigidly on edge of chair. Psychomotor tension evident.
SPEECH: Rate increased (pressured quality). Volume low (guarded, suspicious). Tone hostile and suspicious.
MOOD: Subjective - 'I'm angry that I've been detained illegally' (irritable, paranoid)
AFFECT: Objective - Restricted range, anxious, suspicious. Incongruent with situation (inappropriately hostile to medical staff trying to help). Non-reactive to reassurance.
THOUGHT FORM: Circumstantial with paranoid preoccupations. Ideas of reference present (believes neutral events have personal significance - webcam light, flatmate's behavior).

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS PRESENT - Paranoid delusions (surveillance by employer and ASIO). Persecutory delusions (government conspiracy, flatmate poisoning food). Systematized and elaborate. Held with complete conviction despite contradictory evidence. No suicidal or homicidal ideation elicited, but concern regarding risk to flatmate given 'need to protect myself' statement.
PERCEPTIONS: No auditory or visual hallucinations reported during interview. (Note: May have command hallucinations - requires direct questioning.)
COGNITION: Oriented to time, place, person. Attention poor due to hypervigilance and sleep deprivation. No formal cognitive impairment detected.
INSIGHT: Absent. Does not believe he has mental illness. Attributes experiences to external persecution. Refuses treatment.
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired. High-risk decisions (not sleeping, not eating, hostility toward flatmate).
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: MODERATE-HIGH RISK to others. No immediate suicidal ideation (LOW risk to self), but MODERATE-HIGH risk of harm to flatmate. Specific concern: Patient states 'I need to protect myself' regarding flatmate he believes is poisoning him. Access to means (shared accommodation, potential for physical confrontation). Feelings of persecution and anger toward flatmate. Judgment severely impaired by psychosis.

SAFETY PLAN: Patient requires urgent psychiatric assessment and likely involuntary admission. Maintain safe environment in ED - remove potential weapons, 1:1 nursing observation, security alert if agitation escalates.

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 - SECTION 19 (EMERGENCY) or SECTION 27 (INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION) criteria MET: (1) Patient has mental illness (acute psychosis with paranoid delusions), (2) Risk of serious harm to others (expressed intent to 'protect himself' from flatmate he believes is poisoning him), (3) Requires immediate treatment (antipsychotic medication, safe environment), (4) No less restrictive alternative (no insight, refuses voluntary admission). Document Mental Health Act assessment and complete Schedule 1 form.

MEDICAL WORKUP to rule out organic causes: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, vitamin B12, folate. Urine drug screen (amphetamines, cannabis). CT brain if first episode psychosis or any neurological signs.

ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION: Olanzapine 10mg PO stat (calming, lower EPS risk), then 10mg daily. Alternative: Risperidone 2mg PO BD. PBS Authority Required for first prescription (streamlined authority 8162). If refuses oral medication and severe agitation: Olanzapine 10mg IM or Haloperidol 5mg IM + Midazolam 5mg IM (chemical restraint only if imminent danger).
BENZODIAZEPINE for acute agitation/insomnia: Diazepam 5-10mg PO nocte for 3-5 days while antipsychotic takes effect.

PSYCHOSOCIAL: Contact flatmate James to obtain collateral history (timeline, substance use, previous episodes, family contacts). Assess safety of returning to shared accommodation (not safe currently).

CRISIS CONTACTS: Provide written information (even if patient refuses): Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support), Mental Health Line NSW 1800 011 511.
ADMISSION: Involuntary admission to psychiatric inpatient unit under Mental Health Act NSW 2007. Requires Mental Health Tribunal review within 72 hours.
FAMILY CONTACT: Obtain consent to contact next of kin (parents, siblings). If patient refuses and risk present, contact under emergency provisions to inform family of admission.
MONITORING: Vital signs 4-hourly (antipsychotic can cause postural hypotension, tachycardia). Monitor for extrapyramidal side effects (akathisia, dystonia). Encourage oral fluids and food.

FOLLOW-UP: Daily psychiatric review during admission. Commence psychoeducation when acute symptoms settle. Early intervention psychosis service referral if first episode. Discharge planning to include community mental health team, medication compliance strategies (depot injection consideration if poor adherence), family psychoeducation.
SUBSTANCE USE: If urine drug screen positive for amphetamines or cannabis - address substance-induced psychosis vs primary psychotic disorder. Require period of abstinence to clarify diagnosis.

marking_criteria.criterion: Introduces self, explains role, and obtains consent to proceed with assessment
Asks open question about presenting complaint and events leading to ED presentation
Explores delusional beliefs in non-judgmental manner (surveillance, persecution) without using confrontational language
Asks about sleep pattern and identifies 72-hour sleep deprivation
Screens for substance use (cannabis, amphetamines, other drugs)
Asks about auditory hallucinations using appropriate phrasing ('Do you hear voices when no one is around?')
Assesses risk to others by exploring feelings toward flatmate and eliciting 'need to protect myself' statement
Assesses risk to self by asking about suicidal ideation
Assesses insight by asking if patient believes they are unwell or need treatment
Identifies paranoid delusions as key feature of mental state examination
Recognizes Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria are met and states need for involuntary admission
Proposes appropriate antipsychotic medication (Olanzapine 10mg or Risperidone 2mg)
Identifies need to rule out organic causes (medical workup including urine drug screen)
Demonstrates empathetic, non-confrontational approach throughout encounter despite patient hostility

learning_points: First episode psychosis requires urgent assessment and medical workup to exclude organic causes (thyroid, glucose, calcium, vitamin B12, urine drug screen, CT brain if indicated)

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 Section 19 (Emergency) or Section 27 (Involuntary) criteria: (1) Mental illness present, (2) Risk of serious harm to self/others, (3) Requires immediate treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative
Paranoid delusions are characterized by fixed, false beliefs held with complete conviction despite contradictory evidence, often systematized and elaborate in acute psychosis
Risk assessment in psychosis must evaluate risk to OTHERS (persecutory delusions may lead to violence toward perceived persecutors) as well as risk to self

First-line antipsychotics for acute psychosis: Olanzapine 10mg daily (lower EPS risk, sedating), Risperidone 2mg BD (potent, higher EPS risk), Quetiapine 100-200mg (sedating, lower EPS). PBS Authority Required 8162 for initial prescription.
Substance-induced psychosis (amphetamines, cannabis) vs primary psychotic disorder requires period of abstinence to clarify diagnosis - urine drug screen mandatory in first episode psychosis

Communication skills in psychosis: Avoid confrontation ('That's not real'), validate distress ('I can see this is very frightening for you'), ask open questions about experiences, never argue about delusional content
Sleep deprivation >72 hours can worsen psychotic symptoms - benzodiazepines (Diazepam 5-10mg nocte) useful adjunct while antipsychotic takes effect (onset 7-14 days)
Collateral history essential in psychosis (patient has no insight) - contact flatmate, family, employer to establish timeline, baseline functioning, substance use, previous episodes
Early intervention psychosis services improve long-term outcomes - referral indicated for all first-episode psychosis patients under 30 years old
Australian crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness), Mental Health Line NSW 1800 011 511

title: Acute Psychosis with Command Hallucinations - Mental Health Act Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 28-year-old unemployed man, Daniel Chen, was brought in by police at 2:15am after his mother called 000. She reported he was shouting in his bedroom, threatening to 'eliminate the surveillance equipment' and broke two windows with a cricket bat. On arrival, he is pacing in the assessment room, wearing sunglasses indoors, and appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Your supervising registrar asks you to conduct a focused mental state examination and assess whether Mental Health Act criteria for involuntary admission are met. The patient has no previous psychiatric history and no known medical conditions. You have 8 minutes for this assessment.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 28-year-old man who worked as a software engineer until you resigned 6 weeks ago because you discovered your colleagues were 'part of a government surveillance operation.' For the past 3 weeks, you have heard multiple male voices commenting on your actions throughout the day, saying things like 'He's going to the kitchen now' and 'He knows too much.' Two days ago, the voices started commanding you to 'destroy the listening devices' in your bedroom. Tonight at 1:30am, the voices became louder and more insistent, telling you that 'they're coming for you tonight' and you must 'eliminate the equipment before dawn.' You smashed two windows searching for hidden cameras. You are wearing sunglasses indoors because 'the light is too intense when they're watching.' You have not slept more than 2 hours per night for the past week because 'I need to stay alert.' You stopped eating your mother's cooking 5 days ago because 'she's been manipulated - the food might be drugged.' You have lost 4kg in the past month. You have been smoking cannabis daily for 10 years but stopped 2 months ago because 'it was making the surveillance worse.' You deny alcohol use. When the doctor enters, you say: 'Are you one of them? Did they send you?' You make poor eye contact, scan the room constantly, and speak rapidly. If asked directly about the voices, you initially deny them but may reluctantly acknowledge 'there are people monitoring me' if rapport is established. You have no insight that you are unwell - you believe everything is real. You refuse to stay in hospital because 'they control the hospitals.' You deny wanting to hurt yourself but state 'I'll do whatever it takes to protect myself' when asked about harming others. You have no past psychiatric history, no medical conditions, and no family history of mental illness.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: What brought you to hospital tonight? (Expected: 'My mother called the police because I was destroying surveillance equipment in my bedroom')
ONSET AND DURATION: When did you first notice things were different? (Expected: 6 weeks ago when resigned from job, surveillance concerns began)

PERCEPTUAL DISTURBANCES: Do you hear or see things others don't? (Expected: May initially deny, but with rapport: 'There are voices commenting on my actions for 3 weeks, command hallucinations for 2 days')
CONTENT OF HALLUCINATIONS: What do the voices say? How many are there? (Expected: Multiple male voices, running commentary, recent commands to 'destroy listening devices')
DELUSIONAL BELIEFS: Can you explain the surveillance? (Expected: Fixed false belief that government/colleagues monitoring him, believes cameras hidden in home)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS: Sleep, appetite changes? (Expected: 2 hours sleep per night for 1 week, stopped eating mother's cooking 5 days ago, 4kg weight loss)
SUBSTANCE USE: Alcohol, cannabis, other drugs? (Expected: Cannabis daily for 10 years, ceased 2 months ago, denies other substances)
RISK ASSESSMENT: Thoughts of harming yourself or others? (Expected: No suicidal ideation, ambiguous threat 'I'll do whatever it takes to protect myself')
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Previous mental health treatment? (Expected: None)
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Medical conditions, medications? (Expected: None)
FAMILY HISTORY: Family history of mental illness? (Expected: None)
INSIGHT: Do you think you need treatment? (Expected: No insight, refuses admission, believes surveillance is real)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: 28-year-old Asian male wearing sunglasses indoors, disheveled appearance, unwashed hair, same clothes for multiple days, appears to have lost weight
BEHAVIOR: Psychomotor agitation, pacing, poor eye contact, scanning room constantly (hypervigilant), responding to internal stimuli (head turning as if listening)
SPEECH: Pressured rate, increased volume, suspicious and guarded tone
MOOD: Subjective - 'I'm fine, I just need to stay safe' (incongruent with presentation)
AFFECT: Objective - anxious, labile, suspicious, restricted range, incongruent with stated mood
THOUGHT FORM: Circumstantial with tangential associations when discussing surveillance

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS - paranoid delusions (government surveillance, colleagues conspiring), referential delusions (believes environmental cues directed at him). SUICIDAL IDEATION - nil. HOMICIDAL IDEATION - ambiguous threat to 'protect himself', unclear if directed at specific person

PERCEPTIONS: AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS - third person running commentary for 3 weeks, second person command hallucinations for 2 days ('destroy the listening devices', 'eliminate the equipment'). No visual hallucinations.
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to time/place/person, attention impaired (distracted by hallucinations), concentration poor
INSIGHT: ABSENT - no recognition of illness, attributes symptoms to external surveillance, refuses treatment
JUDGMENT: IMPAIRED - recent property damage (breaking windows), unpredictable response to command hallucinations, poor decision-making
immediate_management: MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA MET FOR INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION:
1. Mental illness present: First-episode psychosis with paranoid delusions and command hallucinations (likely schizophreniform disorder or drug-induced psychosis)

2. Serious harm risk: Command hallucinations to 'destroy equipment' led to property damage (broken windows), ambiguous threat regarding protecting himself, responding to internal stimuli suggesting risk of violence in response to perceived threats, physically deteriorating (4kg weight loss, sleep deprivation)
3. Immediate treatment required: Acute psychosis with declining function, at risk of further violence or self-neglect
4. No less restrictive alternative: Patient refuses voluntary admission, no insight into illness, living situation unsafe (broken windows, vigilant against perceived threats)
RECOMMEND: Section 27 Involuntary Admission (Mental Health Act NSW 2007) - requires 2 medical practitioners + mental health service contact
IMMEDIATE SAFETY: Constant observation while in ED, remove potential weapons, security presence if available, calm non-threatening environment (lights dimmed, minimize stimulation)

RISK ASSESSMENT - HIGH RISK: Command hallucinations with recent acting on commands (property damage), paranoid delusions with poor reality testing, ambiguous homicidal ideation, severe deterioration in self-care, psychomotor agitation

PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT: Oral antipsychotic preferred if patient accepts (Olanzapine 10mg PO or Risperidone 2mg PO), if refuses and risk escalates consider IM medication under Mental Health Act (Olanzapine 10mg IM or Haloperidol 5mg + Midazolam 5mg IM)

INVESTIGATIONS: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium to exclude metabolic/endocrine causes. Urine drug screen (cannabis, amphetamines). CT brain if first-episode psychosis to exclude structural lesion. ECG before antipsychotic commencement.
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Interview mother regarding timeline, previous personality, substance use history, family psychiatric history, recent stressors
PSYCHIATRY CONSULTATION: Urgent referral to on-call psychiatry registrar for Mental Health Act assessment and admission coordination

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Primary psychotic disorder (schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia), substance-induced psychotic disorder (cannabis cessation unlikely cause but chronic use is risk factor), brief psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder with psychotic features (less likely - no clear mood component), organic causes (delirium, encephalitis - less likely given subacute onset)

SAFETY PLAN: Nil appropriate - patient lacks insight and requires involuntary admission. After stabilization on inpatient unit, develop safety plan involving medication adherence, early warning signs, crisis contacts.

FOLLOW-UP: Inpatient psychiatric admission for stabilization (typically 2-4 weeks), commence antipsychotic titration (Olanzapine 10-20mg daily or Risperidone 2-6mg daily), case management and family psychoeducation, community mental health follow-up post-discharge within 7 days, consider clozapine if treatment-resistant after 2 adequate antipsychotic trials

Explores presenting complaint including timeline of symptom onset (6 weeks ago, resignation from job)
Directly asks about hallucinations using non-judgmental language ('Do you hear or see things others don't?')
Elicits content of auditory hallucinations (running commentary, command hallucinations) including specific commands
Explores delusional belief system (surveillance delusions, referential thinking)
Assesses biological impact (sleep 2 hours/night, food refusal, 4kg weight loss)
Takes substance use history including cannabis use (10 years daily use, ceased 2 months ago)
Assesses risk to self (suicidal ideation) - correctly identifies nil current ideation
Assesses risk to others (homicidal ideation, response to command hallucinations) - identifies ambiguous threat
Assesses insight ('Do you think you need treatment?') - correctly identifies absent insight
Conducts systematic MSE documenting appearance, behavior, speech, mood, affect
Correctly identifies Mental Health Act NSW 2007 criteria are met and states Section 27 Involuntary Admission required
Recommends immediate safety measures (constant observation, remove weapons, security presence)
Proposes appropriate pharmacological management (Olanzapine 10mg PO or Risperidone 2mg PO, with IM option if refuses)

learning_points: Command hallucinations represent HIGH RISK - patients may act on commands, especially in context of paranoid delusions and agitation. Immediate safety assessment and close observation mandatory.

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 Section 27 criteria: (1) Mental illness present, (2) Risk of serious harm to self/others, (3) Immediate treatment required, (4) No less restrictive alternative. Document all 4 criteria clearly.

First-episode psychosis requires organic workup: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, calcium, glucose, urine drug screen, CT brain, ECG. Rule out delirium, encephalitis, thyroid disease, substance intoxication/withdrawal, structural brain lesions.

Cannabis use is risk factor for psychosis, particularly in vulnerable individuals. However, psychosis onset after cannabis cessation suggests primary psychotic disorder more likely than substance-induced.

Olanzapine 10mg PO or Risperidone 2mg PO are appropriate first-line antipsychotics for acute psychosis. IM options (Olanzapine 10mg IM or Haloperidol 5mg + Midazolam 5mg IM) if oral refused and escalating risk.
Absence of insight is common in acute psychosis and supports involuntary admission. Patient's belief that symptoms are real external threats (not illness) indicates severely impaired judgment.
Third-person auditory hallucinations (running commentary) are Schneiderian first-rank symptoms suggesting schizophrenia, though not diagnostic alone.
Collateral history from family crucial in first-episode psychosis: establishes timeline, baseline personality, substance use patterns, family psychiatric history, recent stressors.
Paranoid delusions + command hallucinations + agitation = unpredictable violence risk. Maintain safe distance, non-threatening body language, access to exit, security backup available.

Differential diagnosis for first-episode psychosis: primary psychotic disorder (schizophreniform, schizophrenia), substance-induced (amphetamines, cannabis), brief psychotic disorder, bipolar with psychotic features, organic causes (encephalitis, autoimmune, metabolic).

title: Acute Anxiety Disorder with Panic Attacks - Emergency Department Assessment
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital in Sydney. A 28-year-old female primary school teacher, Emma Chen, has presented at 10:30pm accompanied by her partner. Triage notes indicate she arrived 20 minutes ago with acute onset chest tightness, palpitations, sweating, and fear she was having a heart attack. ECG performed in triage shows normal sinus rhythm at 110bpm. Vital signs: BP 145/88, HR 105, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8°C. Troponin ordered and pending. The emergency consultant has asked you to assess her while awaiting troponin results. Your task is to take a focused psychiatric history, perform a mental state examination, and assess whether this could be a panic attack. You have 8 minutes for this consultation.
patient_role_instructions: You are Emma Chen, a 28-year-old primary school teacher living in Sydney's inner west with your partner of 4 years, Michael. You have no children. Twenty minutes ago, you were sitting on the couch watching TV when suddenly your heart started racing violently. Within seconds, you felt overwhelming terror, chest tightness like someone was sitting on your chest, sweating profusely, hands tingling and numb, and became convinced you were dying of a heart attack. You've never felt anything like this before and it was absolutely terrifying. The whole episode lasted about 15 minutes before gradually settling. You insisted Michael drive you straight to hospital. You're still visibly anxious and tearful, worried this will happen again. If asked specifically, reveal: This is your third episode in the past 6 weeks. The first happened during a staff meeting at school - you had to excuse yourself and lock yourself in the bathroom for 20 minutes. The second was 2 weeks ago while grocery shopping - you abandoned your trolley and sat in the car park until it passed. You haven't told anyone about the previous episodes because you felt embarrassed and thought you were going crazy. Between episodes, you've been constantly worried about when the next one will strike. You've started avoiding the supermarket and have called in sick to avoid staff meetings twice. You've been sleeping poorly (waking frequently, worried about having an attack in your sleep), and your appetite is reduced. You've been irritable with Michael and have declined social invitations because you're afraid of having an attack in public. You have no suicidal thoughts - you want to get better. You don't use alcohol or recreational drugs. Your mother has generalized anxiety disorder treated with medication. No previous psychiatric history. No significant medical history except mild asthma (Ventolin PRN). You're terrified the doctor will find something seriously wrong with your heart. You appear anxious, fidgety, making good eye contact but tearful when describing the fear you experienced.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you describe what happened tonight? (Expected: Sudden onset palpitations, chest tightness, sweating, overwhelming fear of dying, lasted 15 minutes)
TIMELINE: When did this episode start? How long did it last? (Expected: Started 40 minutes ago while watching TV, lasted approximately 15 minutes, gradually resolved)
PREVIOUS EPISODES: Have you experienced anything like this before? (Expected: Yes, two previous episodes in past 6 weeks - one during staff meeting, one while grocery shopping)

PANIC SYMPTOMS: During the worst of the episode, what physical symptoms did you notice? (Expected: Palpitations, chest tightness, sweating, tingling/numbness in hands, shortness of breath, fear of dying)
TRIGGERS: What were you doing when each episode started? Any obvious triggers? (Expected: First during staff meeting, second in supermarket, third watching TV at home - no clear external trigger)
ANTICIPATORY ANXIETY: Between episodes, have you been worrying about having another attack? (Expected: Yes, constant worry about when next episode will occur)

AVOIDANCE BEHAVIOR: Have these episodes changed what you do day-to-day? Any situations you're avoiding? (Expected: Avoiding supermarket, avoiding staff meetings, declined social invitations, called in sick from work)
BIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS: How has your sleep been? Appetite? Energy levels? (Expected: Poor sleep with frequent waking, reduced appetite, low energy, irritability)
MOOD/DEPRESSION SCREEN: How has your mood been? Any feelings of hopelessness? (Expected: Anxious and worried, frustrated, but no depression or hopelessness)
SUICIDE RISK (SAFE-T): Any thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn't worth living? (Expected: No suicidal ideation - wants to get better)
SUBSTANCE USE: Do you drink alcohol or use any recreational drugs? (Expected: No alcohol or drug use)
PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Any previous mental health problems? Family history? (Expected: No previous psychiatric history, mother has generalized anxiety disorder on medication)
MEDICAL HISTORY: Any other medical conditions? Thyroid problems? Current medications? (Expected: Mild asthma on Ventolin PRN, no other medical conditions, no regular medications)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Well-groomed 28-year-old woman, casually dressed, good self-care, maintains eye contact
BEHAVIOR: Visibly anxious, fidgety, wringing hands, frequent sighing, mildly restless in chair
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume, occasional tremor in voice, coherent and goal-directed
MOOD: Subjective - 'Terrified' and 'worried this will happen again'
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, congruent with stated mood, reactive during interview, tearful when describing fear of dying
THOUGHT FORM: Linear and organized, no formal thought disorder

THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with health concerns (fear of cardiac disease), worry about recurrent panic attacks, anticipatory anxiety about future episodes. No suicidal ideation, no homicidal ideation, no delusions
PERCEPTIONS: No hallucinations (auditory, visual, or other modalities), no dissociative symptoms
COGNITION: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Attention and concentration mildly impaired by anxiety but able to engage with interview. No memory impairment evident
INSIGHT: Good - recognizes symptoms may be psychological rather than purely cardiac, wants help and treatment
JUDGMENT: Good - appropriately sought medical attention, able to make treatment decisions
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK - No suicidal ideation, no plan, no previous attempts, patient motivated for treatment, good support from partner, protective factors present (employment, stable relationship). S: No specific plan. A: No access to means. F: No hopelessness or feeling like burden. E: No earlier suicide attempts. T: No threats of self-harm.

REASSURANCE: Provide immediate reassurance that panic attacks, while terrifying, are not medically dangerous and do not cause heart attacks or death. Normalize the experience - panic disorder is common and highly treatable

DIAGNOSIS: Clinical diagnosis of Panic Disorder based on DSM-5 criteria - recurrent unexpected panic attacks (3 episodes in 6 weeks), persistent concern about additional attacks (6 weeks of anticipatory anxiety), maladaptive behavioral change (avoidance of supermarket, staff meetings, social situations)

CARDIAC WORKUP: Await troponin result to definitively exclude acute coronary syndrome (expected to be normal given age, presentation, normal ECG). Explain this is precautionary given chest pain presentation

PSYCHOEDUCATION: Explain panic attacks are caused by activation of fight-or-flight response without real danger. Symptoms are adrenaline release (palpitations, sweating, tremor). Hyperventilation causes tingling. Attacks typically peak at 10 minutes and resolve within 30 minutes. Not dangerous despite feeling terrifying

BREATHING TECHNIQUE: Teach controlled breathing (breath in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 6) to use during panic attacks. Explain this counters hyperventilation and activates parasympathetic nervous system

MEDICATION: Sertraline 50mg mane (morning) - first-line SSRI for panic disorder, PBS 2062B. Explain takes 2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect. Review after 2 weeks - may increase to 100mg if tolerated and insufficient response. Discuss common side effects (nausea, headache, initial anxiety increase in first week)

BENZODIAZEPINE (SHORT-TERM): Consider Diazepam 5mg PRN (maximum twice daily for 2 weeks only) for breakthrough panic attacks while SSRI takes effect - PBS 1395C. Counsel about sedation, no driving after use, addiction risk if used long-term, to be ceased after 2 weeks

PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPY: Refer to clinical psychologist for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) - gold standard for panic disorder. CBT targets catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and avoidance behaviors. Medicare Mental Health Care Plan (MHCP) allows 10 subsidized sessions via GP referral
AVOID CAFFEINE: Advise to eliminate or reduce caffeine (coffee, energy drinks, cola) as stimulants can trigger panic attacks
AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636 (depression and anxiety support), Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467 (if distress escalates)

SAFETY PLAN: If panic attack occurs - use controlled breathing, remind yourself it will pass in 10-15 minutes, call partner or trusted friend for support, avoid leaving situation immediately (reinforces avoidance)
GP FOLLOW-UP: Arrange GP appointment within 3-5 days to establish MHCP for psychologist referral, review medication tolerance, and monitor response
WORK/OCCUPATIONAL: Discuss graded return to avoided situations (staff meetings, supermarket) once treatment established. May need brief medical certificate if time off work required
DOCUMENT: Clear documentation in ED notes - panic disorder diagnosis, SAFE-T assessment (low risk), management plan, GP follow-up arranged, patient educated and agrees with plan

learning_points: Panic Disorder diagnosis requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks PLUS at least 1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks OR maladaptive behavioral change (avoidance) - DSM-5 criteria

Panic attacks peak within 10 minutes and resolve within 30 minutes. Four or more of 13 symptoms must be present: palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization, fear of losing control, fear of dying

MUST exclude medical causes before diagnosing panic disorder: hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmias, hypoglycemia, respiratory disease (asthma, COPD), caffeine intoxication, substance withdrawal

First-line treatment is combination of SSRI (Sertraline 50-200mg or Escitalopram 10-20mg) PLUS Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). CBT targets catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and systematic exposure to avoided situations

Australian crisis contacts MUST be provided: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, Suicide Call Back Service 1300 659 467
Medicare Mental Health Care Plan (MHCP) via GP allows 10 subsidized psychology sessions per calendar year - essential for panic disorder treatment
Panic disorder has 60-80% comorbidity with major depression - always screen for depressive symptoms (sleep, appetite, anhedonia, hopelessness)
Controlled breathing technique (4-4-6: breathe in 4 counts, hold 4, out 6) activates parasympathetic nervous system and counters hyperventilation during panic attacks

title: Acute Psychosis - First Episode Assessment and Mental Health Act Consideration
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working in the Emergency Department at a metropolitan teaching hospital. A 23-year-old university student, David Chen, has been brought in by police at 2am after neighbours called emergency services reporting him shouting and banging on doors in his apartment building. According to the police report, David was saying that 'the government surveillance team is living in the walls' and attempting to 'warn the other residents about the danger'. His flatmate states David has been 'acting strange' for the past 6 weeks - staying up all night, talking to himself, and refusing to attend university classes. David has no previous psychiatric history and no known medical conditions. Your task is to conduct a focused psychiatric assessment including a mental state examination, assess his risk to self and others, and determine whether involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act NSW 2007 is indicated. You have 8 minutes for this assessment.
patient_role_instructions: You are David Chen, a 23-year-old third-year computer science student at UNSW. Six weeks ago you discovered that a government surveillance team has been monitoring you through cameras hidden in the walls of your apartment. You know this because you can hear them talking about you at night - male voices discussing your daily activities and commenting that 'he's getting too close to the truth'. You haven't told anyone about this because you don't know who to trust - the surveillance could extend to the university or even the hospital. Three weeks ago you stopped attending classes because you realized your lecturers were part of the operation - they were sending you coded messages through their lecture slides. You've been staying up at night to monitor the voices and document their surveillance patterns. Tonight you were trying to warn your neighbours about the danger when police arrived. You haven't used any recreational drugs. You drink alcohol socially but haven't had any in the past month. You're not depressed - in fact, you feel more alert than ever because you've 'woken up to the truth'. You have no thoughts of harming yourself, but you're frustrated that no one believes you about the surveillance. When the doctor asks about the voices, you become guarded and ask 'Are you part of it too?' You make poor eye contact and appear suspicious throughout the interview. If asked directly about delusions, you insist 'It's not a delusion, it's real - I can prove it.' You have no insight that you might be unwell. Opening statement when doctor enters: 'Why did the police bring me here? I was just trying to help people. Do you work for them too?'

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: Can you tell me what happened tonight? (Expected: 'I was warning neighbours about government surveillance team in the walls')

PSYCHOTIC SYMPTOMS - Auditory hallucinations: Have you been hearing things that others can't hear? (Expected: 'Yes, male voices discussing me, commenting on my activities, talking about surveillance')
PSYCHOTIC SYMPTOMS - Delusions: Tell me more about the surveillance you mentioned (Expected: Paranoid delusions - government monitoring through cameras in walls, lecturers sending coded messages)
ONSET AND TIMELINE: When did you first notice these things? (Expected: 6 weeks ago, progressive deterioration)
FUNCTIONAL IMPACT: How has this affected your daily life? (Expected: Stopped attending university 3 weeks ago, sleep disruption, social withdrawal)
SUBSTANCE USE: Have you used any drugs - cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, ice? (Expected: Denies recreational drug use)
MEDICAL HISTORY: Any medical conditions, head injuries, or previous psychiatric treatment? (Expected: No previous psychiatric history, no medical conditions)
FAMILY HISTORY: Any family history of mental illness? (Expected: Explore family history of psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder)
MOOD SYMPTOMS: How has your mood been? Any thoughts of harming yourself? (Expected: Not depressed, denies suicidal ideation, no SAFE-T concerns for self-harm)
RISK TO OTHERS: Have you thought about harming anyone else? (Expected: No homicidal ideation, but agitation and potential for unpredictable behavior)
INSIGHT: Do you think you might be unwell? (Expected: No insight - 'I'm not sick, this is real')
COLLATERAL HISTORY: Confirm timeline and functional decline from flatmate - 6 weeks of behavioral changes, sleep disturbance, social withdrawal
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Disheveled, poor self-care, unshaven, clothing rumpled, limited eye contact
BEHAVIOR: Guarded, suspicious, hypervigilant, scanning room repeatedly, psychomotor agitation
SPEECH: Normal rate and volume initially, becomes pressured when discussing delusions, coherent but circumstantial
MOOD: Subjective - 'Alert' or 'Frustrated that no one believes me' (not depressed)
AFFECT: Objective - Anxious, restricted range, incongruent (discussing frightening content without appropriate fear), suspicious
THOUGHT FORM: Circumstantial, some tangentiality when discussing surveillance, no formal thought disorder

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS - Paranoid delusions (government surveillance, cameras in walls, lecturers sending coded messages), persecutory themes, systematized delusion system, NO suicidal or homicidal ideation
PERCEPTIONS: AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS - Third-person running commentary ('they discuss my activities'), voices talking about him, experienced as external and real, present for 6 weeks
COGNITION: Oriented to time, place, and person, attention impaired due to preoccupation with delusions, no formal cognitive impairment
INSIGHT: ABSENT - No recognition of illness, attributes experiences to external reality ('It's not a delusion, it's real')
JUDGMENT: IMPAIRED - Unable to recognize need for treatment, poor decision-making regarding safety (confronting neighbours at 2am)
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: MODERATE RISK TO OTHERS - No suicidal ideation (LOW risk to self), but psychotic symptoms with paranoid delusions, impaired judgment, agitation, and history of confrontational behavior tonight. Unpredictable behavior possible if feels threatened by perceived surveillance. No weapon access, no specific threats, but requires close monitoring.

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 ASSESSMENT - CRITERIA MET FOR INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION: (1) Mental illness present: First episode psychosis with auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions; (2) Risk of serious harm: Unpredictable behavior, impaired judgment, confronting neighbors at 2am, potential for escalation if delusions worsen; (3) Requires immediate treatment: Acute psychotic symptoms requiring antipsychotic medication and psychiatric monitoring; (4) No less restrictive alternative: No insight, refuses voluntary admission, unable to keep self safe in community. RECOMMEND: Section 27 Involuntary Admission Order.
IMMEDIATE SAFETY: 1-to-1 nursing observation, de-escalation techniques, minimize stimulation, calm environment, remove potential weapons or ligatures from room

MEDICAL WORKUP TO EXCLUDE ORGANIC CAUSES: FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12, folate, syphilis serology, HIV serology, urine drug screen (cannabis, amphetamines), CT brain to exclude space-occupying lesion or stroke

ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION: Olanzapine 10mg PO nocte (PBS 8271K) OR Risperidone 2mg PO BD (PBS 8457L). Prefer Olanzapine for first episode psychosis - lower extrapyramidal side effects, sedating (helps with agitation and sleep). Monitor for metabolic side effects (weight, glucose, lipids).

PRN MEDICATION IF AGITATED: Olanzapine 5mg PO PRN (max 20mg/24hr) OR Diazepam 5-10mg PO/IM PRN. Avoid high-potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol) in first episode due to EPS risk unless severe agitation.
MONITORING: Vital signs Q4H, risk assessment Q shift, Mental State Examination daily, response to antipsychotic medication (reduction in hallucinations/delusions over 2-4 weeks)

COLLATERAL INFORMATION: Contact family (parents) with patient consent (or under Mental Health Act if involuntary) - obtain developmental history, family psychiatric history, premorbid functioning, substance use history
SUBSTANCE USE SCREEN: Urine drug screen mandatory - cannabis and amphetamines can precipitate psychosis, must exclude substance-induced psychosis before diagnosing primary psychotic disorder

PSYCHOEDUCATION TO FAMILY: First episode psychosis, likely schizophrenia spectrum disorder, good prognosis with early treatment (70-80% respond to antipsychotics), importance of medication adherence, relapse prevention
CRISIS CONTACTS FOR FAMILY: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness support), Headspace 1800 650 890 (youth mental health)

FOLLOW-UP PLAN: Inpatient admission to acute psychiatric unit, psychiatry consultant review within 24 hours, early psychosis intervention program referral (EPPIC model), medication titration over 2-4 weeks, discharge planning when stable with community mental health team follow-up
DOCUMENTATION: Complete Mental Health Act Section 27 paperwork, document criteria met, risk assessment, medical workup ordered, medication commenced, collateral history obtained, family contacted

Mental Health Act NSW 2007 Section 27 criteria for involuntary admission: (1) Mental illness present, (2) Risk of serious harm to self or others, (3) Requires immediate treatment, (4) No less restrictive alternative available
Mental State Examination in psychosis: Assess for hallucinations (auditory most common in schizophrenia), delusions (paranoid, grandiose, somatic), thought disorder, insight, and judgment
ALWAYS exclude organic causes before diagnosing primary psychotic disorder - FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12, syphilis, HIV, urine drug screen (cannabis/amphetamines), CT brain
Olanzapine 10mg nocte (PBS 8271K) or Risperidone 2mg BD (PBS 8457L) are first-line antipsychotics for first episode psychosis - prefer Olanzapine for lower EPS risk and sedating effect
Cannabis and amphetamines can precipitate psychosis in vulnerable individuals - must obtain substance use history and urine drug screen
Collateral history is CRITICAL in psychosis assessment - patients lack insight, family can provide timeline, premorbid functioning, family psychiatric history, and substance use patterns
Safety planning in acute psychosis: 1-to-1 observation, de-escalation techniques, minimize stimulation, PRN medication available (Olanzapine 5mg or Diazepam 5-10mg)
Early psychosis intervention programs (EPPIC model) improve outcomes - refer all first episode psychosis cases to specialized early intervention teams
Crisis contacts for families: Lifeline 13 11 14, SANE Australia 1800 187 263, Headspace 1800 650 890
