title: Acute Psychotic Episode - First Episode Psychosis Assessment in Emergency Department
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor working the night shift in the Emergency Department at a Sydney teaching hospital. A 23-year-old university student, Daniel Chen, has been brought in by ambulance after his flatmate called triple zero. The flatmate reports Daniel has not slept for 5 days, believes the government is monitoring him through his laptop camera, and was found destroying his phone claiming it had tracking devices implanted by intelligence agencies. Daniel was initially reluctant to come to hospital but agreed after police attended. Your task is to conduct a focused psychiatric assessment including a mental state examination and assess whether Daniel requires involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act NSW 2007. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Daniel Chen, a 23-year-old computer science student at University of Sydney. Three months ago you began noticing that people on campus were staring at you and talking about you. Six weeks ago you discovered that ASIO (Australian Security Intelligence Organisation) has been monitoring your internet activity because you are 'too intelligent' and they fear you will expose government corruption. Two weeks ago you began hearing voices through electronic devices - your laptop makes clicking sounds that form words telling you to 'be careful' and 'trust no one'. Five days ago you stopped sleeping because you need to stay vigilant. Yesterday you smashed your phone with a hammer after discovering microscopic tracking chips the government implanted in the battery. Your flatmate Michael overreacted by calling an ambulance - you tried to explain you are not sick, you have simply uncovered the truth. When the doctor enters, you are guarded and suspicious. You maintain eye contact intensely, monitoring for signs they might be part of the surveillance network. You will answer questions but frequently return to themes of government monitoring and your special ability to see patterns others miss. You deny feeling depressed or suicidal. You have never used cannabis or other drugs - you are too careful about what enters your body. Your parents emigrated from China when you were 5 years old. You have no previous psychiatric history. You have not been eating properly (government might poison the food supply) and have lost approximately 8kg over the past month. You become agitated if the doctor suggests you are unwell, stating firmly: 'I am not crazy, I am awake to the truth.' You will reveal the voice hearing only if specifically asked about unusual sensory experiences.

history_taking_structure: PRESENTING COMPLAINT: What brought you to hospital tonight? (Expected: Reluctant, states flatmate overreacted, insists he is not unwell)
TIMELINE: When did you first notice things were different? (Expected: 3 months ago, people on campus behaving strangely toward him)
BELIEFS ABOUT SURVEILLANCE: Tell me about your concerns regarding being monitored? (Expected: Detailed beliefs about ASIO surveillance, government tracking, special significance)
PERCEPTUAL DISTURBANCES: Have you noticed any unusual sounds, voices, or sensations? (Expected: Voices through electronic devices, clicking sounds forming words of warning)
SLEEP: How has your sleep been? (Expected: No sleep for 5 days, states he must remain vigilant)
APPETITE/WEIGHT: How has your eating been? Any weight changes? (Expected: Poor intake due to paranoia about food poisoning, 8kg weight loss)
MOOD: How has your mood been? (Expected: Denies depression, may state feeling 'energized' or 'awakened')
SUICIDE RISK (SAFE-T): Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life? (Expected: Denies suicidal ideation, no self-harm history)
SUBSTANCE USE: Cannabis, amphetamines, alcohol, or other substances? (Expected: Denies all substance use)
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY: Previous mental health treatment or admissions? (Expected: None, first presentation)
FAMILY HISTORY: Mental health problems in family members? (Expected: Need to explore, may be positive for psychotic disorders)
FUNCTIONAL IMPACT: University attendance, self-care, social relationships? (Expected: Stopped attending lectures 2 weeks ago, isolated from friends, self-care deteriorating)
mental_state_examination: APPEARANCE: Casually dressed, disheveled, poor hygiene, appears thin and tired, unkempt hair
BEHAVIOR: Hypervigilant, intense sustained eye contact, minimal psychomotor activity, guarded posture, scanning room for threats
SPEECH: Normal rate initially, becomes pressured when discussing surveillance themes, normal volume and tone
MOOD: Subjective - 'I am fine, just awake to reality' (denies mood disturbance)
AFFECT: Objective - Suspicious, guarded, incongruent (claims to be fine but appears distressed), restricted range, occasionally intense when discussing beliefs
THOUGHT FORM: Circumstantial when discussing persecution themes, occasional loosening of associations, overvalued ideas becoming fixed

THOUGHT CONTENT: DELUSIONS - Paranoid delusions (ASIO surveillance, government monitoring), persecutory delusions (tracking devices in phone), ideas of reference (people talking about him, campus staring), thought broadcasting possible. NO suicidal or homicidal ideation. Insight severely impaired.
PERCEPTIONS: Auditory hallucinations (voices through electronic devices, clicking sounds forming words), possible command hallucinations ('be careful', 'trust no one')
COGNITION: Alert, oriented to time/place/person, attention difficult to assess due to paranoia, concentration likely impaired by sleep deprivation
INSIGHT: Severely impaired - denies mental illness, attributes symptoms to 'awakening' and discovering truth, refuses treatment
JUDGMENT: Severely impaired - destroyed phone, stopped attending university, poor self-care, paranoid ideation affecting decision-making
immediate_management: SAFE-T RISK ASSESSMENT: LOW RISK for suicide - No suicidal ideation, no self-harm history, no depression, no hopelessness. However, HIGH RISK for harm due to psychosis (unpredictable behavior secondary to paranoid delusions and command hallucinations).

MENTAL HEALTH ACT NSW 2007 CRITERIA MET FOR INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION: (1) Mental illness present (first episode psychosis with delusions and hallucinations), (2) Risk of serious harm (deteriorating self-care, 8kg weight loss, sleep deprivation 5 days, unpredictable behavior driven by paranoia), (3) Requires immediate treatment (antipsychotic medication, structured environment), (4) No less restrictive alternative (lacks insight, refuses voluntary treatment). COMPLETE SECTION 19 (EMERGENCY) OR SECTION 27 (INVOLUNTARY ADMISSION) DOCUMENTATION.
IMMEDIATE SAFETY: One-to-one nursing observation, remove potential weapons from environment, de-escalation techniques (calm tone, non-threatening posture, adequate personal space)

INVESTIGATIONS: Urine drug screen (exclude amphetamines, cannabis despite denial), FBC (infection), UEC (electrolytes), LFT (baseline before medication), TFT (exclude thyroid pathology), Vitamin B12/folate, syphilis serology, HIV serology (organic causes of psychosis). CT brain if first episode psychosis to exclude structural pathology.

MEDICATION - FIRST EPISODE PSYCHOSIS: Olanzapine 5mg PO nocte (low dose, titrate slowly in antipsychotic-naive patient), PBS 8254K. Alternative: Risperidone 1mg PO BD, PBS 8662L. AVOID high-potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol) as first-line due to extrapyramidal side effects in first episode.
PRN MEDICATION IF ACUTELY AGITATED: Olanzapine 5mg PO or Diazepam 5-10mg PO. Avoid IM if possible to maintain therapeutic alliance.
PSYCHOEDUCATION (when appropriate, not during acute phase): Explain first episode psychosis, medication rationale, prognosis (70% respond to first antipsychotic trial), importance of adherence

REFERRAL TO EARLY PSYCHOSIS INTERVENTION SERVICE: EPPIC model (Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre) - specialized multidisciplinary service for first episode psychosis ages 15-25 years, provides case management, family therapy, vocational support
CONTACT FAMILY: Obtain collateral history from parents (with patient consent or under Mental Health Act provisions), assess family history of psychotic disorders, provide family psychoeducation
SUBSTANCE USE COUNSELING: Even though denied, educate about cannabis risks (doubles relapse risk in schizophrenia spectrum disorders)
AUSTRALIAN CRISIS CONTACTS: Lifeline 13 11 14 (24/7 crisis support), SANE Australia 1800 187 263 (mental illness information and support), Beyond Blue 1300 224 636

ADMISSION PLAN: Admit to psychiatric inpatient unit under Mental Health Act involuntary status, initiate low-dose antipsychotic, monitor for adverse effects (metabolic syndrome, extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation), nutritional rehabilitation, sleep hygiene

FOLLOW-UP: Psychiatry registrar review within 24 hours, tribunal hearing within 72 hours (statutory requirement for involuntary admissions), discharge planning through early psychosis service with outpatient follow-up within 7 days of discharge

patient_role_instructions: You are Margaret Chen, 67-year-old retired primary school teacher. Your husband died 8 months ago from cancer and you've been very depressed since. You've been on antidepressants for 6 months but still feel hopeless most days. You saw a charity advertisement on TV about helping orphaned children and felt this was your calling - you want to sell your $800,000 house and donate everything to them. You believe this will give your life meaning again. You understand your daughter thinks you're not thinking clearly, but you feel this is the right thing to do. You have fleeting thoughts that life isn't worth living without your husband, but deny any suicide plan. You've lost 8kg, sleep poorly, and have difficulty concentrating. You sometimes think you hear your husband calling your name. You're cooperative but tearful during the interview.
examiner_instructions: Assess the candidate's ability to conduct a comprehensive capacity assessment while simultaneously evaluating suicide risk. Look for systematic evaluation of the four elements of capacity (understanding, appreciation, reasoning, choice), proper application of SAFE-T protocol, and appropriate risk stratification. The candidate should demonstrate understanding of the interaction between depression and decision-making capacity, and provide clear recommendations about the patient's ability to make this major financial decision.

title: Mental Health Act Assessment - Acute Psychotic Episode with Violence Risk
candidate_instructions: You are the emergency department registrar. A 28-year-old male tradesman, Marcus, has been brought in by police under Section 20 of the Mental Health Act after threatening his neighbour with a hammer, believing they are spying on him through cameras. He is agitated, suspicious, and refusing voluntary treatment. The nursing staff are concerned about his escalating behaviour. Conduct a risk assessment and determine if involuntary treatment criteria are met under the Mental Health Act. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Marcus, a 28-year-old electrician. For the past 3 weeks, you have become increasingly convinced that your neighbour is part of a surveillance network monitoring you through hidden cameras. Today, you confronted them with a hammer to 'disable their equipment'. You don't believe you're unwell - everyone else is blind to the truth. You're angry about being brought here against your will. You hear occasional whispers confirming the surveillance but won't admit this unless directly asked. You have no insight into your condition and believe the doctors are part of the conspiracy. You want to leave immediately to 'protect yourself' from further monitoring. You've been sleeping poorly for weeks and haven't eaten properly in days. You've never been in hospital before and don't take any medications.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's systematic approach to Mental Health Act assessment. Look for: comprehensive risk assessment using SAFE-T protocol, assessment of insight and capacity, evaluation of involuntary treatment criteria (mental illness causing serious risk to health/safety), appropriate crisis intervention, and clear documentation of findings. The candidate should demonstrate understanding of legal frameworks while maintaining therapeutic rapport with an agitated, paranoid patient. Note their ability to balance patient autonomy with duty of care.

sample_answer.history_summary: 28-year-old electrician with 3-week history of progressive paranoid delusions regarding neighbour surveillance. No previous psychiatric history. Today escalated to threatening behaviour with hammer. Sleep disturbance, poor oral intake, deteriorating self-care. No substance use reported. Lives alone, works irregularly due to paranoia.

Affect: Restricted, congruent with paranoid content. Thought form: Goal-directed but circumstantial. Thought content: Fixed paranoid delusions about surveillance, no suicidal ideation expressed. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (whispers). Cognition: Alert, oriented, concentration impaired. Insight: Nil. Judgement: Impaired.
sample_answer.diagnosis: Brief Psychotic Disorder (ICD-11: 6A23) or Delusional Disorder (ICD-11: 6A22)

safe_t_assessment.specific_plan: Denies suicidal ideation, but impaired insight limits reliability of assessment
safe_t_assessment.access_to_means: Access to tools/weapons through trade occupation
safe_t_assessment.feelings_hopelessness: Not explicitly expressed, focused on external threats
safe_t_assessment.threat_level: Medium risk - psychosis impairs judgement, paranoid fears may lead to impulsive actions

management.immediate: Involuntary admission under Mental Health Act, secure environment, 1:1 nursing observation, remove potential weapons, contact emergency contact
management.medications: Olanzapine 10mg PO stat then 5mg BD (PBS 8822K) or Haloperidol 5mg IM if refuses oral (PBS 1923H)
management.therapy: Defer formal therapy until acute psychosis resolves, supportive counselling when appropriate
management.follow_up: Daily psychiatrist review during admission, community mental health team involvement pre-discharge
management.crisis_contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, NSW Mental Health Line 1800 011 511

Violence risk factors in psychosis: paranoid delusions with specific targets, command hallucinations, previous violence
Maintain therapeutic relationship even during involuntary assessment - avoid confronting delusions directly
Document clearly for legal purposes - specific behaviours and statements supporting criteria
Consider capacity assessment separate from risk - psychosis often impairs treatment decision-making capacity
Early antipsychotic intervention reduces duration of untreated psychosis and improves outcomes

title: Discharge Planning for a Patient with Suicidal Ideation Following Deliberate Self-Harm
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. Sarah Chen, a 28-year-old marketing coordinator, was brought to ED 6 hours ago following an overdose of 20 paracetamol tablets. She has been medically cleared by the medical team and is now requesting discharge. Your task is to conduct a risk assessment using the SAFE-T protocol and develop an appropriate discharge plan. You have 8 minutes to complete your assessment and discuss your management plan with the examiner.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Chen, a 28-year-old marketing coordinator who took 20 paracetamol tablets 8 hours ago after discovering your partner of 3 years was having an affair. You immediately regretted it and called an ambulance. You feel embarrassed and want to go home now that you're medically stable. You live alone but have supportive parents who live 20 minutes away. You have no previous suicide attempts but have been feeling increasingly depressed over the past 3 months with work stress and relationship problems. You stopped taking your antidepressants (sertraline) 6 weeks ago because you thought you were better. You have access to a large medicine cabinet at home with various medications. You feel hopeless about your relationship but acknowledge you don't actually want to die and are scared by what happened. You're willing to engage with help if offered appropriately.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's systematic approach to suicide risk assessment using SAFE-T protocol. Note whether they gather appropriate history, conduct mental state examination, assess immediate safety concerns, and develop a comprehensive discharge plan. Pay attention to their communication skills, empathy, and ability to engage the patient in safety planning. Assess whether they appropriately consider Mental Health Act criteria and involve appropriate supports. The candidate should demonstrate understanding of discharge planning principles and follow-up arrangements.

marking_criteria.description: Assesses specific plan, access to means, hopelessness, earlier attempts, threat level

marking_criteria.description: Recognises relationship breakdown, medication cessation as risks; family support, regret as protective

marking_criteria.criterion: Develops appropriate safety plan

sample_answer.history_summary: 28-year-old marketing coordinator with 3-month history of low mood, work stress, and relationship difficulties. Impulsive overdose of 20 paracetamol tablets following discovery of partner's infidelity. Immediate remorse and self-initiated emergency contact. Ceased sertraline 6 weeks prior due to perceived improvement. No previous deliberate self-harm or suicide attempts. Supportive family relationships but currently socially isolated. Chronic work-related stress with recent performance concerns.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: casually dressed, appears stated age, mild tremor. Behaviour: cooperative, maintains eye contact, some psychomotor retardation. Speech: normal rate and volume, reduced spontaneity. Mood: 'devastated and scared'. Affect: depressed, anxious, restricted range. Thought: no formal thought disorder, preoccupied with relationship breakdown, denies current suicidal ideation but acknowledges transient death wishes. Perception: no hallucinations. Cognition: alert, oriented, concentration impaired by emotional distress, insight developing.
sample_answer.diagnosis: Major Depressive Episode (F32.1) triggered by relationship stressor

safe_t_assessment.specific_plan: No current plan, previous impulsive overdose without planning
safe_t_assessment.access_to_means: Large medicine cabinet at home with various medications including remaining paracetamol
safe_t_assessment.feelings_hopelessness: Moderate hopelessness about relationship but developing hope for future
safe_t_assessment.earlier_attempts: No previous suicide attempts or deliberate self-harm episodes
safe_t_assessment.threat_level: Medium risk - recent attempt, ongoing depression, but good insight and regret

management.immediate: Safety plan including removal of excess medications, family notification and involvement, crisis contact card, agreement to contact services if suicidal thoughts return
management.medications: Restart sertraline 50mg daily (PBS 2062B) with 7-day supply initially, review compliance and side effects at follow-up
management.therapy: Referral to clinical psychologist for CBT focusing on depression and relationship issues, consider couples therapy if appropriate
management.follow_up: GP appointment within 3 days for mental health care plan, psychiatry outpatient appointment within 2 weeks, case management if deterioration
management.crisis_contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, NSW Mental Health Line 1800 011 511, local ED if urgent

sample_answer.mental_health_act: Does not meet criteria for involuntary treatment - has capacity, willing to engage with voluntary treatment, acceptable risk with safety plan in place

learning_points: SAFE-T protocol provides systematic approach to suicide risk assessment: Specific plan, Access to means, Feelings of hopelessness, Earlier attempts, Threat level
Medium risk patients require careful discharge planning with robust safety nets and early follow-up arrangements
Removing access to means is crucial - involve family in securing/removing medications from home environment
Crisis contacts must be provided in written form: Lifeline 13 11 14 available 24/7 for immediate support
Restart antidepressants cautiously with small quantities initially and close monitoring for increased suicidality in first 2 weeks
Family involvement in safety planning significantly reduces risk when patient consents to disclosure
Early GP follow-up within 3 days is evidence-based practice for post-discharge suicide prevention

title: Substance Use Assessment - Alcohol Dependence with Depression
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the emergency department. Michael, a 35-year-old construction worker, has been brought in by his partner Sarah after she found him intoxicated and talking about 'ending it all'. He has been drinking heavily for the past 6 months following a workplace injury. Sarah is very concerned about his mental state and drinking. Take a focused history including substance use assessment, perform a mental state examination, assess suicide risk using SAFE-T protocol, and formulate a management plan.
patient_role_instructions: You are Michael Thompson, a 35-year-old construction worker. Six months ago, you injured your back at work and have been unable to return to full duties. You've been drinking 15-20 standard drinks daily for the past 4 months - starting with beer in the morning to 'steady your nerves' and continuing throughout the day. Tonight you drank a full bottle of vodka and told Sarah you 'can't go on like this anymore' and that 'everyone would be better off without me'. You feel hopeless about your future, guilty about being a burden, and have been having thoughts about suicide for the past 3 weeks. You haven't made a specific plan but have thought about 'taking all your pain pills at once'. You have a history of depression 5 years ago after your father died, treated with sertraline by your GP. You stopped taking it after 6 months when you felt better. You're irritable, not sleeping well (waking at 3am daily), have lost 8kg, and feel worthless. You love Sarah and your 8-year-old daughter Emma, which is the only thing stopping you from acting on suicidal thoughts. You're embarrassed about your drinking and worried about losing your job permanently.
examiner_instructions: Assess the candidate's ability to: 1) Take a comprehensive substance use history including quantity, frequency, pattern, and consequences of alcohol use 2) Screen for alcohol withdrawal symptoms and complications 3) Assess for co-morbid mental health conditions particularly depression 4) Conduct thorough suicide risk assessment using SAFE-T protocol 5) Demonstrate understanding of dual diagnosis (substance use + mental health) 6) Formulate appropriate management plan including crisis intervention, detoxification considerations, and follow-up 7) Show awareness of Australian crisis resources and Mental Health Act criteria. Look for empathetic, non-judgmental approach and recognition of the complexity of substance use disorders.

marking_criteria.description: Identifies core symptoms: low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, guilt

marking_criteria.criterion: SAFE-T suicide risk assessment - all 5 components
marking_criteria.description: Specific plan, access to means, hopelessness, past attempts, threat level

marking_criteria.description: Documents disheveled appearance, depressed mood, suicidal ideation

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies dual diagnosis and complexity
marking_criteria.description: Recognizes alcohol dependence with major depression

marking_criteria.criterion: Management plan - detoxification and mental health treatment
marking_criteria.description: Considers inpatient detox, antidepressant, specialist referral

sample_answer.history_summary: Michael is a 35-year-old construction worker with 4-month history of heavy alcohol use (15-20 standard drinks daily including morning drinking) following workplace back injury. Co-morbid major depression with 3-week history of suicidal ideation. Previous depressive episode 5 years ago post-bereavement, treated with sertraline. Current symptoms include early morning wakening, 8kg weight loss, guilt, worthlessness, and hopelessness about future employment.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: disheveled, smell of alcohol, tremulous hands. Behaviour: cooperative but agitated. Speech: slightly slurred, normal rate. Mood: 'terrible, hopeless' with congruent depressed affect. Thought form: linear, goal-directed. Thought content: suicidal ideation with passive thoughts of overdose, no specific plan currently. Perceptions: denies hallucinations. Cognition: alert, oriented, concentration impaired. Insight: partial - recognizes drinking problem but minimizes severity.

safe_t_assessment.specific_plan: No specific plan currently, passive thoughts of 'taking all pain pills at once'

management.immediate: Admit for supervised alcohol withdrawal and suicide risk. Remove access to medications and alcohol. Crisis safety plan with partner involvement.
management.medications: Diazepam 10mg QID PRN for withdrawal (PBS 1426G). Consider sertraline 50mg daily after acute withdrawal (PBS 2062B). Thiamine 100mg daily (PBS 8467K)
management.therapy: Addiction counseling, CBT for depression, couples therapy referral. Dual diagnosis treatment program
management.follow_up: Daily medical review during admission. Addiction medicine consultation. Community mental health team referral on discharge. GP within 3 days post-discharge
management.crisis_contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, NSW Mental Health Line 1800 011 511

sample_answer.mental_health_act: Meets criteria for involuntary admission - mental illness (depression with alcohol dependence), serious risk to self (suicidal ideation with means), treatment available, least restrictive option after voluntary treatment declined

learning_points: SAFE-T protocol essential for all patients with substance use - suicide risk significantly elevated in alcohol dependence (15x general population)
Dual diagnosis common - treat both conditions simultaneously, not sequentially. Depression may be substance-induced or independent

Alcohol withdrawal can be life-threatening - assess for seizure/DT risk, consider CIWA-Ar protocol for monitoring
Family/partner involvement crucial in substance use treatment - protective factor and support for recovery

Mental Health Act criteria: mental illness + serious risk + treatment available + least restrictive option considered

title: Borderline Personality Disorder Assessment and Crisis Management
candidate_instructions: You are a junior doctor in the emergency department. Sarah, a 24-year-old university student, has been brought in by her flatmate after she cut her forearms with a razor blade following an argument with her boyfriend. She has a history of multiple presentations to ED for self-harm episodes. Take a focused psychiatric history, conduct a mental state examination, assess her current risk, and formulate a management plan. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Sarah Mitchell, a 24-year-old psychology student. You cut your forearms with a razor blade 2 hours ago after your boyfriend of 3 months said he needed 'space' following an argument where you accused him of cheating. You feel abandoned and describe intense emotional pain 'like my heart is being ripped out'. You have a pattern of intense, unstable relationships that typically last 3-6 months and end when you become 'too needy' or suspicious. You've self-harmed since age 16, usually cutting when feeling rejected or abandoned. You deny current suicidal ideation but admit to previous overdoses during relationship breakdowns. You feel empty most of the time and struggle with your sense of identity, changing career plans frequently. You can be dramatic in presentation but become defensive if you feel judged. You live with a supportive flatmate and maintain contact with your mother, though the relationship is strained.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's ability to: 1) Establish rapport with a distressed patient with personality disorder traits, 2) Conduct systematic risk assessment using SAFE-T framework, 3) Identify features of borderline personality disorder without being judgmental, 4) Formulate appropriate crisis management plan including safety planning, 5) Demonstrate understanding of therapeutic boundaries and splitting behaviors. Look for evidence-based approach to personality disorder assessment and management. Note if candidate addresses both immediate safety and longer-term treatment planning.

Pattern of unstable relationships lasting 3-6 months, chronic feelings of emptiness, identity disturbance with frequent career changes. Lives with supportive flatmate, strained relationship with mother.
sample_answer.mse_findings: Appearance: Casually dressed, visible fresh cuts on forearms with bandages. Behaviour: Cooperative but occasionally dramatic, some psychomotor agitation. Speech: Normal rate and volume, occasionally pressured when discussing boyfriend. Mood: 'Devastated and empty'. Affect: Dysthymic with lability, appropriate to content. Thought process: Coherent and goal-directed. Thought content: Preoccupation with abandonment themes, no current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms. Perception: No hallucinations reported. Cognition: Alert, oriented, memory intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes pattern but limited understanding of personality factors. Judgment: Currently impaired by emotional state.

title: Cognitive Decline in an 82-year-old Woman: Dementia versus Depression
candidate_instructions: Mrs Helen Thompson, an 82-year-old retired teacher, has been brought to the emergency department by her daughter who is concerned about her mother's deteriorating memory and mood over the past 6 months. The daughter reports that Mrs Thompson has become increasingly forgetful, withdrawn, and has expressed feeling 'worthless' and 'a burden'. She has stopped participating in her book club and gardening activities. Your task is to conduct a focused psychiatric assessment to differentiate between dementia and depression, assess suicide risk using the SAFE-T protocol, and formulate an appropriate management plan.
patient_role_instructions: You are Mrs Helen Thompson, an 82-year-old retired primary school teacher who taught for 40 years. You live alone in your own home in Parramatta, NSW. Over the past 6 months, you have noticed significant memory problems - forgetting appointments, misplacing items, and struggling to follow conversations. You feel deeply ashamed about these changes and believe you are 'losing your mind'. You have lost interest in reading (which you previously loved), stopped tending to your garden, and withdrawn from your weekly book club. You feel hopeless about the future and have thought 'everyone would be better off without me', but you have no specific suicide plan. You deny any access to means of self-harm. You have no history of mental illness. Sleep is poor with early morning wakening at 4am. Appetite is reduced. You appear sad and answer questions slowly, often saying 'I don't know' or 'I can't remember'. Show psychomotor retardation. Express feelings of guilt about being a 'burden' to your daughter.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's ability to differentiate between depression and dementia in an elderly patient. Key assessment areas: 1) Systematic psychiatric history taking including onset, timeline, and functional impact; 2) Mental state examination focusing on cognitive assessment and mood; 3) Comprehensive suicide risk assessment using SAFE-T protocol; 4) Recognition that this presentation could represent depression with cognitive symptoms (pseudodementia), early dementia with secondary depression, or mixed presentation; 5) Appropriate management planning including safety measures, Australian crisis resources, and follow-up arrangements. The candidate should demonstrate cultural sensitivity when discussing cognitive decline with an elderly patient and involve family appropriately in management planning.

learning_points: SAFE-T protocol: Essential for all elderly patients with mood symptoms - suicide rates highest in men >75 years in Australia
Pseudodementia: Depression can present with cognitive symptoms that may be reversible with treatment - key distinguishing features include acute onset, intact orientation

Medication considerations: Start antidepressants at half usual dose in elderly; SSRIs preferred over tricyclics due to cognitive and cardiac effects
Family involvement: Essential for collateral history and ongoing safety monitoring - daughter is key protective factor
Cognitive assessment timing: Defer formal neuropsychological testing until mood symptoms treated - depression significantly impacts cognitive performance
Cultural sensitivity: Address dignity concerns about cognitive decline; avoid patronising language; maintain patient autonomy in decision-making where possible

title: Medication Counseling for First Episode Psychosis
candidate_instructions: You are a psychiatry registrar in the outpatient clinic. Marcus Chen, a 22-year-old university student, was recently diagnosed with first episode psychosis and started on olanzapine 10mg daily two weeks ago. He has come to today's appointment with his mother expressing concerns about weight gain and metabolic effects. His mother is also worried about long-term medication use. Provide medication counseling addressing his concerns while assessing adherence and monitoring for side effects. You have 8 minutes.
patient_role_instructions: You are Marcus Chen, a 22-year-old engineering student at UNSW. Two weeks ago you were hospitalized for 5 days after experiencing paranoid delusions that your lecturers were monitoring your computer and hearing voices telling you to drop out of university. You were started on olanzapine 10mg at night. You're feeling much better now - the voices have stopped and you don't feel as paranoid. However, you've gained 3kg in two weeks and are very concerned about this. You've been reading online about diabetes and heart problems with antipsychotics. You're considering stopping the medication because you feel better and are worried about long-term effects. Your mother is with you and is also concerned about the weight gain and whether you really need medication long-term. You should express these concerns but be willing to listen to medical advice. You have no thoughts of self-harm or suicide currently.
examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's ability to: 1) Assess medication adherence and side effects systematically, 2) Provide clear education about olanzapine's benefits and risks, 3) Address patient and family concerns about weight gain and metabolic effects, 4) Discuss monitoring requirements and lifestyle modifications, 5) Assess insight and suicide risk, 6) Provide clear follow-up plan. The patient should initially express strong concerns about weight gain and desire to stop medication, but gradually become more receptive to continuing treatment with proper monitoring.
